articles.title: Canada-Ukraine 100-Year Partnership: What Does It Mean for Both Countries?
articles.body:
Last week, President Zelensky visited Canada and signed the Ukraine-Canada Declaration for a 100-Year Partnership. It is Ukraine’s second 100-year partnership framework, after the agreement signed with the UK in 2025.
Important note: for now, it exists only at the level of a declaration, and the formal agreement is expected to be signed in December 2026.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
This partnership doesn’t really come as a surprise because Canada has historically been one of Ukraine’s most reliable allies, especially in this war against Russia. Throughout years of Russia’s aggression, Canada’s support for Ukraine has remained consistent. There were no major policy swings like those in the US that directly affected the situation on the battlefield. Nor have there been major disappointments like those Ukraine experienced with some European partners that either refused to provide key weapons systems, or delayed their delivery for so long that those delays had negative consequences for Ukraine.
This can be partly explained by the fact that Canada has not been a major producer of many of the defense capabilities Ukraine urgently needed. Nevertheless, it has provided important equipment, including armored vehicles and drones. Canada has also led the way in imposing sanctions on Russia. It seized a Russian-registered Antonov aircraft grounded in Toronto and has been one of the first and strongest advocates for using frozen Russian assets to support Ukraine.
Russia Threatens EU With Court Action as Europe Advances ‘Aggressor Pays’ Model for Ukraine
The new 100-year partnership framework creates much broader opportunities for both Ukraine and Canada.
Canada now has a rapidly growing defense and security ecosystem comprising more than 585 companies nationwide.
For decades, its defense industry has been deeply integrated with the United States. Canadian companies often found it easier to access the US defense market than to sell to their own government. But during these two years of the Trump administration, Canada has changed.
I have lived in Canada since August 2024, and I have seen how dramatically Trump’s annexation threats and economic pressure have shaped the country’s political debate.
The current revitalization of Canada’s defense can only partly be explained by the threat from Russia. A much more immediate factor has been uncertainty surrounding Canada’s most important ally. Although nobody seriously (at least publicly) talks about the prospect of US military action against Canada, the realization that Canada might not be able to rely on its closest partner has been something of a cold shower.
In 2026 we’ve seen a remarkable number of new defense initiatives, institutions, investments, and reforms announced. The most important policy development was the launch of Canada’s Defence Industrial Strategy. The document places much greater emphasis on building sovereign defense capabilities and supporting domestic producers. It identifies ten “key sovereign defense capabilities” that will receive particular attention under the new approach.
At the same time, Canada is clearly trying to diversify its defense partnerships. The strategy calls for deeper cooperation with European partners, the United Kingdom, and countries in the Indo-Pacific. We also need to be realistic: Canada is highly unlikely to become completely militarily self-sufficient or independent from the United States in the foreseeable future. Nor would that be desirable. The two countries remain closely connected through NATO, NORAD, integrated supply chains, and decades of military cooperation. In the event of a major common threat, they would still have to respond together, making interoperability between their armed forces and military capabilities essential.
Interestingly, the Defence Industrial Strategy does not specifically mention Ukraine as a priority partner. Yet that has not prevented the two countries from deepening their partnership.
All types of drones across the land, air, surface, and underwater domains are now officially recognized as one of Canada’s ten key sovereign defense capabilities. Canada has also launched an unusually large number of initiatives in this area over a relatively short period. Compared with many other countries, even those facing immediate threats, Canada appears to be making a particularly significant push in the drone sector.
The list of these initiatives includes:
-  MINERVA – a Canadian Army initiative focused on accelerating the integration of larger numbers of uncrewed aerial, ground, and littoral systems into Army operations and strengthening regular engagement with industry. Advertisement
-  Uncrewed Systems Defence Innovation Secure Hub (UxS DISH) – a secure innovation hub bringing together government, industry, academia, and the military to develop, test, and commercialize uncrewed technologies.
-  Defence Drone Initiative (DDI) – a broader effort to accelerate the development, testing, adaptation, procurement, and domestic production of uncrewed and autonomous systems.
-  Defence Drone Initiative Marketplace (DDIM) – modeled on Ukraine’s Brave1 Marketplace and designed to give the Canadian Armed Forces and Coast Guard faster access to drone and counter-drone technologies.
-  RED COBALT Uncrewed Systems Accelerator – a Canadian Joint Forces Command initiative bringing together operators, government agencies, and industry to test aerial, ground, and maritime drones, as well as other emerging uncrewed capabilities, in realistic conditions.
The Canadian Armed Forces currently have only around 2,000 drones of various types in their inventory. Ottawa has now awarded contracts worth up to C$50 million, expected to expand this fleet roughly tenfold. The first procurement phase focuses on intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance drones, as well as uncrewed ground vehicles, and includes six companies.
During President Zelensky’s visit, Canada and Ukraine signed a Joint Declaration on enhanced defense and security cooperation, which the Ukrainian presidency described as the first step toward a bilateral Drone Deal expected to be finalized at the end of September.
Ukraine has already signed Drone Deals with 10 partner countries. These arrangements include mutually beneficial cooperation formats, including joint production, localization, technology transfer, financing, cyber cooperation, and access to new markets, with the precise model tailored to the partner country.
Currently, Canada and Ukraine cooperate within the Build with Ukraine framework for joint drone production. The first is a joint venture partnership between Ukrainian Airlogix and Canadian Sentinel Research & Development, announced in May, focused on producing Ukrainian reconnaissance-drone technologies in Canada. The second, announced during Zelensky’s latest visit, is a partnership between General Dynamics Mission Systems–Canada and the Ukrainian company Green Tech Harvest.
Additional partnerships are currently under negotiation, most likely including two Ukrainian companies, Ratel Robotics and Skyfall.
The Ukrainian delegation organized an event in Calgary to showcase their technologies. The Ukrainian side was represented by JK Land Vehicles LLC, Airlogix, AIDRONESUA, GreenTech Harvest LLC, UFORCE, Skyfall, and Quantropi. More than 30 Canadian companies also took part, including both current and potential partners of Ukraine’s defence industry.
From the Canadian side, according to social media posts, North Vector Dynamics, which describes itself as Canada’s only domestically owned and controlled missile company, met with President Zelensky. UAS producer Volatus Aerospace was also present at the meeting. Sentinel R&D, which has already established a joint venture with Ukrainian Airlogix, participated as well.
Setting drones aside, Canada also announced more than $2 billion in new support for Ukraine, including over $1 billion in defense assistance. Canada will allocate approximately C$350 million (around US$253 million) to procure urgently needed air-defense capabilities for Ukraine through the JUMPSTART program. JUMPSTART is a US mechanism that allows allies and partners to finance the procurement of American-made weapons for Ukraine through the Foreign Military Sales (FMS) system.
Canada is also ready to contribute technology to the pan-European FREYJA anti-ballistic missile programme and to prepare new sanctions against Russia, including measures aimed at making it more difficult for Russia to produce ballistic missiles.
President Zelensky also visited the International Test Pilots School in Canada, where Ukrainian pilots are being trained to operate F-16 and Gripen fighter jets.
Earlier, Operation UNIFIER, under which Canadian instructors have trained more than 49,000 Ukrainian military personnel, has been extended until 2029.
The 100-year partnership with Canada was received largely positively in Ukraine, although some observers were skeptical about the broad and relatively general nature of the declaration. According to the former Ukrainian Ambassador to the United States Valeriy Chaly, there has been real progress in some areas, particularly defense and security, while cooperation in others, including trade, economic relations, and visa-free travel, has largely remained stagnant. In some areas, such as space cooperation, there is little substance.
At the same time, Chaly stressed that the partnership still has room to grow. He hoped the future Agreement would be more concrete, include clear and detailed commitments, and go beyond simply restating previously agreed positions.
On the Drone Deal partnership, Ukrainian military officer and founder of the Kruk drone training centre Viktor Taran said the Canadian prime minister had described the proposed model quite openly: combining Ukraine’s battlefield experience with Canadian manufacturing capacity, software, and artificial intelligence.
At the same time, Taran cautioned that the key question is not simply how many drones will be produced, but who will own the design documentation, where localization will take place, and whether Ukraine will remain a supplier of complete solutions rather than becoming merely a source of data and combat protocols for foreign production lines.
Protection of intellectual property is an important issue for Ukrainian defense producers and has become a point of discussion in partnerships with Greece and the United States.
Canadian stakeholders also welcomed partnership with Ukraine and pointed to other areas where Canada could play a more active role in supporting Ukraine in its war of survival.
Human rights and disinformation expert Marcus Kolga wrote that “it’s good news for Canadians: we stand to benefit enormously from Ukraine’s hard-won expertise in drone technology.” At the same time, he stressed the importance of helping Ukraine fight the war now: “Ukraine needs weapons now to defend its people from Putin’s escalating nightly bombardment and campaign of terror.”
Kolga argued that Canada should press allies such as South Korea to adjust their policies and allow the immediate sale of surface-to-air missiles to Ukraine, noting that thousands of Ukrainian lives are at stake.
He also called on Canada to designate Russia a state sponsor of terrorism and begin expelling Russian intelligence operatives working under diplomatic cover. Europe has already faced suspected Russian sabotage and terror operations, while Canada has not been immune either. Incendiary devices placed on DHL aircraft in Germany were reportedly intended for flights to Canada.
In his view, supporting Ukraine means helping it defend its skies now, while also strengthening Canada’s own defenses against Russia’s expanding campaign of hybrid warfare.
According to national security expert Wesley Wark, “there is one unique capacity that Canada has been mysteriously reluctant to supply. The capacity is imagery from the latest set of radar satellites that the Government of Canada operates – called the Radarsat constellation mission (RCM)”.
Canada had authorized MDA to provide Ukraine with synthetic aperture radar satellite imagery capable of operating through cloud cover and in all weather conditions. The imagery was combined with other commercial satellite data to produce near-real-time intelligence for Ukrainian authorities.
Wark notes, however, that the Canadian RADARSAT support reportedly lasted only about a year before being quietly discontinued, with no public explanation. The capability had been highly valuable for tracking Russian military movements, targeting weapons systems, and supporting Ukraine’s battlefield defense.
Speaking from my personal experience, what I admire about Canadians is their modesty and willingness to learn. Unlike some others, they are not convinced that their innovations are automatically the best or that there is nothing to improve. They understand their shortcomings, are openly critical of them, and are ready to change.
That said, it remains to be seen how many of the initiatives described above will survive and develop in the coming years, because defense is a long game. We also have to understand that for Ukrainian or European companies coming to Canada, the sense of urgency probably won’t be the same as on NATO’s Eastern Flank.
The coming months will likely bring further updates on Ukraine-Canada defense cooperation, as well as new partnerships between Canadian and European companies, which are developing quickly. Stay tuned!

articles.title: Russia adapts a training missile to lead its ballistic onslaught of Ukraine
articles.body:
Russia adapts a training missile to lead its ballistic onslaught of Ukraine
- Russia uses repurposed RM48U training missiles in large numbers to sustain its missile attacks on Ukraine without depleting more accurate Iskander missiles.
- The less precise RM48Us cause significant civilian casualties, such as the deadly August strike on a Kyiv suburban railway platform.
- Ukraine faces critical defence shortages, urgently seeking US Patriot interceptors to counter Russia's escalating ballistic missile campaign this winter.
AI generated
LONDON/KYIV – The bodies of passengers strewn across a bloodied suburban railway platform near Kyiv in August bore grim testament to the escalating air war dominating the conflict in Ukraine.
They were among eight people killed in a barrage of Russian missiles that was mainly focused on industrial facilities in the Brovary district, where the station is located, according to local officials.
The attack that hit the railway wasn’t carried out by Russia’s main Iskander strike missile, Ukrainian investigators said, but by a less accurate weapon originally designed to serve as target practice for air defence crews.
Russia’s mass deployment of these repurposed training missiles, or RM48Us, has driven its aerial onslaught to record levels in recent months, official Ukrainian data seen by Reuters shows.
RM48Us made up more than half of the 228 ballistic and hypersonic missiles fired at Ukraine in July and early August, according to the figures compiled by military analysts at the General Prosecutor’s Office.
The scale of the RM48U deployment, which hasn’t been previously reported, helps show how Russia has been able to expand its attacks over the summer without running down its stocks of Iskanders and other primary strike missiles.
Moscow has been able to keep up a daily air barrage during a critical window in which Ukraine finds itself highly exposed: It has virtually exhausted its stocks of US-made Patriot interceptors, the only weapons in its arsenal capable of downing Russian ballistic missiles.
There is little clarity on when fresh supplies might arrive, with more Patriots being funnelled to the US military and its allies in the Gulf than to Ukraine.
Russia’s defence ministry didn’t respond to questions about its use of RM48Us and other missiles in Ukraine.
Moscow has denied intentionally harming civilians, saying it only targets military infrastructure.
On Aug 5, the day of the railway deaths, the defence ministry said it struck a logistics centre in Brovary that was being used to store drone components.
Firing large numbers of RM48Us serves as a way for Russia to drain any remaining Ukrainian interceptor stocks and attack lower-value targets without using up its precision strike missiles, according to Sidharth Kaushal, a senior research fellow at RUSI, a London-based defence think-tank.
“Their use allows the Russians to husband the more capable missiles they have, the Iskanders, but also the KN-23s and the Zircons, for winter when they would want to really lean into their ballistic missile campaign,” he said.
Indeed, as the RM48U attacks surged in July, the number of Iskanders fired fell to 38 from more than 100 the previous month, the Ukrainian data showed.
The war in Ukraine has entered yet a new phase.
With battle lines on the ground locked across a ferocious “kill zone”, both sides have launched intensifying air campaigns.
Russia has fired hundreds of ballistic missiles over the summer and is widely expected to pound critical infrastructure including heating and power sites this winter.
Ukraine, which has a far smaller arsenal of missiles, has unleashed hundreds of long-range drone attacks on Russian refineries, ships and ports.
July saw the deaths of at least 437 civilians in Ukraine, the largest toll recorded in a single month since the early months of the invasion, according to the United Nations, which pointed to missile and drone strikes as a key factor.
Russian civilian casualties, while far lower than in Ukraine, are also at record highs.
The Conflict Intelligence Team, an independent open-source investigation group, said 327 civilians were killed in Russia in the first seven months of 2026, compared with 145 in the same period in 2025.
Ballistic trajectory, high speeds
The RM48U – RM for “raketa mishen” or “missile target” – flies on a ballistic trajectory at high speeds, Ukraine’s prosecutor’s office and the country’s GUR military intelligence agency told Reuters.
But it is less powerful and accurate than the Iskander, Russia’s primary short-range ballistic missile, the prosecutor’s office said.
The Ukrainian missiles data shows this summer was the first confirmed time the munitions, which are fired from Russia’s S-400 air-defence systems, have been deployed in large numbers.
The prosecutors linked the RM48U and its lower precision to several strikes that have caused high civilian casualties in the last few months, including the Brovary district railway platform.
They said their military experts found that RM48Us deviate from their intended targets by around 300m on average and that their exploding warheads can unleash metal fragments over a large area.
Forensic investigators concluded the railway strike was conducted with an RM48U after analysing the crater near the rail line beside the platform, metal fragments and damage to the platform, trees and bodies, the office said.
Reuters couldn’t independently verify the Ukrainian findings.
Volodymyr Bihun, head of Brovary’s military administration, said the rail attack happened shortly after midnight.
Russia also fired a number of missiles that hit logistics facilities in the district, he said.
Overhead imagery obtained from commercial satellite company Planet Labs showed that a warehouse complex near the Kvitnevyi railway platform had been damaged.
Two plumes of smoke could be seen rising into the air.
In July, Russia fired the largest number of ballistic and hypersonic missiles in a single month since its 2022 full-scale invasion, according to the official Ukrainian data, which only includes strikes confirmed by on-the-ground analysis.
Of those 158 strikes, 87 were from RM48Us, the data showed.
The pace of the aerial assault has only intensified; there were 70 Russian ballistic and hypersonic strikes in the first eight days of August, the Ukrainian data showed, with 36 of them from RM48Us.
In August, the Ukrainian air force stopped publishing regular readouts of the number of missiles fired and shot down during enemy attacks.
It said the decision was taken to prevent Russia parading reports about the poor performance of Ukrainian air defences for propaganda purposes.
Russia strives to overwhelm depleted defences
Russia has a stockpile of about 100 Iskanders available, compared with 400 RM48Us, the US-based Institute for the Study of War estimated in August.
According to Ukraine’s GUR, the country also has smaller stocks of KN-23 and KN-24 ballistic missiles and Zircon and Kinzhal hypersonic missiles, which can travel faster than five times the speed of sound.
RUSI’s Kaushal put Russia’s Iskander production at around 750 missiles a year. The solid rocket motors are a limiting factor, pushing Moscow to use the weapons judiciously, he said.
Kaushal said Russia could use the cheaper RM48U to attack lower-value and more easily struck targets such as food warehouses, which Ukrainian officials say have been systematically targeted and heavily damaged in recent weeks.
The GUR said Russia plans to more than double production of the RM48U to 480 missiles this year from 200 last year.
Ukraine has been urging the US and other Western allies to supply Patriots to replenish its defences, although production of the munition has failed to keep pace with spiking demand during the Iran war.
A senior US administration official said Washington has more than enough munitions to meet its strategic goals, adding that it must prioritise protecting its critical weapons systems and expanding production.
The US is exploring potential pathways for future defence industrial cooperation with Ukraine, although nothing has been decided, the official added.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky stressed his country’s dire need for Patriots just hours after the Aug 5 attacks, which struck Brovary and other targets in the Kyiv area and involved both Russian missiles and drones.
“Ballistic missile interceptors could have saved the lives of those killed today,” he said. REUTERS

articles.title: What Andy Burnham needs from Donald Trump at their New York meet
articles.body:
What Andy Burnham needs from Donald Trump at their New York meet
Britain’s new prime minister is set for his first meeting with the U.S. president next Tuesday. Unlike Keir Starmer, he won’t be angling for a second helping.
LONDON — When Keir Starmer had his first dinner with Donald Trump, he strained so hard to impress the U.S. president that his host offered the British team a second helping of chicken.
Andy Burnham’s face-to-face introduction next Tuesday will look very different. Instead of the two-hour Trump Tower rendezvous that Starmer enjoyed in September 2024, British officials expect their new prime minister to sit down with his U.S. counterpart on relatively neutral ground in the United Nations headquarters at the far edge of Manhattan.
Their meeting is currently penciled in for Tuesday afternoon, sandwiched between Burnham’s 15-minute address to the U.N. General Assembly on Tuesday evening and Trump’s morning speech to the same hall — which given his past form, may drown out other headlines with whatever he says there.
Advertisement
That may prove convenient for Burnham.
“There will be so much going on that it reduces the intensity and scrutiny,” said Claire Ainsley, a former aide to Starmer who is now at the center-left Progressive Policy Institute think tank.
POLITICO spoke to a dozen current and former senior U.K. officials, ministers and MPs, many of them granted anonymity to speak frankly, about Burnham’s likely handling of the visit. Almost all predicted he would opt for a middle road somewhere between Starmer’s initial charm and the more combative approach of Canadian PM Mark Carney: Get in, smile, press the case for Ukraine, and try to leave without a major upset.
Downing Street’s overwhelming priority for the New York visit has been to squeeze in an IRL meeting with Trump, with whom Burnham has now spoken to by phone twice, according to a person familiar with the preparations. It will allow the two men to engage but with far lower stakes than a one-to-one visit in Washington or London, just one of a series of leader meetings that blend into the noise of a multilateral summit.
The hope, one U.K. government official said, is to “get the Trump meeting done and dusted in a relatively safe environment.”
That was then
The shift away from Starmer’s more high-pressure encounters is driven not so much by Burnham’s laid-back style — the new PM said last month he will “say what I feel” to Trump while also trying to “find a connection” — as by a profound change in the balance of risk since 2024.
Advertisement
Burnham has less to prove. Starmer, who took office shortly before Trump’s second election victory, signed deals on tech, trade and pharmaceuticals from scratch. Warming to Trump was the “medicine required at that period,” said a U.K. diplomat.
His successor’s job is to fix the mess of unresolved threads left behind.
Burnham also has the benefit of hindsight, having watched Starmer’s efforts to praise Trump lead to embarrassment when the president lambasted the PM over the Iran conflict, oil drilling and tech taxes. Trump at one point even dissed Starmer as “no Winston Churchill.”
Donald Trump shakes hands with Britain’s former prime minister Keir Starmer at a joint press conference at the White House on February 27, 2025. | Carl Court/Pool/AFP via Getty Images
The new PM won’t “bend the knee in the way Starmer did,” predicted the same U.K. diplomat. He won’t be going to “kiss the ring,” added the first U.K. government official quoted above. “It’s completely different this time. There’s no drama about having to stay in his good books.”
Yet Trump still has two years left in office, and a smooth relationship will be vital for the U.K. leader who has tried to keep his focus on domestic issues — but is watching his promises to ease living costs be buffeted by rising defense pressures and inflation from the Iran war.
The two men will also meet at a point where Britain and its allies are turning their heads away from the U.S.
Advertisement
Two years ago “Trump was at the height of his powers,” said one Starmer Cabinet minister. “The reality is different now.”
While November’s looming midterm elections threaten to dent Trump’s authority at home, abroad his approaches to NATO and the Middle East have led European allies to find solace elsewhere. Britain and its allies are forming groups of so-called middle powers, while Carney pushes closer ties between Canada and the EU that will still be in negotiation long after Trump’s departure. And Burnham has repeatedly talked about strengthening ties with Brussels — seeing through a reset in relations that Starmer initiated.
Olivia O’Sullivan, director of the U.K. in the World Programme at the Chatham House think tank, said the country is now “testing the waters” of loosening its strategic alignment with the U.S. — even as it continues to rely on America’s security and nuclear weapons architecture. (And even as Burnham continues to let the U.S. use Britain’s air bases for limited strikes on Iran.)
Emily Thornberry, the Labour MP who chairs the House of Commons’ foreign affairs committee, said there’s a reason for that: “I think a couple of years ago, the hopes were high that Trump would help with Ukraine, we would have a proper trade deal, and so on. He hasn’t delivered on those things, so we’re getting used to the disappointment. We don’t expect as much.”
One former senior official under Starmer put it more starkly: “The world is just viewing the United States differently. He is doing enormous long-term damage to the U.S.’s relationship with all of its allies. Institutions that have stood for decades can no longer do the jobs that they used to be able to do, because America is proving to be an unreliable ally. This is hugely significant in the long term.”
No list of deliverables
Burnham, whose two calls with Trump since July have both run far over their allotted time, is at least looking to keep things friendly.
Advertisement
The new prime minister is not expected to take a big list of deliverables or policy goals into his meeting, two people familiar with the planning said.
Burnham is expected to press Trump on U.S. support for Ukraine after paying his first overseas trip there last month. British officials hope there is now a more pro-Ukraine atmosphere on Capitol Hill after the House of Representatives passed a sweeping Russia sanctions bill long championed by the late Senator Lindsay Graham.
Thornberry said the PM should urge Trump to speed up supplies of Patriot missiles to Ukraine ahead of the winter. Ukraine’s forces are “winning without the Americans, but they could actually win if the Americans did help,” she added.
Andy Burnham visits the scene of Russian strikes on Lukanivska Market in Kyiv, Ukraine on August 24, 2026. | Henry Nicholls/WPA Pool/Getty Images
Britain’s wider activities at UNGA — which Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband will also attend — could be dominated by a clash over the hardening stance of the U.K., France and Canada against Israel. The three countries issued joint sanctions against West Bank settlements earlier in September, after what one U.K. official described as a “tag team” coordination effort between Miliband, Burnham and the leaders and foreign ministers of allied countries.
The U.K. is hoping to use UNGA to work on the next steps in the humanitarian response for Gaza. British officials are privately hopeful that the U.S. response will continue to be muted; two U.K. government officials said they believed Secretary of State Marco Rubio viewed the intervention as helpful, given it applies pressure to Israel without it coming from the U.S.
Burnham faces a choice about how hard to lean into the issue of the Middle East in his own speech to UNGA. His closest No. 10 aides have kept a “tight hold” on the thinking around his remarks, said the person with knowledge of the planning quoted above.
Advertisement
Whatever he chooses, plenty of dangers lie in wait — not least Trump’s views on oil and gas in the North Sea. Industry figures believe Burnham’s government has delayed a decision on whether to drill at two fields until after an Oct. 8 special election to replace Starmer, where Labour is battling the Green Party. Trump has long been perplexed by the delay.
Burnham’s government has also delayed a key decision on defense spending until 2027, despite pressure from the U.S. to set out a clearer timetable.
And Britain is stuck over how to proceed with its deal giving up sovereignty of the Chagos Islands, a strategically crucial archipelago in the Indian Ocean, after Trump disowned the pact earlier this year. Mauritius — the beneficiary — could agitate at UNGA to unfreeze the deal.
But it’s the issue of artificial intelligence that has lately rocketed up the news agenda. Here, Burnham faces a conundrum.
On the one hand, Britain can sell a “third way” in AI development between Trump’s free-for-all and burdensome regulation in the EU, argued Emily Darlington, a Labour MP and member of the Commons Science and Technology Committee.
“There are things that [U.S. tech firms] need from us, not least some of the really advanced stuff that we’re doing around quantum, and in the future neuromorphic computing,” she said. “We’re a huge market for them. Large language models are desperate to train on British material that goes back centuries. The BBC archive, all of these sorts of things, are what they’re desperate for. There’s a bit of a fight over whether there is a British advantage to allowing them access to that material, and so there is a bit of a negotiation.”
Advertisement
Yet the U.K.’s digital services tax has drawn Trump’s repeated ire, while PoliticsHome reported this week that U.S. officials warned Britain at the London embassy against its online safety restrictions and plans to ban under-16s from social media. One minister said Burnham’s conversation “can’t be on the digital services tax or regulation like the Online Safety Act, because there’s a tangible risk Trump will go ballistic.”
‘Andy has been a lucky general’
The same minister suggested Burnham will want the sort of relationship that Tony Blair had with George Bush — respectful, even if not as equals.
It is a tall order for a president as mercurial as Trump, yet old allies of Starmer insist he paved the way for it. They point to Starmer’s decision to push back against Trump to defend Greenland’s sovereignty, to bring together a “coalition of the willing” for Ukraine and to welcome Kyiv’s leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy after Trump hectored him in the Oval Office.
Volodymyr Zelensky shakes hands with Andy Burnham ahead of their bilateral meeting at Horodetskyi House in Kyiv, Ukraine, on August 24, 2026. | Henry Nicholls/WPA Pool/Getty Images
Starmer was not being nice to Trump because he liked him, argued the Starmer Cabinet minister quoted earlier in this story, but because he had to bring him back from the brink on NATO and Ukraine.
It means Burnham has inherited an established relationship in which he has no need to lavish the president with praise. All he has to do, argue some, is avoid a barrage of abuse on Truth Social.
“Andy has been a lucky general in the calming of Trump,” argued one U.K. official who worked under Starmer. “Keir was dealing with a completely different beast.”
And yet, this person added: “It could all change in the space of two weeks.”

The new PM won’t “bend the knee in the way Starmer did,” predicted the same U.K. diplomat. He won’t be going to “kiss the ring,” added the first U.K. government official quoted above. “It’s completely different this time. There’s no drama about having to stay in his good books.”
Yet Trump still has two years left in office, and a smooth relationship will be vital for the U.K. leader who has tried to keep his focus on domestic issues — but is watching his promises to ease living costs be buffeted by rising defense pressures and inflation from the Iran war.
The two men will also meet at a point where Britain and its allies are turning their heads away from the U.S.

Two years ago “Trump was at the height of his powers,” said one Starmer Cabinet minister. “The reality is different now.”
While November’s looming midterm elections threaten to dent Trump’s authority at home, abroad his approaches to NATO and the Middle East have led European allies to find solace elsewhere. Britain and its allies are forming groups of so-called middle powers, while Carney pushes closer ties between Canada and the EU that will still be in negotiation long after Trump’s departure. And Burnham has repeatedly talked about strengthening ties with Brussels — seeing through a reset in relations that Starmer initiated.
Olivia O’Sullivan, director of the U.K. in the World Programme at the Chatham House think tank, said the country is now “testing the waters” of loosening its strategic alignment with the U.S. — even as it continues to rely on America’s security and nuclear weapons architecture. (And even as Burnham continues to let the U.S. use Britain’s air bases for limited strikes on Iran.)
Emily Thornberry, the Labour MP who chairs the House of Commons’ foreign affairs committee, said there’s a reason for that: “I think a couple of years ago, the hopes were high that Trump would help with Ukraine, we would have a proper trade deal, and so on. He hasn’t delivered on those things, so we’re getting used to the disappointment. We don’t expect as much.”
One former senior official under Starmer put it more starkly: “The world is just viewing the United States differently. He is doing enormous long-term damage to the U.S.’s relationship with all of its allies. Institutions that have stood for decades can no longer do the jobs that they used to be able to do, because America is proving to be an unreliable ally. This is hugely significant in the long term.”
No list of deliverables
Burnham, whose two calls with Trump since July have both run far over their allotted time, is at least looking to keep things friendly.
Advertisement
The new prime minister is not expected to take a big list of deliverables or policy goals into his meeting, two people familiar with the planning said.
Burnham is expected to press Trump on U.S. support for Ukraine after paying his first overseas trip there last month. British officials hope there is now a more pro-Ukraine atmosphere on Capitol Hill after the House of Representatives passed a sweeping Russia sanctions bill long championed by the late Senator Lindsay Graham.
Thornberry said the PM should urge Trump to speed up supplies of Patriot missiles to Ukraine ahead of the winter. Ukraine’s forces are “winning without the Americans, but they could actually win if the Americans did help,” she added.
Andy Burnham visits the scene of Russian strikes on Lukanivska Market in Kyiv, Ukraine on August 24, 2026. | Henry Nicholls/WPA Pool/Getty Images
Britain’s wider activities at UNGA — which Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband will also attend — could be dominated by a clash over the hardening stance of the U.K., France and Canada against Israel. The three countries issued joint sanctions against West Bank settlements earlier in September, after what one U.K. official described as a “tag team” coordination effort between Miliband, Burnham and the leaders and foreign ministers of allied countries.
The U.K. is hoping to use UNGA to work on the next steps in the humanitarian response for Gaza. British officials are privately hopeful that the U.S. response will continue to be muted; two U.K. government officials said they believed Secretary of State Marco Rubio viewed the intervention as helpful, given it applies pressure to Israel without it coming from the U.S.
Burnham faces a choice about how hard to lean into the issue of the Middle East in his own speech to UNGA. His closest No. 10 aides have kept a “tight hold” on the thinking around his remarks, said the person with knowledge of the planning quoted above.
Advertisement
Whatever he chooses, plenty of dangers lie in wait — not least Trump’s views on oil and gas in the North Sea. Industry figures believe Burnham’s government has delayed a decision on whether to drill at two fields until after an Oct. 8 special election to replace Starmer, where Labour is battling the Green Party. Trump has long been perplexed by the delay.
Burnham’s government has also delayed a key decision on defense spending until 2027, despite pressure from the U.S. to set out a clearer timetable.
And Britain is stuck over how to proceed with its deal giving up sovereignty of the Chagos Islands, a strategically crucial archipelago in the Indian Ocean, after Trump disowned the pact earlier this year. Mauritius — the beneficiary — could agitate at UNGA to unfreeze the deal.
But it’s the issue of artificial intelligence that has lately rocketed up the news agenda. Here, Burnham faces a conundrum.
On the one hand, Britain can sell a “third way” in AI development between Trump’s free-for-all and burdensome regulation in the EU, argued Emily Darlington, a Labour MP and member of the Commons Science and Technology Committee.
“There are things that [U.S. tech firms] need from us, not least some of the really advanced stuff that we’re doing around quantum, and in the future neuromorphic computing,” she said. “We’re a huge market for them. Large language models are desperate to train on British material that goes back centuries. The BBC archive, all of these sorts of things, are what they’re desperate for. There’s a bit of a fight over whether there is a British advantage to allowing them access to that material, and so there is a bit of a negotiation.”
Advertisement
Yet the U.K.’s digital services tax has drawn Trump’s repeated ire, while PoliticsHome reported this week that U.S. officials warned Britain at the London embassy against its online safety restrictions and plans to ban under-16s from social media. One minister said Burnham’s conversation “can’t be on the digital services tax or regulation like the Online Safety Act, because there’s a tangible risk Trump will go ballistic.”
‘Andy has been a lucky general’
The same minister suggested Burnham will want the sort of relationship that Tony Blair had with George Bush — respectful, even if not as equals.
It is a tall order for a president as mercurial as Trump, yet old allies of Starmer insist he paved the way for it. They point to Starmer’s decision to push back against Trump to defend Greenland’s sovereignty, to bring together a “coalition of the willing” for Ukraine and to welcome Kyiv’s leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy after Trump hectored him in the Oval Office.
Volodymyr Zelensky shakes hands with Andy Burnham ahead of their bilateral meeting at Horodetskyi House in Kyiv, Ukraine, on August 24, 2026. | Henry Nicholls/WPA Pool/Getty Images
Starmer was not being nice to Trump because he liked him, argued the Starmer Cabinet minister quoted earlier in this story, but because he had to bring him back from the brink on NATO and Ukraine.
It means Burnham has inherited an established relationship in which he has no need to lavish the president with praise. All he has to do, argue some, is avoid a barrage of abuse on Truth Social.
“Andy has been a lucky general in the calming of Trump,” argued one U.K. official who worked under Starmer. “Keir was dealing with a completely different beast.”
And yet, this person added: “It could all change in the space of two weeks.”

articles.title: How the Air Force Rigged F-15s in the Middle East with Drone-Busting Rockets in a Week
articles.body:
NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.—As the threat of Iranian-made drones rose in recent conflicts, the Air Force rushed last year to equip F-15E Strike Eagles in the Middle East with a cheap, cost-effective way of defeating them.
The Air Force Test Center was able to field the new capability—laser-guided rockets—in roughly a week, the head of the center revealed at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber Conference here Sept. 16.
It’s not the first time the Air Force has turned to this solution, known as Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System, to neutralize enemy drones and cruise missiles.
APKWS was originally designed as an air-to-ground capability, with a laser-guided kit added to Hydra-70 rockets to turn the system into a precision-guided munition.
The Air Force explored using the rockets in an air-to-air role in 2019, testing the system on the F-16 Fighting Falcon. For a few years, the experiment was considered nothing more than a proof of concept, not a real-world capability.
But as the use of Iranian drones was expanded, the program gained new urgency. The system was rushed first to F-16s in 2024 and then prioritized for F-15Es in 2025. Nine days after testing began in May of last year, the system was being equipped on Strike Eagles in the Middle East, said Brig. Gen. Mark A. Massaro.
“At the end of the first week, we had demonstrated, both in a developmental and an operational sense, that it was a usable capability, and we deployed that capability at the end of the first week,” Massaro said. “We deployed that capability into theater. We deployed some of our maintainers and some of our testers into theater to help the first week.”
The initiative is an example of the Air Force Test Center’s ability to quickly “bridge between raw concept and decisive combat-credible power,” said Massaro. He was involved in tests of APKWS in his previous role as commander of the 96th Test Wing, which conducts developmental testing of weapons for the service, and worked alongside the 53rd Wing, which conducts operational tests.
The need for the system was clear. The Air Force had relied on expensive, radar-guided AIM-120 AMRAAM missiles and infrared-guided AIM-9 Sidewinders against Tehran’s relatively cheap Shahed one-way attack drones. AMRAAMs cost roughly $1 million each, and AIM-9s cost hundreds of thousands of dollars depending on the variant. The most capable model is the AIM-9X, which costs around $500,000.
The issue came to a head with a mass Iranian drone and ballistic missile attack aimed at Israel on April 13, 2024. Tehran, which sought to flood the zone, launched a barrage of drones, ballistic missiles, and cruise missiles to confuse and overwhelm Israel’s air defenses—some 300 projectiles in all.
The U.S. had anticipated the engagement, and F-15Es from the 335th Fighter Squadron and 494th Fighter Squadron carried up to eight air-to-air missiles each as they sought to intercept the drones over Iraq along with F-16s from the 121st Fighter Squadron. The Iranian drone barrage was so heavy that many fighters quickly exhausted their air-to-air missiles, and three F-15E crews attempted—unsuccessfully—to drop laser-guided JDAM bombs on drones.
While U.S. fighters had helped to defeat the barrage, it was an expensive proposition, which led to the effort to adapt APKWS rockets, which cost tens of thousands of dollars.
Dubbed the AGR-20F FALCO, the air-to-air APWKS rockets were first used in an air-to-air configuration on F-16s in 2024.
After that, work began at Eglin Air Force Base, Fla., to equip the system on F-15Es. That occurred in mid-2025, led by 96th Wing’s Air Force Seek Eagle Office, known as AFSEO, which had earlier integrated the system into F-16s.
“This was a very integrated test approach between operational and developmental,” Massaro said. “We were overlaying … missions on exactly the same day with each other and flying them together. That second week, where we have our maintainers and some pilots in theater, our operational testers are still refining some of the tactics, and we’re able to then through phone and digital means transmit the upgraded tactics. And then, so at the end of that second week, they had updated tactics, they had equipment, they had everything ready to go, and they were able to use it very quickly after that.”
Early last year, the team initially struggled to find a way to mount the rockets on the F-15E and connect them to the aircraft so they could be fired. In May 2025, a solution was found, and the integration became the top priority for the 96th Test Wing and 53rd Wing at the base, according to Air Force officials.
Aircrew from the 40th Flight Test Squadron and the 85th and 422nd Test and Evaluation Squadrons flew test missions and conducted live-fire tests at targets over land and water.
After the initial demonstrations, the 53rd Wing and 96th Test Wing deployed to deliver equipment and provide training to Airmen to use the new weapons. While the Air Force has declined to identify the location where the system was first fielded, U.S. officials confirmed to Air & Space Forces Magazine that air-to-air APKWS was first used in the Middle East, which is part of U.S. Central Command.
In 2024, Air Forces Central began to equip its F-16s to shoot down drones in the Middle East with APKWS rockets, which were employed to defeat threats from the Houthis in Yemen.
A U.S. F-16 scored its first rocket kill of a drone that year. In October 2024, the 480th Expeditionary Fighter Squadron from Spangdahlem Air Base, Germany, deployed to the Middle East with an advance but limited heads-up that they would be equipped with APKWS for air-to-air use against drones and cruise missiles.
“The first rocket kill was announced just prior to getting there. This was all new and innovative,” Lt. Col. William “Skate” Parks, the unit’s commander, recounted in a December 2025 interview with Air & Space Forces Magazine. “We have these rockets come online. It’s a brand new thing, and we’re the ones doing it. And it’s with guys who are now spending every minute of their day when they’re not flying actual combat missions, preparing and improving on this. It showed because that success rate just started really becoming amazing with these rockets as we’re defending partners and our own forces.”
The 480th scored dozens of kills using the rockets. It also used older AIM-9M Sidewinders, claiming the first air-to-air kill by an AIM-9M in over 30 years. The unit scored 108 total aerial kills of drones and cruise missiles during the deployment. News of the success quickly trickled across the Air Force.
By April 2025, U.S. Air Forces in Europe incorporated the APKWS into its live-fire air-to-air training for F-16s, Air & Space Forces Magazine previously reported. U.S. fighters based on the continent not only routinely deploy to the Middle East, but also increasingly must be wary of Russian drone incursions into NATO airspace. The F-16 experience helped speed up the use of the APKWS as a drone-buster on the F-15E, Massaro said.
“A lot of things had already occurred,” he said. “The F-16 had already integrated APKWS and was flying with that for about a year, so we knew how the system itself worked. We had that knowledge. The F-15E is a known quantity.”
APKWS rockets come in pods of seven, and multiple rocket pods can be fitted. F-15Es can carry up to 42 APKWS rockets.
The work to put APKWS on the F-16 and F-15E would pay off in more than just cost savings for the Air Force. After the start of Operation Epic Fury on Feb. 28, Iran has fired more than 6,000 drones and 1,500 ballistic missiles, with numbers growing, U.S. officials said. What two years ago was an extreme outlier is now a routine threat.
F-16s flying in the area around the Strait of Hormuz, Persian Gulf, and Gulf of Oman, where Iran has repeatedly used drones and missiles to attack ships including U.S. Navy vessels, are flying with APKWS rocket pods to hunt down drones. U.S. Army Apache helicopters can also fire APKWS rockets in an air-to-air role, another recent capability fielded by the military. The U.S. also needs to protect its bases in the Middle East.
The former head of Air Forces Central, Lt. Gen. Derek C. France, said the use of APKWS was a key development during his tenure, which ended last month.
“From a technical aspect, it’s ‘Hey, I need more weapons on my jet,’ and that’s what the APKWS gives you: a pod of seven of those things versus a single AIM-9. You can shoot down a lot more drones when they’re coming in swarms,” France said in a recent interview with Air & Space Forces Magazine. “From an operational perspective, there’s not just the magazine depth of an individual airplane, which I care about, but I care about the magazine depth of the theater and making sure that, across the theater, I’ve got wings with the right weapons in the right place and get them in the air where they can defend their bases. … There’s the cost curve, which is significant as well.”
And the proliferation of the drone threat is only increasing, U.S. military officials and experts say, making further advancements necessary.
“I would say that APKWS is a step in the right direction, but it can’t be the final step,” France said. “The two things that we need to focus on are air domain awareness at range: where are the drones coming from? How many are there? What’s their target? What do I know about them? And then magazine depth, both individual airplanes and theater-wise, to have enough to shoot them down in a layered defense kind of way. So both of those are important.”
“This drone problem is not going away. It’s accelerating in tactics, speed, advancements, and the numbers,” France added. “That’s the direction that we’re going.”

articles.title: US approves $24.3 billion sale of 48 F-35 warplanes to Saudi Arabia
articles.body:
US approves $24.3 billion sale of 48 F-35 warplanes to Saudi Arabia
The United States on Thursday said it had approved a $24.3 billion sale of 48 F-35 stealth warplanes to Saudi Arabia. Israel has previously voiced concerns about Riyadh buying F-35s, despite a push to normalise relations.
The United States has approved a $24.3 billion sale of 48 F-35 stealth warplanes to Saudi Arabia, the State Department said Thursday, the kingdom's latest major arms purchase since the start of the Iran war.
Saudi Arabia has long sought to buy F-35s, but officials from Israel – currently the only country in the Middle East to operate the jets – have voiced concern about their sale to Riyadh despite a push for the kingdom to normalise relations.
Read moreTrump says Saudi nuclear deal contingent on Riyadh normalising relations with Israel
"The proposed sale will improve Saudi Arabia's capability to deter current and future threats by strengthening its homeland defence, and improving interoperability with US forces," the State Department said in a statement.
It "will also augment Saudi Arabia's operational aircraft and enhance its air-to-air, and air-to-ground self-defence capability", the statement said.
The Saudi embassy in Washington praised the transaction, saying it "reflects the strength and enduring nature" of the relationship with the United States.
It added that the security cooperation between the two countries "has contributed to regional stability, strengthened our collective defence capabilities, and advanced our shared security interests".
Saudi Arabia has been repeatedly targeted with drone and missile strikes by Tehran's forces since the United States and Israel launched their war against Iran in February, and has also been hit by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels.
Read moreSaudi Arabia accuses Houthis of targeting Mecca, calls it a 'red line'
Yemen's civil war had been dormant for years, but fighting between Houthis and the internationally recognised, Riyadh-backed government reignited in July, with the rebels declaring a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia and targeting its ships in the Red Sea.
Washington has not directly entered the conflict, but a US official said earlier this week that an American military task force is working to enhance intelligence sharing and planning assistance for Saudi forces.
Congressional approval pending
The State Department has notified Congress about the proposed sale, which would require the approval of US lawmakers. It did not provide a time frame for the delivery of the jets.
The F-35 sale "will not alter the military balance in the region", the State Department said, in keeping with longstanding US policy that Israel must have a military edge over potential regional adversaries.
The United States has so far only allowed the sales of F-35s to its closest allies, including a number of European NATO allies and Israel.
Washington kicked NATO member Turkey out of the F-35 programme in 2019 because Ankara's purchase of a Russian air defence system sparked fears that Moscow could acquire the plane's technology.
Billions in arms sales
Washington also has concerns about potential Chinese espionage related to the jets.
The New York Times reported this week that US intelligence analysts have raised the possibility that Beijing could acquire F-35 technology through its partnerships with Riyadh.
US Representative Raja Krishnamoorthi, a Democratic member of the House Intelligence Committee, expressed opposition to the sale on those grounds.
It should not go ahead "when our own intelligence community is warning that it could put the crown jewels of American military technology within reach of the Chinese Communist Party", Krishnamoorthi said in a statement.
The F-35 sale is the latest in a series of major arms buys by Saudi Arabia this year.
The State Department announced the approval of a $5 billion sale of more than 10,000 bombs – including highly destructive 2,000-pound weapons – to Riyadh earlier in September.
Washington also signed off on the sale of 60 tank engines and related equipment to Saudi Arabia at a cost of $750 million this month, and a $1.96 billion deal in July for the kingdom to buy guidance sections that can convert rockets into precision weapons.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

articles.title: NATO 3.0 marches into Copenhagen
articles.body:
NATO 3.0 marches into Copenhagen
At NATO’s first high-level summit since Ankara, the bloc’s new, Europe-centric incarnation is taking shape. But it’s ordinary Europeans who stand to lose their future, and potentially their lives.
NATO’s Military Committee is meeting in Copenhagen on Friday and Saturday. Chaired by Italian Admiral Giuseppe Cavo Dragone, the Military Committee, which is NATO’s highest military authority, is tasked with turning the bloc’s strategic goals into executable plans. When NATO orders a battlegroup to Lithuania, for example, the Military Committee ensures its tanks will be able to get there across multiple countries’ rail networks, its troops will be supplied and housed, and the deployment will not leave another sector of the bloc’s so-called ‘eastern flank’ unmanned.
Accordingly, NATO is keeping the meeting’s agenda under wraps. The organization’s website simply states that the defense chiefs will take part in a “Session 1” and “Session 2” of talks, followed by a press conference, a photo opportunity, and then a “Session 3” of discussions.
Looking at the political decisions made since the bloc’s headline summit in Ankara in July, the broad aim of the conference becomes clearer: flesh out NATO’s plan to militarize Europe and prepare the continent for war with Russia, all while insulating the US from the consequences of the conflict.
What is NATO 3.0?
Coined by US Under Secretary of War for Policy Elbridge Colby, ‘NATO 3.0’ is an America-first reworking of the Cold War pact. In a speech to NATO defense ministers in February, Colby explained that the US will, going forward, focus on preparing for a potential clash with China in the Indo-Pacific, leaving NATO’s European members to “assume primary responsibility for the conventional defense of Europe.”
Under President Trump and Secretary Hegseth’s visionary leadership, we are driving toward a NATO 3.0 in which Europe takes primary responsibility for its conventional defense. Many said that it could not be done – that Europe couldn’t or wouldn’t step up. That is being disproved… https://t.co/svqGBLPIdE
— Under Secretary of War Elbridge Colby (@USWPColby) July 2, 2026
Europe will increase its military spending to NATO’s current target of 5% of GDP and shift to wartime levels of defense production, Colby explained, all while the US retains control over the bloc’s nuclear weapons. The Europeans will also be expected, US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth stated in June, to guarantee “access, basing and overflight” for American forces.
At Ankara in July, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte sold this one-sided deal as a win for Europe. “We are rebalancing our security for the better, that is what NATO 3.0 is all about,” he said.
We’re rebalancing our Alliance: a stronger #NATO with Europe & Canada spending more, producing more and doing more for their security
Building for our future
This is NATO 3.0 pic.twitter.com/pgmvA4CcAW
In light of US President Donald Trump’s threats to withdraw US forces from Germany and annex Greenland, a more Europe-centric NATO was an easy sell for Rutte at the time. Trump’s threats toward Greenland were likely a key factor in the choice of Copenhagen for this weekend’s meeting. However, in the months since Ankara, Rutte and NATO’s European leaders have revealed what the shift actually means for the continent.
Europe steps up and pays
NATO 3.0 means the death of the European welfare state. In the UK, where living standards have already suffered their worst decline since the Second World War, meeting the bloc’s pre-Ankara 3.5% spending target will involve “eye-watering” cuts to education, transport, and justice budgets, George Robertson, who co-wrote the country’s defense strategy, warned in June. Even before the spending target was hiked to 5%, Robertson claimed that the British public was “too comfortable,” and must accept the “pain and great difficulty” of “preparing for war.”
In Germany, Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s plan to rebuild the Bundeswehr as “the strongest conventional army in Europe” has already precipitated social security cuts and a planned three-year hike in the retirement age. “The welfare state that we have today can no longer be financed,” Merz announced last August, before increasing Germany’s defense budget by almost 40% in a single year and telling Germans to “work harder.”
The Netherlands and Sweden have introduced emergency taxes to fund rearmament, with the Dutch levy branded as the “freedom contribution.” Estonia has increased income tax, Belgium and Finland have cut social spending, and 18 of NATO’s EU members have borrowed money from Brussels to build out their militaries since last May.
“On average, European countries easily spend up to a quarter of their national income on pensions, health, and social security systems, and we need only a small fraction of that money to make defense much stronger,” Rutte told the European Parliament last year. The “small fraction” demanded by Rutte has since almost doubled.
Serving American interests
In return, the Europeans are not getting the strategic autonomy that some, such as France, want. NATO’s “interoperability” standards mean weapons manufactured in Europe are built to American standards, and the AI and cloud computing technology that guides them is provided almost solely by American companies.
The Ankara Summit Declaration states that “we are developing an interoperable transatlantic warfighting cloud and adopting powerful AI models.” With the EU relying on the US for 80% of its digital infrastructure, American companies such as Palantir, Anduril, and SpaceX will be the beneficiaries of this development.
Furthermore, while the US handed control of three operational commands – Norfolk in the UK, Naples in Italy, and Brunssum in the Netherlands – to European commanders earlier this year, Washington took over management of NATO’s highest Land, Air, and Maritime commands in exchange, and maintains the Supreme Allied Commander Europe (SACEUR) post.
Although NATO 3.0 envisions Europe alone deterring Russia, the bloc’s European members are still expected to go along with American wars far beyond their borders. Speaking in the UK this week, Rutte called it “essential” that Britain’s “armed forces continue to provide the hard power NATO needs” to tackle “Russia and its war against Ukraine, terrorism, Iran and the tectonic shifts of global geopolitical competition.”
NATO was not formed to counter Iran, but the US still punished its European members who refused to aid the US-Israeli war on Iran earlier this year, threatening a complete trade embargo on Spain after Madrid denied overflight and basing to American aircraft taking part in the war, and pulling troops from other countries seen as insufficiently supportive of the war.
Bleeding for NATO
In addition to handing over their money and autonomy, Europeans risk handing over their lives, if NATO’s proxy war in Ukraine degenerates into open conflict with Russia. Having dangled the prospect of NATO membership in front of Ukraine since 2008, fomented the pro-Western Maidan coup in 2014, and juiced Ukraine with weapons and training over the next decade, the US has finally succeeded in dumping the resulting conflict on Europe’s lap, with the eager participation of the continent’s Atlantacist leaders.
NATO 3.0 makes it explicit that Europe now owns this conflict, and it is the possibility of escalation that will likely occupy the bloc’s Military Committee in Copenhagen this weekend. Managing the grim minutiae of war – predicting casualty rates in an open confrontation with Russia and preparing hospitals and morgues, for example – is the committee’s remit, and NATO’s European members are already thinking in this direction.
Germany is currently assessing whether its civilian hospitals could handle an influx of 1,000 wounded soldiers per day, and considering reopening a massive subterranean medical bunker in the city of Ulm. The German military practiced moving casualties from field hospitals in Lithuania to operating theaters in Germany during its largest-ever medical exercises in March.
Norway has trained its surgeons in treating combat injuries and ordered that 7,000 hospital beds be made available for wartime casualties. France is preparing for what Paris calls a “major engagement scenario” by equipping civilian hospitals to absorb military casualties. Sweden and Lithuania have begun stockpiling blood.
A short war
NATO’s Military Committee planned for these eventualities throughout the Cold War. However, the bloc’s European members understood that if the war went hot, only US intervention would save them. Charles de Gaulle was famously skeptical of this promise, asking John F. Kennedy whether the Americans would be willing to “trade New York for Paris” in a nuclear war with the Soviets. With NATO 3.0, the US has openly told Europe that Washington’s contribution to its security will be more “limited and focused,” in Colby’s words.
Nevertheless, NATO’s European leaders, from Rutte down to the generals and admirals on the Military Committee, continue to march toward war with Russia, against all logic and self-interest. These preparations have a momentum of their own, which can be accelerated by miscalculation and political commitments; Europe’s leaders learned this lesson the hard way in the opening months of the First World War.
This time around, the potential consequences are even greater. Russia possesses the world’s largest nuclear arsenal, and in a stark warning on Wednesday, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov declared that “if Europe, which talks daily about preparing for war against Russia, attacks Russia, it will be a completely different war, and it will be very short.”
