Saudi Arabia has been repeatedly targeted with drone and missile strikes by Tehran's forces since the United States and Israel launched their war against Iran in February, and has also been hit by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels.
Yemen's civil war had been dormant for years, but fighting between Houthis and the internationally recognized, Riyadh-backed government reignited in July, with the rebels declaring a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia and targeting its ships in the Red Sea.
Washington has not directly entered the conflict, but a US official said earlier this week that an American military task force is working to enhance intelligence sharing and planning assistance for Saudi forces.

articles.title: Mobilization 2.0: Is it inevitable, and what can Putin actually achieve?
articles.body:
Rumors are spreading across Russia that a new wave of mobilization will begin sometime after the State Duma elections conclude on Sept. 20. There is no shortage of cause for such speculation: regions are holding mobilization exercises, employers are being reminded of their obligations regarding military registration of employees, and an electronic register of people who can legally be called up for military service has been compiled. The developments come at the same time the recruitment of voluntary contract soldiers is becoming increasingly expensive. Even if mobilization does take place, however, it is unlikely to significantly alter the situation on the battlefield in Donbas in the near term or to resolve Russia’s financial problems — particularly given that mobilization itself would require substantial funding.
New recruits are getting more expensive
The debate over a new mobilization comes down to a simple question: does the Russian army actually lack manpower? Different methods of counting produce very different estimates of both the potential number of new soldiers and they extent to which they would actually expand the armed forces rather than simply replacing losses.
According to calculations by IStories based on federal budget expenditures for one-time enlistment bonuses, 71,200 people signed contracts with Russia’s Defense Ministry in the first quarter of 2026 and another 60,100 in the second. That puts the six-month total at 131,300 recruits, or an average of about 720 a day. This is almost the same as in the first half of 2025 (127,500), but it is roughly 20% below the 2024 figure. After falling in late 2025 and early 2026, the flow of contract recruits therefore appears to have stabilized.
However, economist Janis Kluge, who tracks regional budget spending, arrived at significantly higher figures: around 79,000 new contract soldiers in the first quarter of 2026 and about 93,000 in the second, or roughly 172,000 over six months — around 1,000 new contract soldiers a day in the second quarter. Deputy Security Council Chairman Dmitry Medvedev, meanwhile, cited an even higher figure: more than 200,000 contracts in the first half of the year.
The discrepancy between official statements and budget-based estimates has of course been seen before, and it is true that federal data on one-time payments probably do not capture the full scale of recruitment. For the calculations that follow, it therefore makes more sense to use a range rather than a single precise figure: roughly 700–1,000 new contract soldiers a day, or 20,000–30,000 a month.
The current rate of recruitment into the Russian armed forces is between 20,000 and 30,000 people a month
New calculations by Kluge published in September confirm this general estimate. According to regional budget data, approximately 234,000 contracts had been signed by the end of August 2026, compared with 260,000 over the same period in 2025. In August, the recruitment rate remained at around 1,000 people a day — a figure that was about 20% lower than a year earlier, despite higher payments and an increase in coercive recruitment.
Actual recruitment rates are probably still below the target set for regional authorities. As the Financial Times reported, the regions have been tasked with securing 409,000 new contracts by the end of 2026. Meeting that target would require an average of about 34,000 new contract soldiers a month, or 1,120 a day.
By itself, the current pace of recruitment is no longer enough to sustain the growth in the size of the Russian armed forces that was seen during the first years of the full-scale war. As military analysts Michael Kofman and Greg Wehner note, in 2023 the Russian military managed to replace its losses while significantly expanding its force, forming two new combined-arms armies, two motor-rifle divisions, and 27 new brigades and regiments. However, in 2024 the growth slowed, and by 2025 it had virtually stopped.
In September and December 2025, Vladimir Putin gave the same figure for the size of the force in the combat zone – around 700,000 troops. According to Kofman and Wehner, this suggests that the force had barely grown over the roughly 18 months since mid-2024. In June 2026, Putin again put the size of the Joint Grouping of Forces at 700,000.
It is difficult to assess the balance between reinforcements and departures more precisely. While estimates of the number of new contract soldiers differ by tens of thousands, estimates of Russian military casualties vary even more widely.
Using budgetary spending on compensation for the families of fallen soldiers, Kluge estimated Russian battlefield deaths in 2026 at roughly 9,000 a month — when compared with recruitment of 20,000–30,000 people a month, that would suggest no manpower shortfall at all.
However, fatalities account for only part of Russia's irreversible losses. They must be supplemented by severely wounded soldiers, those who are no longer medically fit to return to the front, and troops who are missing, captured, deserting, or otherwise removed from active service. Simply adding the numbers of dead and wounded would also be misleading, since a significant share of wounded soldiers return to duty after treatment.
According to The Guardian the number of Russian killed and wounded reached around 30,000 in April 2026. At a recruitment rate of roughly 1,000 people a day, a substantial share of new recruits would go towards simply maintaining the existing strength of military units. The figures cannot, however, be compared directly without accounting for the proportion of wounded soldiers who return to duty.
The Ukrainian General Staff, for its part, puts the Russian army's personnel losses over the summer at 124,200 — 39,300 in June, 42,900 in July, and 42,000 in August – about 26% more than during the three months of the spring and significantly above the current rate of contract recruitment. However, Ukrainian statistics count all personnel losses, not just irreversible ones, meaning the 124,200 figure cannot be directly compared with the number of new contract soldiers either.
The Financial Times reports that the Russian military command is sending most new contract recruits to existing units rather than using them to build a trained reserve. The current pace of contract recruitment is therefore probably somewhat below the target set for the regions.
There is another constraint that gets lost in the aggregate statistics: 30,000 recruits do not equal 30,000 soldiers with the skills the military needs. This is particularly evident in the Unmanned Systems Forces, established in late 2025. According to IStories, the Defense Ministry planned to recruit around 78,800 people for the new branch by the end of 2026. Most were not expected to come from ordinary contract recruits, with a target of 58,000 to be recruited from among students, graduates of DOSAAFtraining courses, former aviation personnel, and “women” with the necessary training. Another 10,800 were to be conscripts transferred to contract service, while only around 10,000 were to be transferred from other military units.
However, on July 17, 2026, Deputy Defense Minister Alexey Krivoruchko said that just over 8,000 specialists had been trained for the Unmanned Systems Forces in the first half of the year. The Conflict Intelligence Team noted that, if the annual target were being met evenly, the figure should have been roughly four times higher by that point. Analysts attribute part of the shortfall to the failure of the campaign to recruit students despite reports from Novaya Gazeta Europe that at least 47 of Russia’s 50 leading universities had campaigned to persuade students to sign such contracts.
After the mass call-up in the fall of 2022, the Russian authorities effectively built an alternative system of continuous military recruitment. The state tried dozens of methods for recruiting people, from advertising contract service and offering large bonuses to using paid intermediaries, conducting raids, targeting men with debts and financial problems, recruiting foreigners, and pressuring conscripts, prisoners, and defendants to sign up for contract service. This system has so far allowed the Russian military command to avoid a second wave of mass mobilization.
Nevertheless, maintaining the previous flow of recruits has become increasingly expensive. Higher payments can indeed temporarily boost recruitment, and after Tyumen region raised its one-time enlistment bonus to 3 million rubles ($35,600), a local military recruitment official reported that the number of inquiries had doubled. However, the need to keep raising both enlistment bonuses and payments to recruiters suggests that the previous level of financial incentives is no longer sufficient to meet recruitment targets. In Moscow, for example, according to sources cited by IStories and Verstka, the flow of recruits fell by roughly a third in the spring compared with the previous year.
The pool of potential recruits is also expanding. In September 2026, Irkutsk region cut the enlistment bonus for Russian citizens from 2.1 million ($24,850) to 1.8 million rubles ($21,300), while introducing a 900,000-ruble ($10,650) payment for foreign citizens and stateless people.
In August, authorities in Zabaykalsky Krai raised the regional payment for foreign citizens and stateless people from 400,000 rubles to 900,000 rubles ($4,750 to $10,650). However, at the same time, they cut the payment for mobilized soldiers who sign contracts from 2 million rubles to 400,000 rubles ($23,650 to $4,750). The contrast illustrates the logic of the current system: regional authorities have little reason to pay as much for someone already serving in the Russian armed forces as they do to bring in a new recruit.
At the same time, the Russian authorities are removing legal barriers to another source of manpower. In August, Putin signed a law expanding the categories of convicts who can sign contracts with the Defense Ministry during periods of mobilization, martial law, or wartime. During the bill’s consideration, Deputy Defense Minister Viktor Goremykin explicitly linked the change to the need to meet the military’s 2026 recruitment target. Kluge views such measures as an additional way to sustain the current recruitment rate.
Here it is important to distinguish between having enough people to replenish infantry units and having enough young, healthy, and trainable recruits for more specialized roles. According to sources cited by Important Stories and Verstka, the share of older recruits and men with serious health problems is growing.
In spring 2026, a source in one military unit claimed that contract recruits had “literally been scraped out of all the villages around here,” forcing recruiters to look for people in other regions. Such accounts cannot be extrapolated to the Russian army as a whole, but they point to another possible limit of the current model: not a shortage of people in general, but a dwindling pool of suitable recruits.
Russian statistics make it possible to count debtors, unemployed people, and those with criminal records, but they cannot show how many are actually fit for military service. It is therefore impossible to calculate mechanically how many months of war Russia can sustain by recruiting from among the poor and indebted.
The extent to which this pool is being depleted can, however, be assessed indirectly by looking at the cost of each next recruit and the effort required to find him. If maintaining roughly the same recruitment rate requires higher payments, more paid intermediaries, searches outside the region, and lower age and health requirements, that suggests the marginal cost of each additional recruit is rising.
That alone, however, does not prove that potential contract soldiers are running out: bonuses of several million rubles remain an enormous incentive for many Russian families.
Why might Putin need mobilization?
What matters is not so much the number of soldiers as the task the Russian military command expects them to perform. Replacing losses may be enough to sustain the current slow advance, but significantly accelerating the offensive, creating an operational reserve, or forming new force groupings would require a much larger pool of troops.
Over the past two years, the Russian military has adapted its offensive tactics in order to fit its limited capabilities. As early as 2024, Russian forces had already largely abandoned attempts to launch repeated attacks with large mechanized formations, instead shifting to small infantry assaults. In 2025, this tactic evolved further — into what has been described as “infiltration,” allowing Russian forces to maintain continuous pressure along a broad front using extremely slow advances that are difficult to turn into an operational breakthrough.
Kofman and Wehner note a paradox: as the Russian force grew, the size of the force the command could deploy simultaneously in direct attacks actually declined. The reason is the battlefield’s saturation with minefields, artillery, prepared defensive positions, and drones of both the reconnaissance and strike variety, all of which combine to make large concentrations of troops highly visible and extremely vulnerable.
As a result, brigades numbering several thousand troops can spend months advancing along a single ravine or toward one or two villages, even as very few of them can take part simultaneously in assaults. The Russian command has numerical superiority across the theater but cannot fully translate it into local superiority on the battlefield.
This is particularly important when assessing the prospects of an offensive against the Ukrainian-held cities of Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, which form the northern part of a larger fortified belt of cities that also includes Druzhkivka and Kostiantynivka. The towns are separated by rivers, high ground, and wooded areas.
As of early September, the nearest Russian positions on the Lyman axis were 7–10 kilometers from Sloviansk — close enough for Russian artillery to shell the city. According to an officer with the 11th Army Corps of the Ukrainian Armed Forces, the Russian command has reinforced the sector with the 123rd Motor Rifle Brigade (which was previously involved in fighting around the Siversk salient), giving it the ability to threaten Ukrainian logistics. The Russian army has therefore moved closer to direct fighting for the Sloviansk–Kramatorsk urban area, while Ukraine’s new commander-in-chief, Mykhailo Drapatyi, is effectively restructuring the defense command system around the expected battle for the area.
Ukraine’s military command system is being reshaped for the coming battle for Sloviansk and Kramatorsk
If the current model remains in place, the most likely first scenario is a continuation of the slow advance without a new mobilization. The Russian command could continue sending reinforcements directly to active units, replenishing assault infantry and gradually attempting to encircle the urban area from several directions while simultaneously degrading Ukrainian logistics and positions with drones, artillery, and airstrikes.
Kofman, however, described the 2026 campaign as significantly less successful for the Russian military than those of previous years. He stressed that the current rate of advance cannot simply be extrapolated to a date when the entire Donetsk region would be captured, as the outcome depends not only on Russian resources but also on the effectiveness of Ukrainian defenses.
Additional mobilization is not a prerequisite for continuing the offensive. The Russian army has sustained its advance for several years with virtually no operational pauses: newly formed or rebuilt units are generally not held in reserve but sent directly to different sectors of the front. Even Russia’s airborne forces and naval infantry are typically pulled from one sector, rapidly replenished, and redeployed to another rather than being kept as a permanent operational reserve. This system allows the Russian command to maintain pressure, but also makes it difficult to accumulate forces for a separate large-scale operation.
The second scenario is an attempt to sharply accelerate the capture of the remaining part of the Donetsk region by deploying a larger mass of infantry. At first glance, a new mobilization might seem the most obvious solution.
Kofman, however, considers this approach unlikely to be effective. In his assessment, if the Russian command simply adds several regiments or divisions to sectors already crowded with troops and continues to use them in the same way, the result will be higher casualties more than anything else. Even 100,000 additional troops would not automatically translate into 100,000 assault troops who could be deployed simultaneously to capture Sloviansk and Kramatorsk quickly.
A radical acceleration of the offensive would require not just more troops, but the ability to conduct larger, coordinated operations. This means a sufficient numbers of trained junior commanders and specialists, engineering support and logistics, and the ability to concentrate forces without allowing Ukrainian reconnaissance and drones to destroy them before they enter the fight.
Linear growth in troop numbers will not work without changes in tactics and organizational support
The third scenario better explains why the Russian leadership might need mobilization: not to reinforce existing assault units, but to form new ones and thereby change the geography of the war.
Kofman considers the most dangerous option to be the creation of additional regiments and several new corps that could be deployed, for example, in the Kharkiv, Sumy, or Chernihiv directions. Even without an immediate objective of capturing major cities, the emergence of substantial Russian troops there would force the Ukrainian command to keep additional brigades in the north and northeast instead of deploying them in Donbas or Zaporizhzhia. In this scenario, mobilization would not be about sending another 100,000 troops toward Kramatorsk, but about creating a shortage of reserves for the Ukrainian Armed Forces across several fronts at once.
This may be the purpose behind the 300,000–500,000 additional troops discussed, among other places, in an analytical memo published by the Black Mirror hacker group. The memo describes a mobilization on this scale as being potentially part of a much more ambitious scenario aimed at achieving a “decisive military advantage” that would allow Russia to establish control over the entire territory of the four annexed regions and Kharkiv region before forcing the Ukrainian authorities into negotiations. The authors consider 300,000–500,000 mobilized troops insufficient on their own, however, as the Russian military would also need to expand air support, strengthen defenses in the rear, and develop its drone capabilities.
Even if a mobilization decision is made, it will not determine the outcome of the 2026 campaign. Mobilized troops have to be assembled, assigned to units, given at least basic training, provided with commanders and equipment, and deployed to the front. And forming new units takes even longer.
Kofman estimates the minimum cycle for building such forces at roughly three months and notes that, in order to significantly accelerate the offensive in 2026, mobilization would have had to begin around May. An autumn mobilization – if it happens at all – would therefore primarily be a decision focused on influencing the 2027 campaign.
What could Putin achieve by expanding the army in 2027?
There is no definitive answer to where Putin’s war aims end. His territorial demands have shifted with the negotiating context. In summer 2024, Putin demanded that Ukrainian forces withdraw from the entire territory of the four Ukrainian regions claimed by Russia — Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson, and Zaporizhzhia — as a condition for a ceasefire (while Russian-annexed Crimea remained non-negotiable).
During U.S.-mediated negotiations in 2025, according to Reuters, he was reportedly prepared to halt fighting along the existing front line in the Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions but continued to demand the entire Donbas. This did not, however, mean that he had abandoned his claims to the other territories: in late June 2026, Putin again publicly described full control of Donbas, plus Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions, as the goal of the “special military operation.”
After capturing the remaining part of Donetsk region, the Russian military would therefore face a much more difficult task in the south. To fully occupy Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions, Russian forces would have to capture the major city of Zaporizhzhia, cross the Dnipro, and retake Kherson (which Russian troops abandoned in fall 2022). These would be operations on an entirely different scale from the current advance by small assault groups in Donbas.
So far, there are no clear signs that such operations are being prepared. In summer 2026, the pace of the Russian advance remained slow. Russian forces are positioned south of Zaporizhzhia, but Ukrainian defenses have so far prevented them from advancing toward the city. There are even fewer signs of preparations for a major operation across the Dnipro to retake Kherson. Meanwhile, Ukrainian forces have stepped up strikes on Russian logistics in the south, including on the port of Mariupol and the Chongar Bridge linking the occupied territories with Crimea.
If Putin intends to use military force to gain full control over all the Ukrainian territories he has incorporated into Russia’s constitution, the Russian military would have to continue its offensive in the south while holding a front more than 1,000 kilometers long. This would seem difficult without recruiting hundreds of thousands of additional troops for next year’s campaign.
But the Russian military’s potential objectives do not end with the territories incorporated into the constitution. Putin also seeks to expand a “security zone” along the Russian-Ukrainian border. Initially, Russian authorities linked the creation of such a zone to protecting the Belgorod region, and later, they invoked Ukraine’s 2024-2025 operation in the Kursk region as justification.
In June 2026, Putin stated explicitly that the Russian military’s objective in the Sumy and Vovchansk sectors was to seize Ukrainian territory along the border, presenting the loss of this territory as Ukraine’s price for its incursion into the Kursk region. In July, following an intensification of Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure, Putin again said that additional territory beyond Donbas needed to be seized in order to expand Russia's “buffer zone.”
There is no predetermined geographic boundary to such an objective. The greater the range of Ukrainian drones and other strike capabilities, the less realistic it becomes to secure Russia’s border regions simply by pushing the front line farther away. Nevertheless, the concept of a “security zone” provides the Russian authorities with a rationale for military operations in Ukraine's Kharkiv and Sumy regions, which Moscow has not formally declared part of Russia.
Still, this does not mean that Putin has decided to pursue such a widespread campaign. For now, the most concrete near-term territorial objective remains the part of Donetsk region that Russia does not yet control, and the timeline for achieving it remains unclear, even if Ukrainian officials have repeatedly claimed that the Russian command aims to do so by the end of 2026. In August, Vadym Skibitskyi, deputy head of Ukraine’s Main Intelligence Directorate, said that this deadline was included in the Russian General Staff’s plans, and in late August, Deputy Head of the Presidential Office Pavlo Palisa made a similar claim. However, there is no independent confirmation that such an order exists.
The Institute for the Study of War contends that the Russian command has repeatedly missed projected deadlines for capturing Donetsk region. The Conflict Intelligence Team, neverthless, argues that reports of yet another deadline allegedly set by Putin for the capture of Donbas should not be taken too seriously. In their analysts’ view, Putin is satisfied with the current pace of fighting, meaning a new mobilization is unlikely to be necessary.
The cost of avoiding mobilization – and the cost of carrying it out
Avoiding mobilization is becoming increasingly expensive for the Russian authorities. In addition to the federal payment of 400,000 rubles ($4,750), new contract recruits receive a regional bonus. According to economist Janis Kluge’s estimate, its average size reached a record 1.65 million rubles ($19,500) by August, up from 1.47 million ($17,400) in March, while the regions’ actual spending on such payments rose by about 30%. Including payments to intermediaries, the regional cost of recruiting a single contract soldier increased from roughly 1.4 million rubles ($16,550) in mid-2025 to 1.8–1.9 million ($21,900) in 2026. Including the federal payment, the state is therefore paying roughly 2.2–2.3 million rubles ($26,600) to recruit each new contract soldier.
At least 11 Russian regions (plus occupied Sevastopol) raised their enlistment bonuses over the summer. In early fall, a number of southern Russian regions followed suit. As Kluge notes, some regions are funding the higher bonuses by cutting other areas of spending, from pay increases for public-sector workers to regional payments to the families of fallen soldiers.
The increase in payments to recruits has been accompanied by an expansion of the recruitment machinery itself. By August 2026, 56 Russian regions were offering rewards for bringing in a new contract soldier, compared with 31 in fall 2025. According to The Moscow Times, at least 38 regions have formally established such payments through regional or municipal regulations. The state has effectively created a market of intermediaries that are paid to find new soldiers.
IStories calculated that in 2026, the regions’ average monthly spending on recruiter bonuses had more than doubled, from 358 million rubles ($4.2 million) to 802 million ($9.5 million). By mid-May, regional authorities had spent at least 7.7 billion rubles ($91.1 million) on such payments. In some regions, recruiters receive 100,000 rubles or more for each contract recruit they bring in.
At current payment levels, recruiting an additional 100,000 people would require roughly 220–230 billion rubles ($2.7 billion) in one-time bonuses; 300,000 would cost 660–690 billion ($8.0 billion), and 500,000 would cost 1.1–1.15 trillion rubles ($13.6 billion). This is a rough estimate: payments vary widely between regions and are frequently changed. But the scale makes the key point clear: building an additional force of 300,000–500,000 contract soldiers would cost around a trillion rubles before the state even begins paying them their regular salaries.
Mobilization saves money specifically on buying people’s consent. The state does not have to offer a conscript several million rubles to sign a contract, and it does not have to pay recruiters to find them. However, that is where the savings end. Mobilized soldiers must be trained, clothed, armed, housed, transported to the front, and then paid and maintained like other service members. Simply paying 300,000 mobilized soldiers the minimum monthly allowance of around 195,000 ($2,300) rubles would cost more than 700 billion rubles ($8.3 billion) a year.
Mobilization saves money on buying people’s consent
Finally, mobilization carries a cost that cannot be captured in any budget line. The first wave turned out to be one of the Russian government’s most unpopular decisions since the start of the war and triggered a mass exodus of men from the country numbering in the hundreds of thousands. A new mobilization would exacerbate labor shortages in two ways: several hundred thousand more men would be taken into the army, while countless others would try to evade the draft.
Additional spending would come at a time when the budget is in significantly worse shape than it was in 2022. Beginning in 2026, the government raised VAT from 20% to 22%, with the Finance Ministry explicitly citing the need to finance defense and security, including military pay and support for soldiers’ families, as a reason for the additional trillion rubles in revenue. In the first eight months of 2026, the federal budget deficit reached 5.8 trillion rubles ($68.6 billion), while the government’s ability to cover it with reserves and cheap borrowing has diminished.
The contract system, by contrast, allows the economic and social cost of drawing people into the military to be spread over time. Instead of drafting several hundred thousand people simultaneously, the state recruits hundreds of volunteers every day, many of them from groups for whom several million rubles is worth more than the income they would otherwise earn.
In other words, contract recruitment does not necessarily remove every new recruit from an already tight labor market. Russian authorities can continue recruiting among homeless people, people with alcohol or drug dependencies, and other socially disadvantaged groups, some of whom have no regular employment. The size of this pool, however, is unknown. The official 2020 census counted only 11,000 homeless people, while experts in 2024 estimated the actual number at around 2 million, including roughly 1.1 million men. In 2024, about 980,000 Russians were registered as having alcohol dependence and 208,000 as having drug dependence. It is not known, however, what proportion of these people are fit for military service, have not already been recruited, and are willing to sign a contract.
Notably, the threat of mobilization itself helps sustain the contract recruitment system. As The Guardian reports, recruiters use it as an argument: it is better to sign a contract now and get paid than risk being drafted into the army later without receiving a bonus. The result is a paradox: fear of a new mobilization helps the Russian authorities recruit more people than they otherwise would have, thereby allowing them to postpone mobilization.
What is known about preparations for mobilization
The Russian authorities are far better prepared technically for a new mobilization than they were in the fall of 2022. The clearest example is the Unified Register of Military Registration, created after the first wave.
As IStories found in a leak of documents from Mikord, one of the companies that developed the system, mobilization was built into it from the outset as a separate scenario. The register allows authorities to identify people liable for military service, send out draft notices (without any limit on their number), track the potential number of mobilized troops, and transmit information for imposing travel bans and other restrictions. The system’s capacity is currently designed to send up to one million draft notices a year.
In summer 2026, more explicit signs of mobilization-readiness testing emerged. In June, officials from the administrations of neighboring regions took part in mass-mobilization exercises in Volzhsky, Volgograd region. They practiced setting up a preliminary assembly point, notifying citizens, receiving military equipment, and operating a mobilization headquarters. In July, according to The Wall Street Journal (citing Western intelligence agencies), the military conducted a similar exercise in Kaliningrad region, practicing the accommodation, feeding, and arming of mobilized troops. The newspaper’s sources claim that similar exercises are being held in other regions.
The organizers of the Volzhsky exercises, however, offered a more prosaic explanation: mobilization preparedness is a “peacetime process,” and such drills are held every year.
At the same time, mobilization has become more prominent in the government’s dealings with employers. In July, three professional publications for accountants, HR specialists, and business executives published or updated guidelines on what employers should do in the event of mobilization. According to a source at the Alabuga industrial complex, the management there also received mobilization instructions in August. There were reports that major companies were compiling lists of employees exempt from mobilization, as well as an alleged order for a mobilization drill at a Gazprom facility. The Alabuga account and the authenticity of the document attributed to Gazprom could not be independently verified.
At the same time, the surge in guidance for employers does not in itself prove that a new mobilization is being prepared. Since 2022, requirements for military registration and the liability of organizations have been steadily tightened.
On September 4, Sberbank held an internal meeting on reserving employees against mobilization, according to sources at the state-owned bank cited by Mozhem Obyasnit. According to the sources, beginning September 10, Sberbank would begin cross-checking the military-registration records of all its employees. Notably, this was the first time the bank had held such a meeting.
The Russian authorities are also continuing to build out the administrative infrastructure that could be used in a mobilization. In August, the government introduced Bill No. 1322096-8, which would establish administrative penalties for failing to comply with decisions by regional governors and operational headquarters. The bill’s explanatory note explicitly lists mobilization measures and meeting the needs of the armed forces among the tasks of these bodies.
Earlier, the Prosecutor General’s Office updated its procedures for overseeing military registration, including the transfer of information on people liable for military service, employee exemptions, and deferments. None of these measures necessarily points to preparations for a new wave of mobilization on its own. Taken together, however, they show that the state continues to keep the mobilization machinery operational.
Russia is steadily strengthening its administrative infrastructure for mobilization
This is the main difference from September 2022. Back then, the authorities first announced the call-up of 300,000 people, but many of the mechanisms for registration, notification, and oversight had to be created or reworked after mobilization had already begun. Military recruitment office databases were incomplete, businesses and regional authorities often had to work out the rules as the campaign unfolded, and there was no electronic draft-notice register. Now, by contrast, much of this infrastructure exists on a permanent basis.
Still, this does not mean that a decision on a new mobilization has already been made, and as The Wall Street Journal's intelligence sources say, no such decision has yet been made. The Guardian reached the same conclusion: in mid-August, two people familiar with discussions in Moscow, plus a Western official, saw no sign that Putin had decided to launch a new mass call-up. For now, the Russian authorities’ actions can be interpreted equally plausibly as preparations for creating the option of future mobilization, or as an effort to put everything in place in order to avoid actually having to mobilize.
In recent months, Russian officials have conspicuously denied that a new call-up is being considered. In July, Deputy Security Council Chairman Dmitry Medvedev called reports of mobilization a “lying provocation.” On Aug. 20, Russia’s UN ambassador Vasily Nebenzya said that it was “neither planned nor expected.” On August 25, presidential spokesman Dmitry Peskov dismissed the reports as “information hoaxes,” while three days later Medvedev again said that mobilization was unnecessary because there were enough contract soldiers. Then, on Sept. 1 and 3, Putin joined them, calling the mobilization rumors (1, 2) “complete crap” and an “information attack.” For now, however, these repeated denials are the strongest public indication that the authorities are concerned enough about the mobilization issue to address it repeatedly.
In any case, the state is maintaining and refining the infrastructure needed to carry out a mass call-up quickly while simultaneously spending ever more money and resources to replenishing the army without one.
So, are the Russian authorities preparing for a new mobilization? The answer is: they are preparing for the possibility. The electronic register, system of restrictions, mobilization exercises, work with employers, and legal framework make a repeat of the organizational chaos of September 2022 less likely. The decision will depend primarily on whether Putin wants to expand military operations in 2027 or if he limit his aims to eventually capturing Donbas. In other words, it will depend on whether he has a military objective important enough to justify the political and economic cost of forcibly recruiting several hundred thousand more Russians quickly.

articles.title: U.S. Navy advances first new nuke since Cold War
articles.body:
- The U.S. Navy awarded JRC Integrated Systems a $47.4 million contract modification for engineering support of its SLCM-N nuclear cruise missile program.
- The missile is also planned for the new Trump-class battleships Trump announced in December 2025, reviving a surface nuclear strike role after decades.
The U.S. Navy has awarded JRC Integrated Systems a $47.4 million contract modification to provide engineering and technical support for the Nuclear-Armed Sea-Launched Cruise Missile, or SLCM-N, the service’s effort to field its first new nuclear weapon since the Cold War.
The modification adds to a contract Strategic Systems Programs, the Navy office overseeing the program, awarded earlier and covers work through Nov. 30, 2030. Tasks include systems engineering and integration, test and flight test engineering, modeling and simulation, oversight of prototype work, system design documentation, and configuration management. The contract also covers nuclear command, control and communications support and both executive and tactical subject matter expertise on nuclear weapons, along with broader program management and acquisition support.
The Navy is obligating $10.1 million in fiscal 2025 research funds now, with the rest tied to optional line items. The work was awarded without competition under a legal provision allowing sole-source nuclear weapons contracts, after being posted publicly on the government’s contract announcement portal.
Work will be split mostly between Washington, D.C., where 80 percent of the effort will take place, with 15 percent at Naval Base Kitsap-Bangor in Washington state, home to the Navy’s Trident submarine fleet, and the remaining 5 percent in Norfolk, Virginia.
The award follows a separate, larger contract The Defence Blog reported earlier, when the Navy gave General Dynamics Missions Systems $194.1 million for engineering support on SLCM-N’s Fire Control Subsystem, with work split between Pittsfield, Massachusetts, and Manassas, Virginia. Rear Adm. Randy Wolfe, director of Strategic Systems Programs, told Congress in May 2025 that the prior year had been spent defining the missile’s overall system architecture, spanning the missile itself, its fire control and launcher systems, platform and warhead integration, and support equipment and training materials.
The SLCM-N traces back to 2018, when the first Trump administration proposed it in that year’s Nuclear Posture Review as a way to restore a low-yield, sea-based nuclear cruise missile option the Navy had given up when it withdrew the nuclear-armed Tomahawk Land Attack Missile from service in 2010. The Biden administration tried to cancel the program in its 2022 Nuclear Posture Review, arguing it was redundant given the submarine-launched W76-2 warhead, but Congress overruled that decision in the fiscal 2024 defense policy act, establishing SLCM-N as a formal program of record. Wolfe has said the Navy expects to deliver the capability in 2034, and Sandia National Laboratories announced in January 2026 that the missile would use a new W80-5 warhead variant.
The program’s surface-ship role became clearer in December 2025, when President Trump announced approval to build an initial pair of nuclear-armed “Trump-class” battleships, with the Navy eventually aiming for a fleet of 20 to 25 of the roughly 30,000- to 40,000-ton ships. As The Defence Blog reported at the time, the design includes Conventional Prompt Strike hypersonic missile launchers, more than 100 vertical launch cells, and is expected to carry the SLCM-N, restoring a surface-based nuclear strike role the Navy has not fielded in decades. Navy Secretary John Phelan said the lead ship, the future USS Defiant, would serve as the Navy’s flagship.

articles.title: Russian forces conduct two massive, five group strikes on targets in Ukraine in past week
articles.body:
MOSCOW, September 18. /TASS/. Russian forces carried out two massive and five group strikes in the past week, particularly targeting Ukrainian defense industry sites and military supply distribution centers, as well as metallurgical and automotive industry sites, and energy and transport infrastructure facilities, the Russian Defense Ministry said in a statement.
"The Russian Armed Forces carried out two massive and five group strikes on September 12-18. The strikes hit defense industry sites, metallurgical, automotive and radio-electronic industry enterprises, logistics and distribution centers for military supplies, energy, fuel, railroad and road transport infrastructure used by the Ukrainian army, as well as production and storage sites for unmanned aerial vehicles, ground-based robotic systems and their components, ammunition, fuel and supply depots, along with temporary deployment points of Ukrainian troops and foreign mercenaries," the statement reads.
Russian forces strike Nova Post logistics hub near Odessa
Russian forces struck a Nova Post logistics hub near Odessa used to store military supplies from Europe overnight, the Defense Ministry said in a statement.
"Last night, the Russian Armed Forces carried out drone strikes on Ukrainian ports and vessels, as well as logistics hubs used by the Ukrainian armed forces. The strikes hit <...> a Nova Post logistics hub located six kilometers northwest of Odessa that was used to store and distribute military supplies delivered to Ukraine from European countries," the statement reads. In addition, a dry cargo ship carrying military cargo was hit at the port of Chernomorsk.
Air defenses shoot down 629 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions overnight
Air defenses shot down 629 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions overnight, the Defense Ministry said in a statement.
"On-duty air defenses intercepted and destroyed 629 Ukrainian fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles last night, from 8:00 p.m. Moscow time on September 17 to 8:00 a.m. Moscow time on September 18 (5:00 p.m. - 5:00 a.m. GMT). The drones were downed over the Astrakhan, Belgorod, Bryansk, Vladimir, Kaluga, Kursk, Oryol, Rostov, Ryazan, Smolensk, Tula, Krasnodar, Moscow and Adygea regions, as well as Crimea, the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov," the statement reads.
Geran drones destroy Ukrainian radar stations, electronic warfare system
Russian Geran-4 drone crews have destroyed radar stations and an electronic warfare system used by the Ukrainian army in the Dnepropetrovsk and Odessa Regions, the Defense Ministry said in a statement.
"Moving vehicles of the 79K6 Pelikan radar station were detected near the settlement of Dalnik in the Odessa Region. The vehicles were tracked, and a Geran-4 drone operator carried out a strike when the radar began to deploy," the statement reads.
The ministry also said that a P-19MA radar station and a dome electronic warfare system had been destroyed near Shirokoye in the Dnepropetrovsk Region.
Russia’s Battlegroup South eliminates over 1,240 Ukrainian troops over week
Over the past week, the Ukrainian armed forces lost more than 1,240 troops in the area of responsibility of Russia’s Battlegroup South, the Defense Ministry reported.
"The Ukrainian armed forces lost more than 1,240 personnel, six armored combat vehicles, 141 motor vehicles, and 10 field artillery weapons," the ministry said in a statement.
Ukraine loses over 1,500 troops in Russia’s Battleground North area in past week
Ukraine lost over 1,500 troops in the area of responsibility of Russia’s Battlegroup North in the past week, the Defense Ministry said in a statement.
"The enemy lost a total of over 1,505 troops, three tanks, 19 armored combat vehicles, 91 motor vehicles, four field artillery systems, and three electronic warfare systems and counter-batter radars in the area of responsibility of Battlegroup North," the statement reads.
Ukrainian forces lose over 390 soldiers in Kharkov over past week
The Ukrainian armed forces’ losses in the encircled areas of the Kharkov Region over the past week exceeded 390 soldiers, the Defense Ministry reported.
"Over the past week, in areas where Ukrainian forces were encircled, the enemy lost more than 390 soldiers, eight armored combat vehicles, five motor vehicles, a field artillery weapon, two all-terrain vehicles, and 15 ground robotic systems. In the Sumy and Kharkov Regions, personnel and equipment of two tank brigades, four mechanized brigades, two motorized infantry brigades, two airborne brigades, two assault regiments of the Ukrainian armed forces, and four territorial defense brigades were destroyed," the ministry said in a statement.
Ukraine loses almost 2,000 troops in Russia’s Battleground East area in past week
Ukraine lost over 1,955 troops in the area of responsibility of Russia’s Battlegroup East in the past week, the Defense Ministry said in a statement.
"The Ukrainian army lost over 1,955 troops, five armored combat vehicles, 65 motor vehicles and four artillery systems in the area of responsibility of Battlegroup East," the statement reads.
Ukraine loses over 2,865 troops in Russia’s Battleground Center area in past week
Ukraine lost over 2,865 troops in the area of responsibility of Russia’s Battlegroup Center in the past week, the Defense Ministry said in a statement.
"The enemy lost over 2,865 troops, 17 armored combat vehicles, 83 motor vehicles, five field artillery pieces and five electronic warfare systems in this area," the statement reads.
Kiev loses over 1,480 troops in Russia’s Battlegroup West responsibility area
The Ukrainian armed forces lost more than 1,480 personnel in the area of responsibility of Russia’s Battlegroup West over the past week, the Defense Ministry reported.
"Enemy losses in this sector (Battlegroup West’s responsibility area) totaled more than 1,480 personnel, five armored combat vehicles, 96 motor vehicles, 11 field artillery weapons, and six electronic warfare and electronic surveillance stations," the ministry said in a statement.
Russian air defenses down 5,706 Ukrainian fixed-wing UAVs over past week
Russian air defense systems shot down 5,706 Ukrainian fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) over the past week, the Defense Ministry reported.
"From September 12 to 18 of this year, air defense systems shot down 44 guided aerial bombs, eight rockets from the US-made HIMARS multiple launch rocket system, two Neptune long-range missiles, and 5,706 fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles," the ministry said in a statement.
According to the ministry, since the start of the special military operation, Russian forces have destroyed 674 enemy aircraft, 284 helicopters, 239,109 unmanned aerial vehicles, 672 anti-aircraft missile systems, 30,944 tanks and other armored combat vehicles, 1,778 multiple rocket launchers, 36,483 field artillery weapons and mortars, and 72,194 tactical wheeled vehicles.
Russian forces disable several Ukrainian port infrastructure facilities this week
Over the past week, the Russian Armed Forces disabled a number of infrastructure facilities at Ukrainian ports used by the Ukrainian military to receive and store cargo and fuel and lubricants.
A number of infrastructure facilities at Ukrainian ports that facilitated the receipt and storage of military-grade cargo, as well as fuel and lubricants intended for the Ukrainian military, have been disabled," the Defense Ministry stated.
Russian forces liberate Verolyubovka, Zolotoy Kolodez in Donetsk People’s Republic
Russian forces have liberated the settlements of Verolyubovka and Zolotoy Kolodez in the Donetsk People’s Republic, the Defense Ministry said in a statement.
"Last week, units of the Battlegroup South improved their frontline positions; the settlement of Verolyubovka in the Donetsk People’s Republic was liberated yesterday through active operations. <...> As a result of active offensive operations by units of the Battlegroup Center, <...> the settlement of Zolotoy Kolodez in the Donetsk People’s Republic was liberated," the statement reads.
Russia’s Battlegroup Dnepr eliminates over 280 Ukrainian troops in past week
Russia’s Battlegroup Dnepr inflicted losses on six Ukrainian formations and eliminated over 280 Ukrainian troops over the past week, the Defense Ministry reported.
"Battlegroup Dnepr units inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of two mechanized brigades, a mountain assault brigade, an assault regiment of the Ukrainian army, and two territorial defense brigades. Over the week, more than 280 troops, an armored combat vehicle, 129 motor vehicles, a field artillery gun, and eleven electronic warfare and counterbattery radar stations were destroyed," the ministry said in a statement.
Russian Armed Forces liberate 5 villages, secure control over 5 others this week
Russian troops have liberated five settlements over the past week. Control was also established over five additional settlements, the Defense Ministry reported.
According to the ministry, the communities of Verolyubovka, Vesyoloye, and Zolotoy Kolodez in the Donetsk People's Republic, as well as Rozovka and Novoandreyevka in the Zaporozhye Region, were liberated this week. Meanwhile, troops from the Battlegroup North secured control of Chernyakov, Shirokoye, Shevchenkovo, Olkhovatka, and Malaya Volchya in the Kharkov Region.
Russian forces strike 16 vessels supporting Ukrainian military over week
Russian forces struck 12 dry cargo ships, two sea ferries, a tanker and a tugboat operating in the interests of the Ukrainian armed forces over the past week, the Russian Defense Ministry said.
"Over the week, 12 dry cargo ships, two Ro-Ro sea ferries, a tanker and a tugboat operating in the interests of the Ukrainian armed forces were hit," the ministry said.
Russian army hits four dry-cargo ships in Ukrainian ports and Black Sea
Russian operators of Geran-4 Seeker UAVs have hit four additional dry-cargo ships in the ports of Chernomorsk and Odessa, as well as in the Black Sea.
"In order to limit the logistical capabilities of the Ukrainian forces regarding the transport of weaponry and military hardware, Russia’s Armed Forces carried out a strike using Geran-4 Seeker unmanned aerial vehicles against four enemy dry-cargo ships in the ports of Chernomorsk and Odessa and in the Black Sea. All targets were hit," the Russian Defense Ministry said in a news release.

Poland Assembles Largest Military Aid Package Yet for Ukraine
Poland is preparing its largest and most comprehensive military aid package for Ukraine since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski announced the upcoming assistance package on Polskie Radio, emphasizing that Warsaw will not reduce its support for Kyiv despite ongoing Russian attacks.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The Polish Foreign Minister stated that increased Russian bombardments will only result in stronger solidarity with Ukraine.
He emphasized that Warsaw does not expect Russian behavior to change through diplomatic statements alone and is actively preparing for further escalation, noting that Russia’s hybrid warfare actions—including sabotage attempts, arson, drone attacks, and airspace violations—have already taken on a kinetic character.
"Russian generals have been threatening us with nuclear war for 20 years now," he recalled. He noted that Kremlin propagandists do this constantly. "This is an area where Russia obviously has an advantage, but, as it discovered in the case of Ukraine, this advantage is difficult to convert into use," Sikorski analyzed. "After all, if Russia could end this war through nuclear blackmail, it would have already done so," he argued.
When asked on Polskie Radio about potential Polish involvement in accelerating the delivery of Patriot air defense missile systems to Ukraine, a measure previously mentioned by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, the minister noted that specific defense deliveries remain under the purview of the Ministry of National Defense.
To further reinforce Ukraine’s air defense, the European Union has recently approved $7.1 billion under the Ukraine Support Loan, explicitly clearing the way for Kyiv to procure American PAC-3 missiles for its Patriot systems via NATO mechanisms.
Announced by EU Defense Commissioner Andrius Kubilius, the package includes special exemptions allowing Ukraine to acquire critical US interceptors alongside domestic long-range drones, missiles, and potential Gripen fighter jets.
On September 13, a Russian drone strike targeted a Kyiv-Warsaw passenger train in Ukraine’s Volyn region, occurring just two kilometers from the Polish border.
While no injuries were reported aboard the train, the attack also hit infrastructure near the Yahodyn-Dorohusk border crossing, damaging several parked trucks and a nearby gas station.
Following the strike, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha called for a full trade embargo and comprehensive sanctions against Moscow, stating that Russian strikes near the border showed Moscow’s terror was knocking on the doors of the EU and NATO.

articles.title: Russia and China veto UN Iran sanctions proposal
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Russia and China veto US proposal for UN experts to keep monitoring sanctions on Iran
Russia and China vetoed a United Nations resolution Thursday that would have authorized UN experts to keep monitoring sanctions that were reimposed against Iran last year over its nuclear program.
The UN Security Council sanctions are still in effect, which freeze Iran’s assets abroad, halt arms deals with Tehran and penalize any development of Iran’s ballistic missile program, among other measures.
Using a provision in the 2015 nuclear deal between Iran and major powers France, Germany and the United Kingdom triggered the “snapback” mechanism, which reimposed the sanctions on Sept. 27, 2025. It restored the Security Council sanctions committee and authorized a panel of UN experts to monitor implementation.
The United States had drafted a resolution to extend the U.N. expert panel’s mandate for a year. The proposal was defeated by a vote of 11-2, with Somalia and Pakistan abstaining, because of the Russian and Chinese vetoes.
It comes as the Trump administration is pursuing a wider campaign to isolate Tehran from its remaining economic partners as the more than six-month-old war in Iran has hit a stalemate.
Separately, Thursday, the administration went after digital currency networks that it says are illegally providing sanctioned Iranian entities with access to the international financial system.
The Treasury and State Departments announced that they had targeted two companies — BitBank and the Pishtaz Simorgh Electronic Trade Co. — and three associates of BitBank’s previously sanctioned chief, Babak Zanjani, who are accused of playing a role in helping Iran evade sanctions.
At the United Nations, Iran's UN mission thanked China and Russia for vetoing the US resolution, saying on social media that the countries “prevented yet another cynical attempt by the United States and its allies to abuse the Security Council for their political purposes.”
Since Israel and the US struck Iranian nuclear sites in June 2025, UN nuclear inspectors have been unable to verify the status of Iran’s stockpile of enriched uranium. The UN nuclear watchdog has said Iran maintained a stockpile of 440.9 kilograms (972 pounds) of uranium enriched up to 60% purity — a short, technical step away from weapons-grade levels of 90%.
U.S. deputy ambassador to the UN Jennifer Locetta said the United States wasn’t surprised by the vetoes on Thursday because the experts “would have shined the light" on prohibited cooperation between Iran and its partners.
She said the vetoes are part of a broader effort to prevent expert monitoring of sanctions, and even the appointment of panel members, “to stifle reporting that implicates their own activities in support of rogue regimes.”
In March 2024, a Russian veto ended UN monitoring of sanctions against North Korea over its nuclear program. In Mali, sanctions were terminated, and Locetta said that in Yemen and the Central African Republic expert appointments have been delayed or refused.
While the panel of experts for Iran was authorized a year ago and Secretary-General Antonio Guterres proposed members, they were never approved.
“Without an independent panel of experts, this council loses its principal source of impartial, evidence-based reporting on sanctions violations, creating a monitoring gap that only benefits the Iranian regime and those who profit from evading those measures,” Locetta warned.
Russian U.N. Ambassador Vassily Nebenzia reiterated Moscow’s claim that the “snapback” of sanctions against Iran was illegal, and therefore the resolution to extend the mandate of the panel of experts “was deeply flawed and did not have any legal basis.”
Russia and China had strongly urged the US and its allies not to put the resolution to a vote, which would only increase tensions in the council, Nebenzia said, but Washington “decided to opt for confrontation.”
French UN Ambassador Jerome Bonnafont, the current council president, said implementing sanctions is “a crucial instrument to encourage Iran” to return to its nuclear obligations. France will study how to ensure sanctions are enforced, he said.
One possibility would be to follow what happened after the North Korea panel of experts was abolished: establishing a monitoring team that includes France, Germany, the UK and the United States.

articles.title: As Iran war grinds on, Trump to face skeptical world leaders at UN
articles.body:
As Iran war grinds on, Trump to face sceptical world leaders at UN
WASHINGTON, Sept 18 - When President Donald Trump addressed the United Nations a year ago, he touted the US bombing of Iran’s nuclear sites just months earlier as "totally obliterating everything" and said he had brought peace between Israel and Iran.
Returning to the world body on Tuesday, Trump will face a deeply skeptical audience increasingly rattled by six months of war between US forces and an emboldened Iran, growing regional instability and a nuclear threat that has not disappeared despite his claims.
Though battered militarily and economically, Tehran has remained defiant, obstructing oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz and in recent days gaining new leverage as its Houthi allies in Yemen tighten their grip on a Red Sea chokepoint, further spiking global energy prices.
The lightning advance by the Houthi militants has put Trump in an ever-tighter bind over the unpopular conflict, dealt a blow to US ally Saudi Arabia and exposed the limits of Washington’s ability to protect its regional partners.
Most European and Asian allies have spurned Trump's demands for assistance in a conflict he launched without consulting them and which has had damaging fallout for their economies.
And with US gasoline prices high and his approval ratings low, Trump could pay a price in November’s midterm elections when his Republican Party’s control of Congress is at risk.
“We are seeing what happens when a president launches a war of choice without anticipating the unintended consequences,” said Aaron David Miller, a former adviser on Middle East policy to Republican and Democratic administrations.
In Trump’s speech to the annual gathering of heads of state and government in New York, he is likely again to frame as a victory a military campaign he promised would be over in weeks.
The conflict has instead hardened into an uneasy stalemate that has failed to achieve Trump’s shifting goals while depleting the Pentagon's missile stockpiles.
Trump’s problems have only deepened since Houthi fighters overcame Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces, sweeping down the Red Sea coast and seizing islands at the mouth of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a crucial shipping corridor that allows Iran to further threaten global oil supplies.
In response to Reuters' questions, a senior Trump administration official said the US is focused on security interests such as ensuring freedom of navigation in the Red Sea "while empowering our regional partners to take the lead in managing and resolving regional security challenges."
DOUBTS ABOUT NUCLEAR CLAIMS
Iran took up only a small portion of Trump’s speech at last year's UN General Assembly.
He recounted how, three months before, he had sent B-2 bombers to drop 30,000-pound bombs that “demolished” Tehran’s uranium enrichment capacity. However, experts determined the strikes had only seriously set back the program.
“No other country on Earth could have done what we did,” Trump said.
The US president – who campaigned on a vow to avoid foreign military entanglements - also presented himself as a peacemaker, repeating claims to have ended conflicts around the world, including a 12-day war between Israel and Iran in 2025, and again insisted he should receive the Nobel Peace Prize.
Events since then stand in contrast to his remarks.
Trump joined Israel in striking Iran on February 28, citing what he said was an imminent nuclear threat to the US. Experts have disputed his claim that Iran was close to developing a nuclear weapon, which Tehran has always denied seeking.
But Trump underestimated Iran’s resilience, analysts say. Despite airstrikes that killed many of Iran’s top leaders, it has hit back at Gulf neighbors and the US bases they host.
At the same time, Iran has retained a stockpile of near-weapons-grade highly enriched uranium believed buried by the US strikes in June 2025.
White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly said Trump alone had “possessed the courage” to confront Iran over its nuclear program, that he had achieved all his objectives and Iran's economy was being crippled by stepped-up sanctions and a US maritime blockade.
Trump, meanwhile, has rebuffed Saudi pleas for direct military intervention against the Houthis, who agreed to a ceasefire with the US last year.
This has dented confidence about US security guarantees among Gulf states, whose doubts had already been fed by Trump’s decision to go to war over their objections, analysts say. He plans to meet Gulf leaders on the UN sidelines next week, Axios reported.
TRUMP'S DILEMMA
The dilemma for Trump is that while the US can ill afford to have the Houthis close a second major shipping corridor, he is reluctant to undertake a dangerous new mission for a US military stretched by the fighting against Iran.
US officials met the Houthis last weekend in Oman, where the group said that while it was targeting Saudi shipping it had no intention of attacking American vessels, according to five people familiar with the matter.
“The US clearly has (military) capacity challenges but even so the cost of inaction here is likely to intensify tensions among Gulf allies,” said Jonathan Panikoff, a former deputy national intelligence officer on the Middle East.
The Houthis’ sudden re-emergence as a regional threat has further complicated Trump’s efforts to find a way out of the conflict.
With the war grinding on in a seventh month, the US is mired in a battle of attrition while Trump tries to intensify economic pressure on Tehran.
Trump, who has offered shifting timelines, told reporters on Wednesday that “hopefully we are towards the end.”
But analysts warn that the conflict is likely to drag on well past the midterm elections.
“Iran isn’t about to let him off the hook here while they have so much leverage to damage him in the midterms and make him a lame duck,” Brett Erickson, a geopolitical analyst and managing principal at Obsidian Risk Advisors, wrote on X. REUTERS

articles.title: EDF intel chief: Russian losses at over 10,000 soldiers for third consecutive week
articles.body:
EDF intel chief: Russian losses at over 10,000 soldiers for third consecutive week
Russian armed forces losses in the war of aggression against Ukraine have remained above 10,000 troops for the third consecutive week, exceeding the number of new soldiers being recruited, said Col. Ants Kiviselg, head of the EDF Intelligence Center.
"For the third week in a row, Russia has lost more than 10,000 troops, including both wounded and killed. This week's average daily losses are around 1,600 troops, meaning that just over 11,000 were lost over the course of the week," Col. Kiviselg said at the Defense Ministry's regular Friday briefing, giving an overview of the 238th week of the war.
"The trend therefore continues, with Russia losing more troops on the battlefield than it is able to recruit," he added.
The head of the Estonian Defense Forces Intelligence Center also noted that Ukraine had for the first time released figures on its counteroffensive toward Lyman in Donetsk Oblast where around 85 square kilometers were liberated and cleared during the counteroffensive. "Ukrainian operations in Donetsk Oblast are currently continuing," Kiviselg added.
Turning to other Ukrainian successes, Kiviselg listed continued airstrikes against Russian oil facilities in Krasnodar Krai, Saratov and Samara oblasts and the Republic of Tatarstan, a strike on the port of Makhachkala on the Caspian Sea, attacks on chemical plants in Perm Krai and Volgograd and a strike on a drone factory in Rostov Oblast.
"Among military targets, there have been attacks on airfields in Rostov Oblast, as well as air defense systems and launch sites used to store long-range drones in Rostov and Oryol oblasts. The damage is still being assessed, but the Ukrainians have probably managed to either put some aircraft out of action or damage them and the same applies to helicopters," the colonel added.
Kiviselg also cited a report by the International Energy Agency (IEA), according to which the condition of Russia's oil refineries has deteriorated as a result of Ukrainian long-range strikes, while sanctions are hampering efforts to repair damage caused by the airstrikes. The IEA estimates that Russia's oil refining capacity will remain 30 percent below its prewar level for the next 18 months.
Russian continues hitting civilian infrastructure
Although Russia has stepped up pressure on Ukraine by attacking its civilian infrastructure, surveys show that Ukrainians are unwilling to give in despite the hardships caused, Kiviselg said.
"Russian long-range strikes have continued to hit critical and strategic infrastructure in Ukraine this week, as well as residential buildings, potential warehouses, shopping centers, gas stations, vehicles and businesses in at least 17 Ukrainian oblasts. In approximately half of those oblasts, the attacks have also caused disruptions to energy supplies," he said.
Russia has once again begun using relay stations in Belarus to carry out such attacks after they had been out of operation for a period, meaning Russian strikes can now reach western Ukraine and are likely to be more accurate and effective, Kiviselg added.
The head of the EDF Intelligence Center also noted that Russia has attacked around 500 locomotives in Ukraine over the course of the full-scale war. This year, around 10 warehouses holding U.N. humanitarian supplies have been attacked, along with four pharmaceutical warehouses in September.
"So it is very clear that the Russians continue to target civilian sites," he said. "The Russian Federation is doing everything it can to make the coming winter and getting through it as difficult as possible for Ukrainians."
At the same time, recent polls in Ukraine show that around 77 percent of the Ukrainian population do not want to give in to Russia's demands or accept Ukraine's defeat and believe resistance should continue even if they have to cope for periods this winter without electricity, hot water or sewage services, Col. Kiviselg said.
The intelligence chief also highlighted a Russian drone strike on September 13 against a train at Yahodyn station near the Ukrainian-Polish border. Foreign guests who had attended the Yalta European Strategy forum and were traveling to Poland were also nearby. "The guests included many former heads of state and government, former and current senior government officials, lawmakers and experts. The good news is that none of the foreign guests were injured in the attack," he said.
Russia has said it attacks only military targets and logistics infrastructure used for military purposes and has previously warned Ukrainians and Western countries about similar attacks, saying it cannot guarantee the safety of foreign visitors in Ukraine and advising foreign nationals to leave the country, Kiviselg recalled. He said this latest incident was another Russian attempt to influence Western policymakers to withdraw their support for Ukraine.
"In response, NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte has said that Russia's hopes of undermining unity among Ukraine's supporters and bringing support for Ukraine to an end will not be realized and that assistance to Kyiv will instead be increased," the colonel said.
Commenting on an idea raised last week for both sides to halt attacks on energy infrastructure, Kiviselg noted that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has proposed ending attacks on Russian oil refineries and other fuel infrastructure on the condition that Russia stops attacking Ukraine's electricity grid and gas infrastructure.
"Ukraine wants an agreement banning all attacks on all energy infrastructure and is waiting for Russia to provide a list of facilities that would be exempt from attack under a potential ceasefire covering energy infrastructure," he added.
--

articles.title: South Korea says US-North Korea talks possible, rules out Hormuz deployment
articles.body:
South Korea says US-North Korea talks possible, rules out Hormuz deployment
South Korea will continue efforts to facilitate talks between Washington and Pyongyang.
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung said on Friday that United States President Donald Trump wants dialogue with Pyongyang and confirmed Seoul will not be deploying troops to intervene militarily in the Iran war.
“Trump clearly wants dialogue with North Korea,” Lee said on Friday.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items

- list 2 of 3South Korea embraces Central Asian leaders, looking to boost regional clout
- list 3 of 3Seoul court orders North Korea to pay $32.5m for blowing up office
He added that while such talks are uncertain, they are not impossible.
South Korea was continuing “preliminary coordination efforts” to facilitate dialogue between North Korea and the US.
“The resumption of North Korea-US dialogue would be far easier than resuming inter-Korean dialogue,” he said, according to South Korean news agency Yonhap.
Trump, seeking to revive the bond he claims to have forged with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in his first term, said he plans to meet Kim later this year.
The US president said it was important to “get along” with Kim, adding that Pyongyang now had 57 “very powerful” nuclear weapons.
Seoul has assessed that Pyongyang has about 80-120 nuclear warheads.
North Korea, which has secured critical backing from Russia in recent years, did not clearly respond to Trump.
Inter-Korean relations reached a high in 2018 but deteriorated after talks between Kim and Trump collapsed in February 2019.
On Thursday, a court in Seoul ordered North Korea to pay roughly $32.5m for blowing up the Inter-Korean Liaison Office building in 2020. The office was intended to improve relations on the peninsula but was destroyed amid rising tensions between the neighbours.
South Korea is working to strengthen relations with other regional partners. The first-ever presidential summit between Seoul and five Central Asian states was held on Wednesday, aiming to establish deeper economic engagement with the Russian-allied countries.
South Korea will not dispatch troops
Despite growing pressure from the US, Lee reiterated three times that South Korea will not deploy troops to the Strait of Hormuz.
“Let it be clear. There will be no dispatch of troops that will lead to involvement in a conflict. There will be no engagement or involvement in war,” Lee said.
The South Korean government found itself at odds with large parts of Korean society as protests broke out in recent weeks opposing a potential deployment of South Korean military assets to the Strait of Hormuz.
Lee added that South Korea will “carry out the minimum necessary activities” to protect its own merchant ships and oil shipping routes.

articles.title: “What Ukraine needs right now”: Poland to provide Ukraine with scarce F-16 missiles to shoot down jet-powered drones
articles.body:
Poland will provide another aid package to Ukraine, which will include, among other things, “what Ukraine needs right now,” Deputy Minister of National Defense Stanisław Wziątek said, reports Polskie Radio. He said the package would include missiles for F-16 fighter jets, which the Ukrainian military uses to shoot down Russian drones.
Ukraine is critically short of missiles for F-16 fighter jets, which shoot down Russian UAVs. Recently, it was reported that pilots sometimes took off without missiles, using only the aircraft’s built-in M61A1 Vulcan cannon, which is dangerous for civilians. Poland’s newly promised aid will include these missiles for Ukraine.
Among other things, Poland will provide aviation equipment, the report said. Media reports added that the aid package may be worth around €50 million.
Ammunition for F-16s and possible aviation equipment
“Our aid is in the process of being prepared. Everything will happen in a moment. I cannot say what it contains, I can only say that it is what Ukraine needs right now. This includes basic ammunition. These are the ones mounted on F-16s to shoot down Russian drones,” Wziątek said.
AIM-9 and AIM-120 are air-to-air missiles that the Ukrainian Armed Forces use with F-16s to fight Russian aviation, Militarnyi says. The outlet adds that last year Ukrainian F-16s were spotted with APKWS II missiles, which are effective against drones. As for the aforementioned aviation equipment, Poland may provide decommissioned MiG-29 fighter jets or drones, the media outlet suggests.
The MiG-29 does not use the same scarce stocks of AIM-9 and AIM-120 missiles.
Missile shortage is not new
In July 2025, America abruptly suspended arms supplies to Ukraine, affecting some types of weapons. Among them were more than 90 US-made AIM air-to-air missiles that were in Poland and on their way to Ukraine, but were withdrawn by the US, according to a Wall Street Journal article. Since then, Ukraine has received Western aid for air defense systems, but missiles have remained among the items in short supply.
Ukraine faced a severe shortage of F-16 missiles from late November to mid-December, according to Reuters. One source said Ukraine had "nothing to put on its jets for almost a month."
While F-16s likely rank first by number in the Ukrainian Armed Forces, the Soviet-made MiG-29 ranks second, Euromaidan Press. Ukraine had enough R-73 missiles for this fighter, but when the Ukrainian Armed Forces also began using them for ground-based launchers after 9M33 missiles for Soviet Osa air defense systems ran out, the rate of consumption increased sharply.
Ukrainian forces were observed resuming the use of older missiles that had been considered obsolete. There is an alternative: using the fighter’s cannon. However, this practice is dangerous.

articles.title: Russia’s plans may include strikes against Ukraine’s allies, Poland says
articles.body:
Russia’s plans may include strikes against Ukraine’s allies, Poland says
Warsaw also says it has scrambled military planes in response to a Russian attack in western Ukraine, close to its border.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk says that intelligence information suggests Russia plans to launch drone and missile attacks against countries supporting Ukraine.
Warsaw’s leader outlined the assessment during an address to parliament on Thursday, saying that the attacks will be meant to weaken NATO’s ability to act collectively in response.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
