- list 2 of 4Poland, Ukraine accuse Russia of ‘escalation’ after strikes near border
- list 3 of 4NATO pledges more Ukraine support after Russia strikes near Poland
- list 4 of 4NATO jet shoots down suspected Russian drone over Lithuania
“According to intelligence assessments, Russia’s plan … includes hybrid drone and missile strikes against countries supporting Ukraine, including Poland,” Tusk said.
European countries suspect Moscow of being behind a series of acts of sabotage in recent months to put pressure on the allies, especially Germany, helping Kyiv in its bid to resist Russia’s full-scale invasion – something the Kremlin has vigorously denied.
“These potential strikes would be quote-unquote ‘accidental’ in nature, intended to paralyse or at least weaken the resolve of NATO states to invoke the relevant NATO provisions in the event of aggression against a member country,” Tusk added.
He did not elaborate on which intelligence agencies had provided the warning.
He also said such attacks by Russia could coincide with “political changes in certain European countries granting power – or at least a powerful voice – to those who, increasingly invoking noble slogans of peace, pacifism and needless casualties, will call for peace – or rather, the total capitulation of Ukraine”.
Tusk appeared to be referring to the advance of more Russia-friendly parties such as Alternative for Germany (AfD) and National Rally in France.
Air raid near border with Poland
Earlier on Thursday, Poland said it had scrambled military planes in response to a Russian attack in western Ukraine, close to the Polish border.
Airports in Rzeszow and Lublin were temporarily closed, and residents of two eastern regions of Poland received air raid warnings. Local media reported that sirens had sounded and that pupils in some schools had sought shelter.
“Very close to the Polish border, not far from Dorohusk, a petrol station was most likely attacked again,” Tusk said.
On Sunday, a Russian drone hit a passenger train in Ukraine, just two kilometres (1.6 miles) from the Polish border.
Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said Poland was strengthening airspace protection.
“We have increased F-16 and helicopter activity, and are reinforcing our air defence and rapid response systems,” he wrote on X.
Tusk said he would visit Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Friday to discuss cooperation within the Integrated Anti-Ballistic Missile Coalition, a group of European countries developing an air defence system with Ukraine as a cheaper alternative to the US-built Patriot.

articles.title: Ukraine kept this strike drone secret for two years—its maker says it has destroyed more than 350 Russian systems
articles.body:
A Ukrainian drone maker has revealed it built a strike weapon it kept classified, deputy director Andrii Rymaruk told Radio NV. For two years, Ukrspecsystems, known for manufacturing Ukraine's SHARK reconnaissance drones, hid its connection to the RAM-2X strike drone, even as crews used it to hunt Russia's costly air defenses and missile launchers deep behind the front. By 2025, it had quietly become the Defense Forces' flagship mid-strike drone.
Ukraine's war on Russia's air defenses increasingly runs on drones its own industry builds and fields in secret, revealed only once they have already destroyed the enemy's costliest launchers and radars. Holding one back that long lets its crews rack up strikes before Moscow can study the weapon and build a counter—and this maker went public only once wrecked drones had reached Russian hands.
Why come out now
The RAM-2X first flew in combat in early 2024, but the maker kept its role secret. Rymaruk said the company wanted the drone and its crews to finish the job first—destroy what needed destroying—before talking. Once shot-down units reached the enemy and turned up on social media, silence no longer protected anything. So after two years, Ukrspecsystems unveiled the drone at the MSPO defense expo in Kielce, Poland.
What it kills
This is a mid-strike drone—a loitering munition that flies deep behind the lines, circles, and dives into its target. Its victims include S-400 and S-300 air defenses, the systems Russia uses to shoot down aircraft, and Iskander launchers that fire ballistic missiles at Ukrainian cities.
Rymaruk put the RAM-2X's own tally at more than 350 Russian systems destroyed since 2024, while Defender Media, which interviewed him, reported more than 1,000 targets over two years. Ukrspecsystems credits the wider RAM series, which reaches back to a fixed-wing model supplied from late 2022, with more than 450 target engagements, over 400 of them against air defenses. Today, it destroys 50 to 60 pieces of Russian equipment a month.
How far, how many
The drone has grown fast. It flew 140 km in 2024 and now hits targets up to 180 km, almost 230 km in good conditions, and a crew from the 429th Achilles unmanned-systems brigade set a range record at 215.5 km. It has spread from a few crews to about 100 military units and 250 trained teams, and one operator can fly it from anywhere in Ukraine. It also works in pairs with the SHARK-M reconnaissance drone—one finds the target, the other kills it. In July, Ukrainians crowdfunded 30 of the drones for military intelligence and the security service through Serhii Prytula's foundation.

articles.title: Russia has ramped up ballistic strikes on Ukraine using repurposed S-400 missiles – Reuters
articles.body:
Russia has ramped up ballistic strikes on Ukraine using repurposed S-400 missiles – Reuters
New data on Russian missile strikes shows that Russia has been increasingly using RM-48U missiles, originally designed as targets for air-defence crews, against Ukraine.
Source: Reuters, citing official Ukrainian data
Quote: "RM48Us made up more than half of the 228 ballistic and hypersonic missiles fired at Ukraine in July and early August, according to the figures compiled by military analysts at the General Prosecutor's Office."
Details: Reuters reported that in July Russia used the highest number of ballistic and hypersonic missiles in a single month since the start of the full-scale invasion.
Quote: "Of those 158 strikes, 87 were from RM48Us, the data showed. The pace of the aerial assault has only intensified; there were 70 Russian ballistic and hypersonic strikes in the first eight days of August, the Ukrainian data showed, with 36 of them from RM48Us."
More details: The mass use of RM-48Us could be intended to deplete Ukraine's stockpiles of interceptor missiles, said Sidharth Kaushal, a senior research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), a London-based defence think tank.
"Their use allows the Russians to husband the more capable missiles they have, the Iskanders, but also the KN-23s and the Zircons, for winter when they would want to really lean into their ballistic missile campaign," Kaushal said.
Reuters also points to a shift in the ratio of RM-48U missiles to Iskander-system missiles used by Russia.
Quote: "Indeed, as the RM48U attacks surged in July, the number of Iskanders fired fell to 38 from more than 100 the previous month, the Ukrainian data showed."
More details: "RM" stands for "raketa mishen", meaning "missile target" in Russian. RM-48Us are launched from Russian S-400 surface-to-air missile systems. The Ukrainian Prosecutor General's Office and Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU) say the missile travels along a high-speed ballistic trajectory. The Prosecutor General's Office noted that the RM-48U is less powerful and accurate than Iskander ballistic missiles.
The Prosecutor General's Office said military experts have also established that RM-48Us deviate from their intended target by an average of around 300 m. Their warheads can also scatter metal fragments over a wide area when they detonate.
DIU reported that Russia plans to produce over 480 RM-48Us this year, more than double the 200-plus missiles it manufactured last year.
Background: DIU recently revealed the structure and component base of the Russian RM-48U missile, as well as the companies involved in its production.

articles.title: EU pledges €3.3 billion for Ukraine, von der Leyen says “more is coming” as Russia’s escalating air war makes life in Ukrainian cities increasingly difficult
articles.body:
EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen says Europe will provide Ukraine with another €3.3 billion for missiles and drones as Russia intensifies attacks on Kyiv and seeks to make daily life in Ukraine's cities impossible.
Ukraine has repeatedly appealed to its partners for more air defense as Russia develops increasingly sophisticated ways to attack Ukrainian cities, while Ukraine’s stocks of air-defense interceptors have fallen to critically low levels.
Following a call with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, von der Leyen said the EU would disburse the funds on 18 September. She also said the EU had approved funding for Patriot air defense systems through its Ukraine Support Loan.
Ukraine needs more air defense
Russia has increasingly combined large numbers of attack drones with ballistic and cruise missiles, forcing Ukraine to defend vast areas while facing shortages of high-end interceptors.
The most difficult targets are Russia’s ballistic missiles, which can reach Ukrainian cities within minutes and require specialized systems such as Patriot to intercept. Ukraine has repeatedly called for more Patriot batteries and interceptors as Russia increases missile attacks.
Ukraine also needs additional air defense capabilities to counter Russia’s increasingly sophisticated drone attacks. Russia is deploying faster, more advanced Geran-type drones that are more difficult to intercept, increasing pressure on Ukraine’s already limited air-defense stocks.
Von der Leyen said the EU had approved funding for Patriot systems last week, but acknowledged that “clearly more is needed.”
The new €3.3 billion package will fund the procurement of missiles and drones for Ukraine, strengthening its ability to defend against Russian attacks.
Europe proposes joint air defense development
Von der Leyen also announced that the EU is prepared to use remaining funds from its Security Action for Europe (SAFE) program to launch a new joint EU-Ukraine defense initiative.
The proposed program would focus on developing a European air and missile defense system, building on the jointly developed anti-ballistic Freya system.
The goal is to combine Ukraine’s battlefield experience and defense innovation with European technology and industrial capacity, according to von der Leyen.
The announcement comes as Ukraine is trying to strengthen its air defenses ahead of another winter of Russian attacks, when strikes against energy and other critical infrastructure could have an especially severe impact on civilians.
The EU has billions in unspent defense funds. It wants to use them for projects with Ukraine
Von der Leyen calls for broader support
Von der Leyen said the EU has already mobilized nearly €15 billion for Ukraine in 2026, with additional support planned. She added that “more is coming.”
She also said Ukraine needs to complete reforms in the Verkhovna Rada to unlock further funding and continue its path toward EU membership.
“Europe is stepping up,” von der Leyen said. “Now others must step up their support too.”

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: Poland’s Tusk heads to Kyiv after warning of Russian strikes on Ukrainian allies
articles.body:

  Russia is planning hybrid strikes with drones or rockets on European countries supporting Ukraine, among them Poland according to its prime minister, Donald Tusk. Russia will pretend the attacks are “accidental” in order to “paralyse or at least weaken the motivation of Nato countries” to rush to the defence of the member state coming under attack, Tusk said in a speech to the Polish parliament. “There is a real risk that drones or other types of projectiles will enter the territory of one or several countries on the eastern flank and even cause destruction,” Tusk said, vowing that “if anyone dares to attack us, they will face a resolute response from us and our allies”.
- 
  Tusk announced he would travel to Ukraine overnight, arriving on Friday, in what might be seen as an act of defiance against Russia after European leaders were in transit during a drone strike on a train near the Polish-Ukrainian border on Sunday. Officials usually keep their travel plans to Ukraine secret for security reasons. In Kyiv, he said he would discuss with Volodymyr Zelenskyy how to defend against the new types of drones, as well as discuss with partners including Slovakia further sanctions against Russia.
- 
  The Slovak prime minister, Robert Fico, also said he would be in Kyiv as he claimed Europe is closer than ever to a large-scale war erupting from the war in Ukraine and politicians must strive for peace. Fico has kept warm relations with Russia while criticising EU and Nato aid to Ukraine, though Slovakia’s arms industry is simultaneously a producer of artillery shells supplied to Kyiv’s forces. On Friday the European Union will disburse €3.3bn to Ukraine to buy missiles and drones, Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, has announced.
- 
  Tusk said Russia was not ready for any peace talks “without the total capitulation of Ukraine”. “They are convinced the winter will be tragically critical for Ukraine.” He said last winter Poland stepped in with deliveries when Ukraine’s energy infrastructure came under attack, but if border crossings are destroyed it will be much harder for Warsaw to offer such help this winter. “Russia’s goal is to destroy as much as possible the economy and logistics of Ukraine,” Tusk said, adding that intelligence indicates continuous attacks of “very high frequency and intensity” on six main Ukrainian cities should be expected in the near future.
- 
  A drone hit a petrol station near Ukraine’s border with Poland on Thursday, Tusk said separately at a press conference in Warsaw. A spokesperson for the Polish military told TVN24 that air defences were activated on Thursday after a jet-powered drone approached Polish airspace before exploding about 4km (2.5 miles) from the Polish border. Poland’s Lublin and Rzeszow airports temporarily suspended operations on Thursday as the air force responded to Russian drone activity, Polish authorities said.
- 
  Russian missiles and drones injured at least 19 people in Ukraine’s capital and the surrounding region, authorities said on Thursday. Kyiv’s military administration said more than 10 locations were hit, while 33 sites were damaged in the wider region. A 10-year-old girl and a 12-year-old boy were among the injured, the administration said.
- 
  Ukraine’s air force said it destroyed or suppressed 131 Russian aerial targets during the overnight attack in the Kyiv, Zaporizhzhia and Odesa regions. The attack involved ballistic and cruise missiles as well as drones and decoys. In Odesa, seven people were injured, including two children, according to Ukraine’s state emergency Service. Apartments on the 14th through 16th floors of a residential building were damaged. A private residential building in Odesa was also destroyed and others damaged.
- 
  Ukrainian forces struck an oil refinery in Yaroslavl and a military airfield in the Rostov region, Zelenskyy said on Thursday. Zelenskyy said Ukraine’s operation against the Yaroslavl oil refinery was conducted jointly by the country’s Security Service, special operations forces, military intelligence and the foreign intelligence service. The security service also struck a military airfield in Rostov, damaging an An-12 aircraft, two An-26s and three helicopters. Reuters said that according to its industry sources, the refinery halted crude processing after the Ukrainian attack. The local Russian governor confirmed the damage.
- 
  A Russian drone struck a civilian vessel flying the flag of Tanzania in the Black Sea on Thursday, killing the ship’s captain and injuring three crew members, according to Oleh Kiper, the regional head in Odesa. Russia damaged the Bilhorod-Dnistrovskyi bridge in the Odesa region, significantly limiting Ukraine’s ability to transport grain to its Danube river ports, Ukrainian state railway operator Ukrzaliznytsia said on Thursday. According to Ukrzaliznytsia, about 3,000 grain wagons are bound for the Danube ports. Without the bridge, they would need 26 days to reach the ports. “The situation is very difficult. We are working to restore the Bilhorod-Dnistrovskyi bridge,” a company official said.

articles.title: U.S. May Have Committed War Crimes in Iran, U.N. Report Says
articles.body:
The U.S. may have committed war crimes when its strikes allegedly hit an elementary school and a sports facility in Iran, according to a United Nations report publicly released on Thursday.
The U.N.’s Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran said it found “reasonable grounds to believe that the United States committed a war crime by launching indiscriminate attacks that killed or injured civilians or damaged civilian objects.”
The U.S. and Israel launched strikes on Iran on Feb. 28, triggering a war that has stretched into its seventh month. Among those attacks, the mission identified U.S. Tomahawk missile strikes that hit Tree of Tayyiba Elementary School in Minab, killing more than 150 people, including 120 children, and an alleged U.S. missile strike that dispersed tens of thousands of tungsten pellets over a sports complex and residential area in Lamerd, killing 22 civilians. (The U.S. denied carrying out any strike within the vicinity of Lamerd on Feb. 28.)
Both civilian facilities were “clearly identifiable,” the report said.
“The U.S.’s failure to update information in relation to the school in its targeting databases and to verify that the building was a military objective before launching the attack went beyond mere negligence,” the report said. “Rather, the U.S. directed the strikes at the building of the school while being aware of a substantial risk of striking a civilian object and acting recklessly as regards the possibility that this would happen.”
The mission is expected to present its findings, which also conclude that Iranian authorities likely committed crimes against humanity during their deadly crackdown on protesters in December and January, to the U.N. Human Rights Council on Monday.
“People in Iran are caught between intensified repression and violence by their government and renewed armed conflict and insecurity resulting from the hostilities between Iran and the U.S and Israel,” the report said.
The war has produced a significant civilian toll, with at least 2,100 people killed across the region by late April. In Iran, human rights groups estimate that more than 1,700 civilians were killed by the end of April, including more than 1,000 civilians who were killed in the first five days of the U.S.-Israeli bombing campaign. That includes hundreds of women and children, dozens of health care workers, and at least nine journalists. Iranian authorities reported another 18 deaths from U.S. strikes on Sept. 1, which included several civilians. Israel’s strikes on Lebanon have also killed more than 4,300 people and displaced more than one million since early March, according to Lebanon’s Health Ministry, which does not distinguish between civilians and combatants.
U.S. conduct in its war against Iran has come under growing scrutiny. On Sept. 1, an apparent U.S. strike hit a wedding celebration in Kuhestak, killing five people and wounding more than 60. Washington has not accepted responsibility, although it launched an internal probe into the strike. An analysis by Reuters indicated that the damage was likely caused by a direct hit from a U.S. munition.
The U.S. also carried out strikes on bridges and electrical infrastructure in Iran in July, after President Donald Trump repeatedly threatened attacks on Iranian bridges and power plants. In March, Trump threatened to “blow up” Iran’s desalination plants if Tehran did not reopen the Strait of Hormuz, a move that legal experts said could violate international law. He also warned in April that a “whole civilization will die tonight” unless Iran acquiesced to U.S. demands. Israel’s bombing of Iranian fuel depots, which shrouded Tehran in plumes of toxic black smoke, also raised warnings of potentially decades-long harm to public health.
The State Department told the Associated Press that it did not consider the latest U.N. report credible. The Trump Administration withdrew from the Human Rights Council, which comprises 47 countries, in February 2025, over its “anti-American rhetoric and antisemitism,” the department said.
White House spokesperson Anna Kelly told news outlets the Human Rights Council has “accomplished nothing for human rights while spouting unserious nonsense for decades.”
“The only party in this conflict that has committed war crimes is the Iranian regime, which has murdered thousands of its own people, killed Americans overseas, executed acts of terrorism in the Strait of Hormuz, and launched indiscriminate attacks against its neighbors in the region,” Kelly said.
What the U.S. has said about the strikes
In March, the Pentagon launched a formal command investigation into the Minab school strike following a preliminary review. It has not released its preliminary findings, although a U.S. official told the Associated Press that the strike was likely the result of outdated target coordinates supplied by the Defense Intelligence Agency. The school was adjacent to an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps complex, but satellite imagery showed the school had been separated from the compound in 2016. It had been publicly listed as a girls’ elementary school for years.
Members of Congress have also questioned whether the Pentagon used artificial intelligence tools to identify the school as a target. No publicly disclosed evidence has established that an AI model independently selected the school as a target.
In June, Trump said the incident was still under investigation. “Nobody did that on purpose,” he told reporters at a press conference in France.
The Pentagon told Reuters on Thursday that the investigation is ongoing.
The U.S. was also accused of carrying out strikes with precision missiles that scattered clouds of tungsten pellets in the city of Lamerd, which the U.N. report also mentioned.
On March 28, BBC Verify reported that weapons experts had identified the type of missile used in Lamerd from video footage as a probable U.S.-made Precision Strike Missile (PrSM). A visual analysis by the New York Times also indicated the same type of missile.
A review by the conflict monitor Airwars last month mapped three apparent missile detonations over a sports complex and two residential neighborhoods in Lamerd. Weapons experts told AP that the missiles appeared to be PrSMs and were unlikely to have been fired by Iran or Israel.
On March 31, U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) refuted claims that the U.S. struck Lamerd and said U.S. forces did not launch strikes in Lamerd or within 30 miles of the city on Feb. 28.
CENTCOM said that the missile visible in video footage was too long to be a PrSM, and suggested it was instead an Iranian Hoveyzeh cruise missile.
“U.S. forces do not target civilians, unlike the Iranian regime which has attacked civilian locations in neighboring countries more than 300 times,” CENTCOM said on March 31. No formal investigation into the alleged strike has been announced since.
In May, CENTCOM commander Adm. Brad Cooper told Congress that the military was investigating only one case involving possible U.S.-caused civilian deaths: the Minab school strike.
Iran may have committed crimes against humanity in deadly crackdown
The mission also found grounds to believe that the Iranian government committed crimes against humanity during their “violent” crackdown on mass protests beginning late December. Iranian security forces killed 3,038 people and injured 25,000, according to official counts, although the report said the toll is likely higher. At least 221 children, including two two-year-olds, were killed in the crackdown, the report said, citing a human rights organization.
The government arbitrarily detained tens of thousands of people, some of whom were subjected to torture, solitary confinement and denial of legal advice, the report said.
Security forces also attacked health care facilities, arresting wounded protesters and health care workers, the report said.
The mission said at least 29 men were executed, five publicly, in connection with the protests following summary trial. More than 70 people, including five women and three children, are at “imminent risk” of execution, the report said.
Iran has not publicly commented on the report.
In January, Iranian protesters urged Trump to make good on his promise that “help is on its way.” Trump said he was considering military action, although he ultimately declined to launch a strike at the time, and called on demonstrators to continue standing up to the theocratic regime.
In recent weeks, amid renewed U.S.-Iran hostilities, Trump has again urged the Iranian public to resist their government, asking “When are the Iranian people going to rise up and fight?”

Poland Warns Russia May Target Ukraine Supporters With "Accidental" Strikes
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned that the most likely scenario for the coming months involves Russian hybrid drone and missile attacks against countries supporting Ukraine, including Poland, according to Onet on September 17.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Speaking in Poland’s Sejm , Tusk said recent attacks near the Polish border were a particular cause for concern. He stressed the need to provide the public with detailed information about possible developments based on currently available intelligence.
“I want to present to the public the most likely scenario for the next few months, because this scenario involves serious events and requires focus, seriousness, and the mental readiness to face difficult tests,” Tusk said.
According to the Polish prime minister, there is a risk that drones or missiles could enter the territory of one or more countries on NATO’s eastern flank and potentially cause damage, while such incidents could subsequently be presented as accidental.
“In short: there is a real risk that drones or other types of missiles could enter the territory of one or more countries on the eastern flank, even cause destruction, while the official version would be that it was an accident,” Tusk said.
Tusk emphasized that this was not the only possible scenario, noting that unpredictability has become a defining feature of contemporary politics.
He added that intelligence assessments point to the possibility of Russia carrying out hybrid drone and missile strikes against countries providing support to Ukraine.
“According to intelligence assessments, the Russian plan also includes hybrid drone and missile strikes against countries supporting Ukraine, including Poland. These possibilities have been discussed for a long time, but today this information is very consistent and, unfortunately, convincing,” Tusk said.
According to Tusk, such attacks could be made to appear “accidental” in an effort to weaken NATO countries’ willingness to invoke the Alliance’s provisions in response to aggression against one of its member states.
His remarks come amid heightened concerns over Russian drones near Poland. On September 14, Polish forces recovered a Russian-origin military drone from the Baltic Sea off the country’s northern coast.
Polish Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz reported the discovery the same day, saying troops had located and retrieved the aircraft from the water near the beach in Rusinowo, close to Jarosławiec.
Further details emerged on September 16, when Polish military prosecutors told the Polish Press Agency that the recovered drone had been carrying a live warhead, which was neutralized at the scene. Preliminary findings identified the Russian aircraft as a Gerbera 2 drone.

articles.title: Trump 'clearly' wants dialogue with Pyongyang: S Korean President
articles.body:
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung said it was "clear" that U.S. President Donald Trump wants dialogue with Pyongyang (AFP Photo)
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung said on Sept.18 that U.S. President Donald Trump clearly wants dialogue with Pyongyang and confirmed Seoul will not be deploying troops to intervene militarily in the Iran war.
Trump, seeking to revive the bond he claims to have forged with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in his first term, said last month that he plans to meet Kim later this year.
The U.S. president also said it was important to “get along” with Kim, adding that Pyongyang now had 57 “very powerful” nuclear weapons. Seoul says there are around 80-120.
North Korea, which has secured critical backing from Russia in recent years, did not clearly respond to Trump’s overtures.
Lee said on Sept. 18 it was “clear” that “Trump wants dialogue, and I am also urging President Trump to engage in dialogue.”
South Korea, which Pyongyang has repeatedly labelled as its enemy, was continuing “preliminary coordination efforts” to facilitate dialogue between North Korea and the United States, Lee told reporters at the presidential Blue House.
He added that such a meeting “remains difficult, but is not impossible.”
“I cannot say for certain how likely it is, but it is also clear that we must make every possible effort to turn that possibility into reality,” he said.
Lee’s comment came hours after the North Korean leader’s powerful sister accused the United States of escalating regional tensions through frequent military drills and warned of a “more offensive” response from Pyongyang.

articles.title: Pentagon, Lockheed to Expand Production of Secretive New Joint Advanced Tactical Missile
articles.body:
The Pentagon announced a deal with Lockheed Martin on Sept. 17 to expand production of the AIM-260 Joint Advanced Tactical Missile, an advanced new Air Force and Navy air-to-air missile meant to equip fifth- and sixth-generation fighters.
The “framework” agreement aims to give Lockheed a “long-term demand” signal, part of a push by President Donald Trump’s administration to build and sustain a more robust munitions manufacturing industrial base.
The announcement “establishes the framework for future multiyear procurement of JATM,” according to the Pentagon release.
“We will deliver JATM at the speed our nation and allies demand while providing value for taxpayers and our shareholders,” Tim Cahill, president of Lockheed Missiles and Fire Control, said in a company release.
A Lockheed spokesperson declined to answer further questions from Air & Space Forces Magazine, deferring to the Department of Defense. A Pentagon press officer also declined any further comment about the announcement.
The announcement should signal to Lockheed and other munitions-makers that a stable market is taking shape, said Mark Gunzinger, director of future concepts and capability assessments at the Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies.
“It is difficult for industry to justify expenditures needed to accelerate and scale up production,” the retired Air Force colonel said. “This is a key reason why this is an important framework.”
Next-Gen Option
The JATM is the successor to the AIM-120 Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missile, which has been in service since 1991.
The radar-guided, medium-range, supersonic AMRAAM has undergone major upgrades since its inception, most recently in 2020. The F-22 Raptor, F-35 Lightning II, F-15 Eagle variants, and the F-16 Fighting Falcon can all carry it, and the Air Force isn’t looking to stop buying the missile even as it looks to the JATM.
The service is seeking $953 million for 618 AMRAAMs in its fiscal 2027 budget request, while the Navy is asking for $673 million to buy 388 AMRAAMs.
The JATM seeks to overmatch the Chinese military’s PL-15 and PL-17 missiles and will reportedly double the AMRAAM’s range and hit targets in excess of 120 miles away, though much of its capabilities have been shrouded in secrecy for years.
In its fiscal 2026 budget request, the Air Force revealed it had bought 144 JATMs in 2024-2025 and planned to buy at least another 112 missiles. The fiscal 2027 request, still pending before Congress, has $1.5 billion in procurement to scale up production, but budget documents don’t list any quantities.
While upgraded AMRAAMs provide an improved strike option for fighter aircraft, the JATM is necessary for advanced aircraft already fielded and those in the pipeline, such as the F-47 and Collaborative Combat Aircraft variants, the FQ-42 Vengeance and FQ-44 Fury.
“It doesn’t make sense to invest in highly survivable and incredibly capable fifth- and sixth-gen fighters and bombers just to saddle them with payloads of weapons that will not survive to reach their targets in a fight with a peer adversary,” Gunzinger said.
Mix for the Future Fight
Though reports on the current conflict with Iran don’t indicate the U.S. is using large numbers of air-to-air missiles, a future conflict with a peer adversary such as the Chinese military is likely to look much different.
“Multiple Mitchell Institute wargames have spotlighted the need to rapidly grow the U.S. Air Force’s inventory of advanced air-to-air weapons, which could be nearly depleted within a couple of weeks of high-intensity combat with a peer adversary,” Gunzinger said.
This isn’t the first time the Pentagon has announced plans for multiyear procurement of key missiles.
In July, the Pentagon announced a similar framework for a USAF program known as the Family of Affordable Mass Munitions, which will produce lower-cost cruise missiles that experts believe will be needed in future conflicts for higher strike volumes.
That deal anticipates 8,000 missiles annually once production is at full strength. Work is expected to ramp up by 2028 with 5,300 missiles produced, increasing to the 8,000-missile mark by 2031.
While the FAMM deal will bulk up low-cost options for the Air Force, work on more expensive but more capable munitions are an important part of the equation.
“Our air forces will have a future high-low mix of counter-air weapons, but it’s far more important to focus on the cost to achieve an effect in the battlespace like countering an enemy air threat than the unit cost of a weapon,” Gunzinger said. “The key is to determine the right high-low mix based on optimizing cost per effect instead of simply chasing lower unit costs.”
Allies and Partner Purchases
The U.S. isn’t the only country interested in JATM—Australia announced $736 million in spending to equip its Royal Australian Air Force with the weapon.
That move, along with potential deals with other allies and partners, could also help reduce missile costs for the U.S.
“I believe sharing production with key allies as soon as possible is critical to improving their interoperability with U.S. air forces and lead to cost-sharing agreements that can accelerate weapon development and acquisition,” Gunzinger said.
Beyond cost savings, having allies buy the next-generation missile for their fleets also gives the U.S. ways to standardize weapons loaders across a coalition and share munitions when needed, he said.

articles.title: Tusk warns of ‘accidental’ Russian strikes against Ukraine’s allies in fall and winter
articles.body:
Donald Tusk looks on during a joint press conference with the Austrian Chancellor in Warsaw on September 17, 2026. | ROLAND Schlager/AFP via Getty Images
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned Thursday that Russia could launch drone or missile strikes in the coming months against countries supporting Ukraine and play them off as accidents.
Speaking in the country’s parliament, Tusk said intelligence assessments from NATO, Ukraine and Poland indicated that “the most likely scenario for the next few months” is that Russia will step up attacks against Ukraine and its allies, including Poland.
Tusk said Russia’s aim was to “weaken NATO’s integrity” and convince its members that “Article 5 is more theoretical than practical.”
“There is a real risk that drones or other types of missiles could enter the territory of one or several NATO countries on the eastern flank and cause damage. And the official narrative will be that it was an accident and that there is no reason for anyone to consider any kind of NATO response,” Tusk said.
He also said that “not all politicians in the West, in the United States or Europe are thinking about how to defend Poland, Lithuania, Latvia or Estonia, dreaming of immediately proving that they are ironclad allies and will come to Poland’s aid under Article 5.”
“You know that yourselves,” Tusk added.
U.S. President Donald Trump has on numerous occasions cast doubt on the principle of collective defense.
The prime minister also said that some politicians and political groups in Europe were “just waiting for an excuse” to declare, in the event of a conflict, that “we are not going to die for Poland, we are not going to die for Latvia or Lithuania.”
The warning came as Tusk said the coming fall and winter months could prove “tragically critical” for Ukraine, with Russia expected to carry out continuous, high-intensity strikes on major Ukrainian cities while targeting warehouses, rail infrastructure and other logistics essential to the country’s defense.
Such attacks have intensified in recent weeks, also covering western Ukraine close to the Polish border, as Russia has increased its use of jet-powered drones that Ukraine has struggled to intercept.

articles.title: US intelligence warns of China spying risk in Saudi F-35 sale: Report
articles.body:
Berk Kutay Gokmen
17 September 2026•Update: 17 September 2026
US intelligence officials have warned that a proposed $24 billion sale of F-35 fighter jets to Saudi Arabia could expose sensitive technology to China, The New York Times reported Wednesday.
Analysts said China could gain access to the technology through espionage in Saudi Arabia or its military and security cooperation with the kingdom, the newspaper reported, citing US officials.
An assessment prepared by the Pentagon’s Defense Intelligence Agency several months ago examined China’s military access to Saudi bases and Riyadh’s use of Chinese technology in its telecommunications infrastructure, a US official told the newspaper.
The assessment also questioned whether Washington and Riyadh could maintain secure facilities to protect sensitive F-35 technology, the report said.
It has been shared with several US administration agencies and congressional offices, alongside analyses from other intelligence agencies, according to the newspaper.
The Defense Intelligence Agency issued a broader assessment outlining similar concerns in fall 2025, when the administration was considering the potential sale of dozens of the jets to Saudi Arabia, The New York Times previously reported.

articles.title: Ukraine Drones Make Orchestrating Russia’s Elections Tougher
articles.body:
Kremlin-orchestrated voting in the Russian Black Sea resort city of Sochi on Friday was halted, and voters and officials were ordered to head underground or into concrete bunkers following a regional alert warning of possible Ukrainian drone strikes.
Sochi Mayor Andrey Proshunin, in a statement published on his official Telegram channel, ordered election commission members, observers, and voters present at the polling stations to move to shelters and stay there until an all-clear, before ballot-casting might continue.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Please observe safety precautions; the threat is currently being countered. Polling stations will resume operations as soon as it is safe to do so,” Proshunin said.
Air defenses were tracking and attempting to engage Ukrainian drones operating in regional airspace, and all citizens should remain calm, he said.
According to unconfirmed reports in local media, on Friday at least one Ukrainian drone struck and damaged a Sochi voting site, blowing out windows and breaking up fixtures and furniture inside a public building.
Authorities moved the polling station “to a reserve site,” and ballot-casting would continue once polling sites re-opened, Ella Pamfilova, Chairperson of the Central Election Commission, said in a briefing as reported by the news platform BFM.RU.
Russian national elections taking place between Sept. 18-20 will select representatives for all 450 seats in the State Duma, the lower house of parliament. Regional governors and legislature members will also be determined by around 111 million eligible voters.
Slovakia’s Fico Pours Cold Water on Fulfilling NATO’s Article 5 Mutual Defense
On Wednesday, on the eve of polls’ opening, a Ukrainian drone struck and killed Elena Astanina, a Ukrainian citizen collaborating with Russian occupation authorities in the Ukrainian city of Tokmak in southern Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region, pro-Russia news sites reported.
Astanina had served as a Russian election council member since 2022 and was attacked by a drone while helping prepare a voting site, the news magazine Zhivaya Kuban reported.
The independent Russian news agency SOTA, and later Kremlin state media TASS, confirmed the strike and Astanina’s death. A statement from Zaporizhzhia region occupation authority chief Sergei Obertas praised Astanina as a Russian patriot and said the state would assist her family.
Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova on Thursday said that Ukraine was launching drone strikes with the intent of undermining “democratic elections” in her country, and spun the Ukrainian strike on Astanina as a terrorist attack against a peaceful Russian citizen.
In occupied districts of Ukraine’s southern Kherson region, voting was proceeding as planned on Friday, according to Ukrainian news agencies, but officials were using paper records to conduct voting and track ballots after Ukrainian drone strikes targeting electric transformers in the region cut off power.
A statement from the Russia-run local power utility Khersonenergo confirmed the loss of electricity deliveries to some 150,000 customers, but blamed the outage on “a technical problem.”
Russia’s defense ministry on Friday morning claimed its forces had shot down 629 Ukrainian drones in Russian airspace, making the night’s raids by shootdown claims one of the four or five most massive drone attacks of the entire Russo-Ukrainian War.
Ukrainian military sources and independent media said that the night’s attacks targeted port facilities in the city of Taganrog on the Azov Sea, and a nearby military airfield in Rostov-on-Don. Both air raids were follow-up attacks, with dozens of Ukrainian aircraft having hit and damaged a Taganrog aerospace factory and megawarehouse on Tuesday, and a power substation and military airfield near Rostov on Thursday.
Some Ukrainian drone sorties have reached 3,000 km (1,250 miles) deep into Russia, with massed drone attacks usually targeting Russian Federation military- or energy-linked infrastructure. Although initially scoffed at by authorities as pinpricks mighty Russia might ignore, actual or threatened Ukrainian drone attacks are now taken more seriously by local officials.
On the first day of national elections, which the Kremlin traditionally has used to pump up patriotism and state-manage an image of a stable and prosperous Russia under President Vladimir Putin’s leadership, Russia’s Central Election Commission published instructions to election officials about what to do if Ukrainian kamikaze aircraft seemed en route and potentially able to disrupt the voting process, a major Russian daily reported.
Officials at a voting site forced to shut down because of a potential or actual Ukrainian drone attack should turn over voter registers, voting boxes, and ballots to the election site boss for storage in a safe, while police and emergency response officials would supervise the orderly evacuation of the voting site, official step-by-step procedures at a voting site in the Volga region city of Kazan mandated, according to a Friday BiznesOnline report.
A policeman stationed by the safe until an all-clear was called would ensure a fair poll without fraud, the article says.
Although more than 1,200 km (750 miles) from probable Ukrainian launch sites, industrial sites in Kazan have been regularly hit by Ukrainian drones for more than a year. Probably the most frequently attacked facility has been the Nizhnekamsk oil refinery, which Ukrainian drones have hit at least seven times since November 2025, Kyiv Post’s records show.
United Russia, the ruling party backed by Putin, is widely expected to retain its dominant position and supermajority thanks to state-controlled media and state repression of opposition parties.
Sochi, with a permanent population of over 500,000 that rises to more than 3 million during the high season, is Russia’s wealthiest and most exclusive beach resort. Putin’s luxurious 40-hectare Bocharov Ruchei summer home, with a helipad, yacht mooring, tennis courts, orchards and fresh and seawater swimming pools, sits in Sochi’s elite northern district.
Ukraine, since launching a long-range drone bombardment of Russia in mid-2025, has hit port, oil refining and fuel storage structures around greater Sochi at least 10 times, but never attacked Putin’s residence, Kyiv Post’s strike records show.
The most recent confirmed Ukrainian attack in Sochi’s vicinity took place on Sept. 14, with at least four drones destroying an advanced Russian S-400 air defense system deployed to protect the city and Bocharev Ruchei from Ukrainian air strikes, those records show.

articles.title: Russians vote in election that Putin sees as barometer of public support for his war in Ukraine
articles.body:
Russians began voting on Friday in a three-day parliamentary election which President Vladimir Putin has said will show that millions of people back his army fighting in Ukraine, even though most anti-war candidates were not allowed to run.
The State Duma election, the first since Russia launched its full-scale war in Ukraine in February 2022, is widely expected to see the ruling pro-Putin United Russia party retain its dominance in Russia's tightly controlled political system.
The result is likely to be held up by the Kremlin as evidence of widespread public support for Putin's policies and, in particular, for his prosecution of Europe's deadliest conflict since World War Two, now in its fifth year.
"Your choice, and your will, will once again demonstrate that millions of people stand behind our soldiers, that we are a united people bound together by shared values, historical memory, and love for our homeland, and that no one will succeed in dividing or intimidating us," Putin said in a televised address before the vote.
An advert on state TV urging people to vote showed Russian military commanders down the ages before cutting to soldiers holding up the national flag after winning a battle in Ukraine with the slogan: "Their voice is the voice of victory. Your vote is the strength of Russia!"
In another move to boost morale and support for fighting on until victory, bone fragments from the sword hand of a medieval Russian prince who won a famous victory over the Mongols were sent to the front in Ukraine in the run-up to the vote.
Voting in Moscow, Anatoliy Simonenko, 76, said he was sanguine about what might happen after the election amid speculation, repeatedly denied by the authorities, that a new wave of mobilization may be announced.
"There are some very grim predictions, and others that are more optimistic. I expect the outcome will likely fall somewhere in the middle. War is war. It entails expenses, defense spending, and cuts to various social benefits. Well, it’s necessary; there’s no getting around it," he told Reuters.
Another voter, who declined to give his name, said he believed the results were easy to rig and raised doubts about an electronic voting system being used in some parts of the country. The electoral commission has rejected such suggestions as false.
Candidates against Ukraine-Russia War have been excluded from Moscow's Duma election ballot
Most anti-war candidates were excluded from the ballot before voting across Russia's 11 time zones got underway, after the Supreme Court ruled last month that the liberal Yabloko party, which wants a ceasefire in Ukraine, had breached electoral rules, something it denied.
Some candidates from Yabloko, which has traditionally only got single-digit support in opinion polls, are still running in individual constituencies that account for half the 450 seats in the lower house of parliament.
In the run-up to the vote, Lev Shlosberg, a senior figure in the Yabloko party, was jailed for 11 years for comments about the war. Its deputy leader, Maxim Kruglov, was jailed for seven years on similar charges in June.
Discrediting the army or spreading what authorities regard as fake news is punishable with long jail terms.
Some opinion polls show public support for peace talks has risen to over 60%, and the Kremlin has repeatedly said that it is ready to resume such talks.
However, it has also made clear, as its troops push to take control of the rest of the Donetsk region in eastern Ukraine, that any settlement must leave it in full control of all of that territory and that it only wants a long-term deal, not a ceasefire.
Voting is taking place at a time when opinion polls show some Russians have become more anxious about how the conflict affects them.
The economy is also under strain, and the authorities are expected to use the vote to gauge the depth of society's war weariness as fuel shortages caused by Ukrainian drone strikes on oil refineries roil some parts of the country, and businesses grapple with drone attacks on their warehouses, high interest rates, a labor crunch and Western sanctions.
National unity vital amid Ukraine attempting to stir unrest, Kremlin claims
The Kremlin says national unity is vital because of what it says are increasingly dangerous efforts by Ukraine's intelligence services and other enemies to stir unrest inside Russia.
Initial and partial results are expected to begin trickling out on Sunday evening, and near-complete results to be available on Monday.

articles.title: India’s homegrown air defense system finds new buyers
articles.body:
- Former DRDO Chairman Samir Kamat said India has exported its Akash air defense missile system to Tajikistan and Turkmenistan.
- Armenia remains the only other confirmed foreign Akash buyer, having signed for the Mk 1S variant with deliveries starting in late 2024.
Former DRDO Chairman Samir Kamat said India has exported its Akash surface-to-air missile system to Tajikistan and Turkmenistan, extending New Delhi’s defense export reach into Central Asia for the first time.
The Akash is a medium-range air defense system built to intercept aircraft, helicopters, drones and cruise missiles. Bharat Dynamics Limited manufactures the missile, using radar and command-and-control systems developed by India’s Defence Research and Development Organisation. Kamat did not specify how many systems were delivered, their configuration, or the value of the deals.
His statement follows earlier reporting in August that said Turkmenistan and Tajikistan were negotiating purchases of the newer Akash Mk 1S variant but had not yet signed formal contracts. It is not clear whether the exports Kamat described represent those same deals reaching completion, or a separate delivery. Neither Indian officials nor the two Central Asian governments have released further detail.
Armenia was the first, and until now the only confirmed, foreign buyer of the Akash system, signing a deal for the Mk 1S variant and beginning deliveries in late 2024. That sale gave India a track record it has pointed to since in pitching the system elsewhere in the former Soviet space.
The Mk 1S upgrade adds an Indian-developed active radio-frequency seeker for terminal homing, on top of the command guidance the missile uses during its mid-course flight. That combination is meant to improve accuracy against maneuvering targets and make the missile harder to defeat with electronic jamming than the original, purely command-guided Akash. The system uses India’s Rajendra phased-array radar to track and engage multiple targets at once, a capability suited to defending fixed sites and stretches of border rather than a single point target.
Tajikistan and Turkmenistan currently rely mainly on older Soviet and Russian-made air defense equipment, including S-125, Kub, Buk and S-300 systems. Aging stockpiles and changing aerial threats have pushed both countries to look at diversifying their suppliers, a dynamic Armenia’s earlier purchase is seen as having encouraged elsewhere in the region. As with Armenia, where the initial missile sale was followed by additional purchases of Indian radar, artillery, rocket systems and vehicles, further Indian defense sales to Tajikistan and Turkmenistan could follow if the Akash purchases are confirmed.
The moves would add to a broader shift in Central Asia’s arms market, a region long dominated by Russian suppliers, toward a wider set of options that now includes India’s defense industry.

articles.title: Ukrainian air defense shoot down 69 of 93 enemy UAVs; hits recorded at 13 locations
articles.body:
Ukrainian defense forces shot down 69 out of 93 enemy drones overnight into Friday, though enemy aerial weapons struck 13 locations, the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported.
"According to preliminary data, as of 08:00, air defense systems shot down or suppressed 69 enemy UAVs—including Shahed and Gerbera types, other drone types, and three Banderol/Dan-T units," the message reads.
In total, overnight into September 18 (starting at 18:00 on September 17), the enemy launched an attack using 93 strike UAVs—including Shahed types (46 of which were jet-powered), Gerberas, Parodiya decoy drones, and Banderol/Dan-T units—from the following directions: Orel and Millerovo (Russian Federation), temporarily occupied Donetsk and Hvardeyske (temporarily occupied Autonomous Republic of Crimea), and the Sea of Azov.
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile troops, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of the Ukrainian defense forces.
Meanwhile, attacks from enemy aerial weapons were recorded at 13 locations, and debris from downed objects fell at three locations. Additionally, some enemy munitions failed to reach their targets; information regarding them is being clarified.
The attack is ongoing, and enemy UAVs remain in the airspace, the command added.

articles.title: Zelenskyy seeks drone deal, closer defense technology ties with Japan
articles.body:
Elena Teslova
17 September 2026•Update: 17 September 2026
Ukraine wants to expand defense technology cooperation with Japan, including through a proposed drone deal, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Thursday.
In an interview with Japanese broadcaster NHK, Zelenskyy said Japanese companies could benefit from Ukraine’s experience in maritime monitoring, reconnaissance, mine clearance, air defense and cybersecurity.
“We very much want to build military-technology cooperation between Ukraine and Japan,” he said, expressing interest in partnerships at both government and business levels.
More than 70% of Ukraine’s defense industry was in the private sector, he said, suggesting that closer defense ties could also boost bilateral trade. Any decisions on defense equipment would be up to Japan, he added.
Zelenskyy said cooperation could contribute to security in the Asia-Pacific region, warning that North Korea was gaining combat experience through its military involvement in Russia.
He alleged that Pyongyang had sent between 30,000 and 50,000 troops to Russia, where they had gained experience in modern warfare, including drone operations, that could later be applied elsewhere.
Turning to China, Zelenskyy accused Beijing of failing to use its influence over Moscow to help end the war.
“I don’t see China putting pressure on Russia to stop the war,” he said.
He described himself as “vexed” by China’s lack of political support for Ukraine and said Beijing was “a little bit more” on Russia’s side.
Zelenskyy said he had not personally seen Chinese-made missiles in Ukraine. While alleging that Chinese equipment and technology were reaching Russia, he clarified that he was not referring to direct Chinese weapons supplies.
China has said it is not a party to the conflict and has called for a political settlement.

articles.title: “Possible casualties” – Sārts warns of escalation of Russia’s hybrid war in Europe
articles.body:
As Russia intensifies its hybrid war in Europe, more serious attacks could be expected, according to Jānis Sārts, Director of the NATO Strategic Communications Centre of Excellence.
The expert said on X that reports of planned Russian attacks against European countries have once again appeared in foreign media in recent days.
The reports refer to hybrid attacks, something Latvian officials have also warned about. Sārts, however, believes that “hybrid attacks” is not the best description of what is happening.
In his view, the growing number of such reports most likely indicates that new intelligence has become available.
“As the hybrid war in Europe is already underway, this signals Russia’s decision to intensify it –
more serious attacks, possible casualties and less caution in carrying out attacks,”
he said.
According to Sārts, intelligence and security services apparently believe that efforts in recent months to deter Russia from such an escalation have been unsuccessful. Therefore, Europe must be prepared for such a development, he stressed.
Sārts said that if a larger attack takes place, the key factor determining what happens next will be how strong the collective response is and how painful it proves for Russia.
As previously reported, the number of Russian hybrid attacks against NATO member states has increased significantly, a senior Alliance official revealed in September.
More than 200 such incidents were recorded last year alone,
the official said, adding that this figure does not include routine cyberattacks. NATO headquarters itself faces thousands of cyberattacks every month.
The official said Russia is seeking to undermine political and practical support for Ukraine while preparing for possible further escalation. This includes spying on critical infrastructure and logistics chains, as well as pre-positioning malware in key industrial control systems.
NATO is particularly concerned about changes in the nature of the attacks, the official said, explaining that their “number is increasing, their severity is increasing, and the appetite for risk is increasing”.
NATO is seeking to strengthen deterrence through military measures and better protection of critical infrastructure.
The Alliance also plans to establish a critical energy infrastructure network to exchange security information with operators and support joint emergency exercises, counter-drone measures and cyber defence.
In particularly serious cases, NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander could ask member states to use offensive cyber capabilities, the official said.
Latvia’s Constitution Protection Bureau (SAB) told LETA in August that Russia currently does not pose a direct military threat to Latvia, although a number of indicators point to potential longer-term plans.
National Armed Forces (NBS) Commander Kaspars Pudāns has also said that Latvia currently faces no direct military threat. At the same time, the NBS is preparing for possible hybrid provocations by Russia.

articles.title: From ‘city of camels’ to Israel’s new dream: Beersheba reinventing itself under Mayor Danilovich
articles.body:
“When I was a child in Beersheba, between Beersheba and Tel Aviv it was like light-years,” the mayor told The Jerusalem Post. “They called us the city of camels, the end of the world, a desert city.”
Danilovich, born in Beersheba in 1971 and mayor since 2008, has spent much of his political life trying to dismantle that image. Today, the city has around 223,600 residents and some 30,000 students studying at its higher-education institutions. Ben-Gurion University of the Negev alone has around 20,000 students and says roughly a third of Israel’s engineers graduate from BGU.
Those numbers help explain why Danilovich’s enthusiastic outlook on his hometown suggests a place seen less as Israel’s periphery and more as a place where several of the country’s largest national projects are now converging.
The IDF began moving units into its new technological campus in Beersheba in May, next to the Gav-Yam Negev high-tech park and close to BGU. Around 8,000 soldiers and career officers are ultimately expected to serve there. Northeast of the city, the Intelligence Campus near Shoket Junction is being built for well over 10,000 Intelligence Directorate personnel.
Across the road from the university, Gav-Yam says some 2,500 engineers already work for around 70 companies at its Beersheba technology park. Nvidia, meanwhile, has been expanding its presence in the city, tripling its office space and planning to recruit hundreds of employees.
Beersheba’s tech ecosystem draws global companies
“The companies come by themselves,” Danilovich said. “They are not philanthropic. They are business companies. They come where it is worthwhile for them.”
He reeled off Microsoft, Dell, Nvidia, IBM and Deutsche Telekom before turning to the geography itself: the university, Soroka University Medical Center, the National Cyber Directorate, military technology units and defense companies, all clustered within a relatively small area.
“Show me another city – not in Israel, in the world – where in such a small radius there is such a concentration of knowledge,” he said.
That concentration is at the heart of what Danilovich repeatedly calls the “new Israeli dream.” The Negev accounts for around 60% of Israel’s territory and is home to roughly 1.5 million people. He argues that successive governments have allowed too much of the country’s population and economic activity to remain concentrated in the center, while neglecting the South's sheer size and potential.
“The Negev is not the problem of the State of Israel,” he told the Post. “The Negev can be the solution.”
Beersheba mayor looks to aliyah to reshape Israel’s periphery
Aliyah is central to that proposal. Danilovich wants Israel to set a national target of one million new immigrants over five to seven years, paired with housing incentives, employment, and community infrastructure intended to encourage many to settle in the Negev and Galilee.
Beersheba has precedent for immigration changing the character of the city. More than 60,000 immigrants from the former Soviet Union arrived during the great aliyah wave of the 1990s, bringing doctors, engineers, academics, and a substantial new Russian-speaking community to Beersheba. Danilovich points particularly to Soroka, where some of the young immigrant physicians who arrived then would later rise to head hospital departments.
“When did we become the Start-Up Nation?” Danilovich asked. “When the gates of the former Soviet Union opened.”
Since October 7, he has also framed his aliyah drive around the rise in antisemitism abroad, particularly in countries such as Britain, France and Canada. His complaint is that while Israel has mechanisms for absorbing newcomers, it lacks the kind of large-scale national plan that could take advantage of a major new wave of immigration if one materialized.
“Come home,” he said. “We will receive you with open arms.”
Another part of that thinking is already taking shape in Beersheba. JNF-USA is developing a $350 million World Zionist Village in the city, whose master plan was approved in 2025. The organization now expects it to open in 2029, with plans for educational programs, accommodation and a center intended to bring young Jews and community leaders from around the world to spend meaningful periods of time in Israel.
Danilovich hopes some will stay. He is almost as interested, however, in those who eventually return to London, Toronto, Johannesburg, Melbourne or elsewhere after a year spent in Beersheba.
“Maybe you will want to make aliyah,” he said. “And even if you don’t, you will go back... but you will be a good ambassador for the State of Israel.”
War leaves its mark on Beersheba’s growth
Beersheba’s development has taken place alongside a less welcome constant: war. Soroka, the main hospital serving southern Israel, took a direct hit from an Iranian ballistic missile on June 19, 2025. The government subsequently approved NIS 360 million toward reconstruction, while philanthropist Sylvan Adams pledged another $100 million.
For Danilovich, the cranes that will rise at Soroka are something he has been through before. He was in his mid-30s when he defeated veteran mayor Yaakov Turner in the November 2008 election, after already serving a decade as deputy mayor. Within weeks, Beersheba was under rocket fire from Gaza during Operation Cast Lead.
Since then, he has led the city through repeated rounds of fighting, each followed, in his memory, by the return of construction.
“After every round ended, I would see the cranes in Beersheba,” he recalled. “Suddenly we are building another neighborhood, suddenly the lake, suddenly the amphitheater, suddenly the high-tech park, suddenly the stadium. We don’t stop for a moment.”
The physical change is obvious to anyone who remembers the older city. Beersheba River Park occupies land where sewage, rubbish and industrial waste once lined the banks of Nahal Beersheba; the rehabilitation project now stretches for kilometers through the city.
From football stadium to high tech, Danilovich eyes the next stage
Danilovich has his own, rather less grandiose benchmark. A former amateur football player, he remembers Beersheba’s old stadium as so uninviting that women and children rarely attended, and even decent toilets were a problem.
Today, he can list the stadium alongside the high-tech park, university, cultural institutions and national park River Park when describing how far his hometown has traveled. Yet after nearly 18 years as mayor, he is wary of sounding satisfied.
“A mayor who is satisfied is not a serious mayor,” Danilovich told the Post. “A mayor should never be satisfied, because he always has to aspire to the next thing.”
Danilovich has received many offers over the years to make the move into national politics, including approaches from prime ministers and other political leaders. He said he turned them down.
“My mission for the State of Israel, for my people and for my country is here,” he said. “It is in the Negev.
“If we do not make it flourish, if we do not strengthen it, if we do not build it and make it attractive, if it does not become the new Israeli dream, the State of Israel will be in danger.”

articles.title: Poland’s prime minister says Russia is preparing ‘accidental’ drone and missile strikes on NATO countries that support Ukraine
articles.body:
Poland’s prime minister says Russia is preparing ‘accidental’ drone and missile strikes on NATO countries that support Ukraine
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk told parliament that Russia is planning “hybrid” strikes using missiles and drones against countries that support Ukraine.
Tusk cited intelligence assessments, the Reuters news agency reports. “There is a real risk that drones or other types of missiles may fly into the territory of one or more NATO countries on the eastern flank, even cause destruction,” he said.
“These potential strikes would be quote-unquote ‘accidental’ in nature, intended to paralyze or at least weaken the resolve of NATO states to invoke the relevant NATO provisions in the event of aggression against a member country,” Tusk said.
According to Tusk, these Russian attacks could coincide with “political changes in certain European countries granting power […] to those who, increasingly invoking noble slogans of peace, pacifism and needless casualties, will call for peace,” but which in fact call for ”the total capitulation of Ukraine.”
Drones have repeatedly entered the airspace of Estonia, Lithuania, and Latvia in recent months. Authorities in those countries said the drones were Ukrainian and had strayed into their airspace because of Russian electronic warfare.
NATO fighter jets shot down a drone that entered Lithuanian airspace overnight on September 15, the first time a drone has been destroyed in the country’s history. Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda later said the drone was Russian.
Russian forces also used drones to attack a gas station near the Yahodyn border crossing on the Polish–Ukrainian border and a passenger train on the Kyiv–Warsaw railway line overnight on September 13. Another train carrying Western politicians returning from Ukraine was traveling nearby when the drone struck. Tusk said the incident showed that “escalation by the Russian Federation is becoming a fact, and examples of it are getting closer and closer to our border.”
