articles.title: Scores killed as Houthis, Yemen govt, Saudi Arabia trade attacks
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Scores killed as Houthis, Yemen govt, Saudi Arabia trade attacks
Fresh fighting left scores of combattants dead in Yemen on Thursday, as Saudi Arabia reported its first death since hostilities flared anew and its Yemeni government allies sought to roll back the group's recent gains.
The sides have been locked in increasingly violent exchanges since Yemen's civil war roared back to life, with the Iran-backed Houthis launching a new offensive that saw them capture all of the country's Red Sea coast.
At least 23 government soldiers were killed over the previous 24 hours in missile and drone attacks by the group in two southwestern provinces, a government military official told AFP on Thursday.
Houthi military sources reported 40 fighters killed in Saudi airstrikes and fighting on the ground during the same period.
Earlier in the day, Saudi Arabia's civil defence agency reported the country's first fatality since the Houthis began targeting their territory as part of their revived campaign.
"The fall of shrapnel from a downed drone in Taif governorate resulted in one death, two injuries, and material damage to several buildings and vehicles," the agency said, in a statement posted on social media, adding that the person killed was a Yemeni national.
Images posted by Saudi state media showed windows in cars and shop fronts shattered by the shrapnel, with nearby buildings also damaged.
The incident came a day after Riyadh accused the Houthis of launching a "cowardly" thwarted drone attack targeting Islam's holy city of Mecca, a claim the group denied.
The EU voiced its "full solidarity" with Saudi Arabia as it condemned the recent Houthi strikes.
"We urge the Houthis to cease all military action," said a statement from EU foreign affairs spokesman Anouar El Anouni, adding "the targeting of civilians and civilian infrastructure is unacceptable".
Earlier in the day, the Houthis said "Saudi enemy warplanes targeted three telecommunications towers" in Taiz province, with one civilian killed and another injured in strikes on the town of Abs, Almasirah television said.
The Houthi-backed outlet later reported that "three children were killed and several Yemeni nationals were injured in strikes by the Saudi-backed mercenaries", a reference to the country's internationally-recognised government.
The Houthis have been reporting dozens of daily Saudi strikes since they launched their new offensive and seized control of strategic areas overlooking the Red Sea's Bab al-Mandab Strait from government forces.
With Iran already throttling the Strait of Hormuz since the outbreak of the wider Middle East war, their Yemeni allies' latest gains cement their hold on the other main shipping corridor for Gulf oil and gas.
The route had been especially important to Saudi Arabia, the world's top crude exporter, which had used a pipeline to bypass the Hormuz and send oil to the Red Sea, which links Europe and Asia via the Suez Canal.
In July, a fragile 2022 truce between the Houthis and the government fell apart after the group allowed an Iranian plane to land in the capital Sanaa in defiance of Riyadh's control over Yemeni airspace, setting off a spate of attacks.
They also announced a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia and began striking its ships and territory.
The conflict in the Arabian Peninsula's poorest country has forced more than 100,000 people to flee their homes, according to the United Nations.

articles.title: ‘You’re Eroding Trust’: What Trump Shifting Tens of Millions in Military Aid Means for U.S. Alliances
articles.body:
The Trump Administration announced this week that it plans to shift tens of millions in military aid from countries in Europe and the Middle East to nations in Latin America with right-leaning governments.
A State Department official confirms to TIME that the department notified Congress that $52 million in foreign military funding for Iraq, North Macedonia, Slovakia, and Tunisia will be diverted to Colombia, Ecuador, Panama, and Peru, and that the funds will be used to “combat narcoterrorism in our own backyard and help continue to secure the Panama Canal.” The department did not specify how much military funding the U.S. will continue to provide those Middle Eastern and European nations following the shift.
“The proposed reprogramming in the Western Hemisphere will reduce opportunities for adversaries to establish or sustain strategic footholds in our hemisphere,” the State Department official says.
The reallocation of military funding reflects a broader shift in the U.S.’s priorities when it comes to foreign policy. Since Trump’s return to office last year, his Administration has worked to buttress the U.S.'s presence in the Western Hemisphere in the name of curbing drug trafficking from Central and South America and squashing the influence of other nations, such as China, in the region.
The Trump Administration has also sought to recalibrate its foreign policy regarding the Middle East and Europe. A national security strategy laid out by the White House at the end of last year stated that the Administration intended to take a more hands-off approach to armed conflict in those regions and allow them to become more militarily self-reliant. The diversion of foreign military aid marks the latest in several moves Trump has made to cut U.S. troops and funding in Europe during his second term—though in the Middle East, his war in Iran has engaged the U.S. in months of conflict.
Experts warn that the shift in military funding—and the broader plans of realigning U.S. foreign policy it fits into—threatens to weaken the country’s alliances around the world over the long term.
“You're eroding silently, quietly, bit by bit, this trust in the United States,” Jim Townsend, who served as Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense for European and NATO Policy for eight years in the Obama Administration, tells TIME of the Administration diverting military funding from European and Middle Eastern countries. “And then when we need them to do something … well, you're turning to a weaker country because you have been pulling their assistance and all of these tools that we have to make them a stronger ally.”
And the Trump Administration’s increasing support for conservative-led nations in the Americas carries its own risks, contends Rebecca Bill Chavez, who served as the Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense for Western Hemisphere Affairs in the Obama Administration.
“U.S. security relations, these are some things you build over time, and if they start to become relationships only with particular governments rather than with countries, that's risky,” she says. “We have to show the region that we are a reliable partner. And one of the best ways to do this is to be consistent.”
How—and why—the Trump Administration is ramping up U.S. military involvement in the Western Hemisphere
During Trump’s second term his Administration has increased military funding to Latin American countries, as well as boosting the U.S.’s own military presence in the region.
The U.S. has also conducted a number of military operations in the region since Trump returned to the White House, including a series of lethal attacks on what federal officials claimed were vessels transporting narcotics to the U.S. from the Caribbean that have drawn blowback from lawmakers on both sides of the aisle in Washington. The Trump Administration has also partnered with Ecuador for a joint military operation targeting “narco-terrorists” in the South American country, while announcing plans for further campaigns of the same kind in other nations in the region.
And in January, the U.S. launched a military operation in Venezuela that resulted in the capture of the country’s then-leader Nicolas Maduro, who had previously been indicted in the U.S. on charges of drug trafficking and corruption. After the operation, Trump pledged that “American dominance in the Western Hemisphere will never be questioned again.”
These moves reflect what the President has referred to as the “Trump Corollary” to the Monroe Doctrine or, later, as the “Donroe Doctrine,” a revival of a 19th century foreign policy framework first articulated by former President James Monroe that was used to justify assertions of U.S. military and economic control in Latin America.
“Reinvigorated by my Trump Corollary, the Monroe Doctrine is alive and well—and American leadership is coming roaring back stronger than ever before,” Trump said in a December proclamation.
A national security strategy released by the White House in November detailed that “Trump Corollary” in effect as an assertion that the U.S. must be “preeminent in the Western Hemisphere … a condition that allows us to assert ourselves confidently where and when we need to in the region.”
“We want to ensure that the Western Hemisphere remains reasonably stable and well-governed enough to prevent and discourage mass migration to the United States; we want a Hemisphere whose governments cooperate with us against narco-terrorists, cartels, and other transnational criminal organizations; we want a Hemisphere that remains free of hostile foreign incursion or ownership of key assets, and that supports critical supply chains; and we want to ensure our continued access to key strategic locations,” the strategy document reads.
The strategy described the Administration’s plans to back like-minded leaders in the Western Hemisphere as well, stating that it would “reward and encourage the region’s governments, political parties, and movements broadly aligned with our principles and strategy.”
Experts warn about the potential consequences of shifting military aid
Townsend warns that reducing military funding for European and Middle Eastern countries will weaken their ability to collaborate with and support the U.S.
“It creates allies who are not as strong as they could have been,” Townsend says. “It creates allies who are not as helpful as they could have been, and they're creating allies that are not as integrated and as pro-U.S. as they could have been.”
This is especially true, he asserts, for members of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO), which include North Macedonia and Slovakia. Trump has repeatedly clashed with the U.S.’s NATO allies during his second term, going so far as to threaten to pull out of the military pact after several other member countries declined to help the U.S. in its ongoing war against Iran.
Foreign military financing (FMF) allows other governments to purchase U.S. military equipment and carry out military trainings in tandem with the U.S. Without it, countries may be left unable to purchase key defensive equipment, such as drones or aircrafts, Townsend explains, which in turn weakens U.S. military alliances in the region.
Chavez meanwhile tells TIME that many Latin America nations could benefit greatly from U.S. military support, but argues that selecting who receives that support based on political ideology isn’t sustainable for U.S. relations in the region.
“All of this raises the question whether U.S. security assistance is increasingly being tied to the political orientation of a president rather than to long-term relationships with countries and institutions, and there's a risk there,” Chavez says.
Townsend contends that there is also risk in supplying military equipment to Latin American governments which could use it for ill.
“In the past, the trouble has come when we've been feeding money to a regime that ends up killing the opposition,” he says. “It's been a very spotty record in terms of assistance that we give to countries in the Caribbean or in Central America, Latin America, where this money ends up going to the wrong people.”

articles.title: Trump says 'major progress' made towards US military base in Poland
articles.body:
Trump says 'major progress' made towards US military base in Poland
US President Donald Trump said that Washington and Warsaw were making "major progress" towards establishing a US military base in Poland, potentially giving the United States a permanent military foothold on NATO's eastern flank even as his administration reviews its broader troop presence in Europe.
US President Donald Trump said Thursday there had been "major progress" towards establishing an American military base in Poland, after Warsaw said it was holding talks with Washington on the issue.
"Thanks to the bold leadership of my friend, Karol Nawrocki, President of Poland, major progress is being made towards establishing a US Army base in Poland," Trump said on social media.
"If this happens, the location will be announced very soon. This will be a historic step for our Great US/Polish Alliance."
Trump's announcement comes despite his administration launching a formal review of its military presence in Europe, raising fears among allies that it could cut back its forces in European nations.
But Poland, which borders both Ukraine and Russia on NATO's eastern flank and spends around five percent of its GDP on defense, is working to strengthen the US presence on its soil.
"We are ready to continue our efforts to strengthen our defence cooperation: seriously, responsibly, and always together," Nawrocki said on X.
"I can assure you that the Polish government will do its utmost to provide the best possible location for the US Army base."
Nawrocki is a conservative ally of Trump, and he visited the White House last year. During that visit Trump offered to send more US troops to Poland.
Polish deputy defence minister Pawel Zalewski said in August that his country was discussing with the United States whether to set up a permanent US base on its territory.
"We have already completed the initial stage (of the process), not to mention the political will, which was expressed long ago," Zalewski told public broadcaster TVP.
Almost 10,000 US soldiers are currently stationed in Poland – which is also an EU member state – but almost exclusively on a rotational basis.
Washington has levied heavy criticism against a number of European countries that refused to allow US forces to use NATO bases on their territory in their war with Iran.
US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth had also threatened to reduce his country's contribution to the alliance's budget if certain states refused to honour the commitments made last year at the NATO summit in The Hague.
At that summit, NATO allies pledged to devote by 2035 at least five percent of their GDP to security spending, including 3.5 percent devoted strictly to military expenditures.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

articles.title: Lithuania's foreign minister confirms Polish intel on Russia preparing hybrid attacks against Ukraine's allies
articles.body:
Lithuania's foreign minister confirms Polish intel on Russia preparing hybrid attacks against Ukraine's allies
Kęstutis Budrys, Minister of Foreign Affairs of Lithuania, has confirmed that his country also possesses intelligence about Russia preparing hybrid attacks against Ukraine's allies after a similar warning from Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk.
Source: European Pravda, citing Baltic states news website Delfi
Details: Budrys' comment concerned a recent statement by Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, who warned of Russian "plans for hybrid attacks using drones and missiles against countries supporting Ukraine, particularly Poland".
As the minister noted, public warnings from politicians regarding the threat are part of coordinated campaigns aimed at discouraging Moscow from staging provocations.
Quote: "I want to assure everyone that Lithuania has the same intelligence information as other countries in the region and countries that have deployed their troops here. There is no other information."
Details: According to the minister, he discussed this topic with the NATO secretary general, his deputy, and commanders of the armed forces of European countries. "I wanted to make sure we were talking about the same thing. The news is this – yes, we are talking about the exact same thing. Lithuania has the same information; we discussed this as a potential false-flag operation by Russia," Budrys stressed.
Background:
- Prior to this, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk claimed that intelligence data indicates Russian "plans for hybrid attacks" against countries supporting Ukraine.

articles.title: US intervention in Yemen 'off the table' despite Saudi pressure
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
US intervention in Yemen war 'off the table' despite Saudi pressure
Saudi Arabia has been pressing the United States to intervene against the Houthis after the Iran-backed group seized Yemen's Red Sea coast and the strategic Bab al-Mandeb Strait, but Washington appears reluctant to enter the conflict.
American military intervention in Yemen is "completely off the table" before November's US midterm elections, a senior Yemeni researcher has told The New Arab, despite Riyadh's calls for military assistance to halt the Houthi advance.
Abdulghani al-Iryani, a senior researcher at the Sanaa Centre, told TNA that unless Iran and the Houthis dramatically escalate the situation, President Donald Trump is likely to stay out of the conflict in a bid to limit potential electoral damage for the Republican Party.
"I don't see a reason for the Republicans to give up their electoral chances for the sake of the Saudis," he said.
His comments come as American and Houthi officials held Oman-mediated talks over the weekend, during which US officials reportedly assured the group they would not intervene in the Yemen conflict.
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman reportedly urged President Trump to launch airstrikes against the Iran-backed group, which seized control of the strategic Bab al-Mandeb Strait on the Red Sea last week.
But sources say the Trump administration reached an understanding with the Houthis that Washington would stay out of the conflict even as the group attacks Saudi energy infrastructure and targets its ships in the Red Sea.
The Oman-mediated discussions saw the Houthis assure US officials that they would not target American ships and would uphold the 2025 ceasefire, according to Reuters.
A Yemeni source said Houthi officials also committed not to attack Israeli vessels or commercial ships that are not linked to Saudi Arabia.
The discussions, held at the US embassy in Muscat, involved senior Houthi officials Mohammad Abdulsalam and Abdelmalik al-Ajiri, sources said.
The Trump administration designated the Houthis as a foreign terrorist organisation in March 2025 before launching a two-month bombing campaign against them to halt their attacks on Red Sea shipping. That conflict ended after the two sides negotiated a ceasefire brokered by Oman.
The Houthis and the Yemeni government have engaged in fierce fighting since the collapse of the ceasefire in July.
The group has declared a blockade on Saudi ports and targeted Saudi ships in the Red Sea. It has also struck several Saudi energy sites, including oil refineries and pipelines.
The Houthis last week captured Yemen's entire Red Sea coastline, including the historic port of Mokha and Mayyun Island in the Bab al-Mandeb.
Since taking control of the area, the group has said it would uphold freedom of navigation through the strait but would continue to enforce its blockade on Saudi Arabia.
Few military options
Trump's refusal to intervene comes as the Houthis and their allies in Iraq attempt to shut down Saudi oil exports. Shipments via the Red Sea have been completely cut off after a drone strike last week took the East-West pipeline offline. The kingdom is now reliant exclusively on covert shipments via the Strait of Hormuz, assisted by the US military.
Saudi Arabia has escalated airstrikes against the Houthis in the week since they captured the Red Sea coast. The Houthis have reported more than 450 strikes as Riyadh tries to help government forces retake the area.
But analysts say Saudi Arabia's military options are limited. Airstrikes have done little to weaken the Houthis since Riyadh first launched its air campaign more than a decade ago, and it is hesitant to deploy ground troops inside the country.
Other allies have followed the US in declining to get involved in the conflict. Turkey and Pakistan have shown no willingness to intervene despite the three countries signing a mutual defence pact last month. Egypt's President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi is also unlikely to weigh in after discussing the situation with bin Salman in Cairo this week.
"I don't think Saudi military escalation will help the Yemeni cause or the Saudi cause," Al-Iryani told The New Arab.
"The best bet for Saudi Arabia is to try to help the government hold its ground until the US-Iran war is over, when it will be in a better position to negotiate with the Houthis," he said.

But sources say the Trump administration reached an understanding with the Houthis that Washington would stay out of the conflict even as the group attacks Saudi energy infrastructure and targets its ships in the Red Sea.
The Oman-mediated discussions saw the Houthis assure US officials that they would not target American ships and would uphold the 2025 ceasefire, according to Reuters.
A Yemeni source said Houthi officials also committed not to attack Israeli vessels or commercial ships that are not linked to Saudi Arabia.
The discussions, held at the US embassy in Muscat, involved senior Houthi officials Mohammad Abdulsalam and Abdelmalik al-Ajiri, sources said.
The Trump administration designated the Houthis as a foreign terrorist organisation in March 2025 before launching a two-month bombing campaign against them to halt their attacks on Red Sea shipping. That conflict ended after the two sides negotiated a ceasefire brokered by Oman.
The Houthis and the Yemeni government have engaged in fierce fighting since the collapse of the ceasefire in July.
The group has declared a blockade on Saudi ports and targeted Saudi ships in the Red Sea. It has also struck several Saudi energy sites, including oil refineries and pipelines.
The Houthis last week captured Yemen's entire Red Sea coastline, including the historic port of Mokha and Mayyun Island in the Bab al-Mandeb.
Since taking control of the area, the group has said it would uphold freedom of navigation through the strait but would continue to enforce its blockade on Saudi Arabia.
Few military options
Trump's refusal to intervene comes as the Houthis and their allies in Iraq attempt to shut down Saudi oil exports. Shipments via the Red Sea have been completely cut off after a drone strike last week took the East-West pipeline offline. The kingdom is now reliant exclusively on covert shipments via the Strait of Hormuz, assisted by the US military.
Saudi Arabia has escalated airstrikes against the Houthis in the week since they captured the Red Sea coast. The Houthis have reported more than 450 strikes as Riyadh tries to help government forces retake the area.
But analysts say Saudi Arabia's military options are limited. Airstrikes have done little to weaken the Houthis since Riyadh first launched its air campaign more than a decade ago, and it is hesitant to deploy ground troops inside the country.
Other allies have followed the US in declining to get involved in the conflict. Turkey and Pakistan have shown no willingness to intervene despite the three countries signing a mutual defence pact last month. Egypt's President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi is also unlikely to weigh in after discussing the situation with bin Salman in Cairo this week.
"I don't think Saudi military escalation will help the Yemeni cause or the Saudi cause," Al-Iryani told The New Arab.
"The best bet for Saudi Arabia is to try to help the government hold its ground until the US-Iran war is over, when it will be in a better position to negotiate with the Houthis," he said.

articles.title: Russia launched 93 drones at Ukraine, 72 of which were neutralized by air defense

Russia launched 93 drones at Ukraine, 72 of which were neutralized by air defense

articles.title: EU to disburse $3.8B for missiles and drones to Ukraine: Von der Leyen
articles.body:
Ayhan Şimşek
18 September 2026•Update: 18 September 2026
The European Union will disburse €3.3 billion ($3.8 billion) to Ukraine for missiles and drones, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Thursday after a phone call with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
“Tomorrow, we will disburse another €3.3 billion to Ukraine,” von der Leyen said in an official readout of the call.
She said the payment comes as Russian strikes continue to hit the Ukrainian capital.
“Russia is relentlessly targeting Kyiv, trying to make daily life impossible for its inhabitants,” she said. “We stand with them. And with all Ukrainians.”
The funds are part of the €28.3 billion set aside for Ukraine’s defense this year under the EU’s Ukraine Support Loan.
Von der Leyen said the bloc last week approved EU funding for Patriot systems through the same loan, a step that also opened the way for Ukraine to buy US-made Patriot interceptors used against ballistic missiles.
“But clearly more is needed,” she said.
She said Brussels was ready to use remaining funds from SAFE — Security Action for Europe, the EU’s defense financing instrument for member-state investment and joint purchases — to start a new program for joint EU-Ukraine defense projects.
“We want to develop together a European air and missile defense system, building on our joint anti-ballistic Freya system,” said von der Leyen, “so that we can combine Ukraine’s battlefield experience and innovation with Europe’s technology and industrial strength.”

articles.title: US clears way for $24.3 billion fighter jet sale to Saudi Arabia
articles.body:
US clears way for $30.9 billion fighter jet sale to Saudi Arabia
WASHINGTON - The US Department of State said on Sept 17 it has approved the potential sale of Lockheed Martin’s F-35 Lightning II fighter jets to Saudi Arabia, as the kingdom is drawn deeper into war in the Middle East.
A sale would mark a significant policy shift from the US, potentially altering the balance of military power in the Middle East and testing Washington’s definition of maintaining its ally Israel’s “qualitative military edge.”
Saudi Arabia made a direct appeal for the jets in early 2025 to US President Donald Trump and has long been interested in Lockheed Martin’s fighter.
The estimated US$24.3 billion (S$30.9 billion) sale would include 48 of the military aircraft and 49 Pratt & Whitney engines along with communications equipment, spare parts and other support items, the State Department said.
Washington weighs weapons sales to the Middle East in a way that ensures Israel maintains a “qualitative military edge”, effectively guaranteeing that Israel gets more advanced US weapons than regional Arab states.
The Saudi embassy in Washington welcomed the proposed sale, describing it as a further step in defence cooperation between the two countries.
“The proposed F-35 sale reflects the strength and enduring nature of the Saudi-US strategic partnership and the continued advancement of our defence cooperation,” the embassy said on X.
The F-35, built with stealth technology that allows it to evade enemy detection, is considered the world’s most advanced fighter jet.
Israel has operated the aircraft for a decade, building multiple squadrons, and remains the only Middle Eastern country to possess the weapons system.
Saudi Arabia, the largest customer for US arms, has sought the fighter for years as it looks to modernise its air force and counter regional threats, particularly from Iran.
The kingdom’s renewed push for what would constitute two squadrons comes as the Trump administration has signalled openness to deepening defence cooperation with Riyadh.
The Saudi Air Force flies a mix of fighter aircraft including Boeing F-15s, European Tornados and Typhoons.
The F-35 issue has also been intertwined with broader diplomatic efforts.
The administration of former US President Joe Biden previously explored providing F-35s to Saudi Arabia as part of a comprehensive deal that would have included Riyadh normalising relations with Israel, though those efforts ultimately stalled.
Trump has made arms sales to Saudi Arabia a priority since returning to office.
In 2025, the United States agreed to sell the kingdom an arms package worth nearly US$142 billion, which the White House called “the largest defence cooperation agreement” Washington has ever done.
Congressional scrutiny could pose challenges to any F-35 sale.
Lawmakers previously questioned arms deals with Riyadh following the 2018 murder of Saudi journalist Jamal Khashoggi, and some members of Congress remain wary of deepening military cooperation with the kingdom.
Saudi Arabia is pursuing ambitious economic and military modernisation plans under Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s Vision 2030 agenda.
The kingdom has sought to diversify its defence partnerships in recent years while maintaining its decades-long security relationship with Washington. REUTERS

articles.title: US approves sale of 48 F-35 jets to Saudi Arabia
articles.body:
(AFP Photo)
The United States has approved a $24.3 billion sale of 48 F-35 stealth warplanes to Saudi Arabia, the State Department said on Sept. 17, the kingdom’s latest major arms purchase since the start of the Iran war.
Saudi Arabia has long sought to buy F-35s, but officials from Israel, currently the only country in the Middle East to operate the jets, has voiced concern about their sale to Riyadh despite a push for the kingdom to normalize relations.
“The proposed sale will improve Saudi Arabia’s capability to deter current and future threats by strengthening its homeland defense, and improving interoperability with U.S. forces,” the State Department said in a statement.
It “will also augment Saudi Arabia’s operational aircraft and enhance its air-to-air, and air-to-ground self-defense capability,” the statement said.
The Saudi embassy in Washington praised the transaction, saying it “reflects the strength and enduring nature” of the relationship with the United States.
It added that the security cooperation between the two countries “has contributed to regional stability, strengthened our collective defense capabilities, and advanced our shared security interests.”
Saudi Arabia has been repeatedly targeted with drone and missile strikes by Tehran’s forces since the United States and Israel launched their war against Iran in February, and has also been hit by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels.
The State Department has notified Congress about the proposed sale, which would require the approval of US lawmakers. It did not provide a time frame for the delivery of the jets.
The F-35 sale “will not alter the military balance in the region,” the State Department said, in keeping with longstanding U.S. policy that Israel must have a military edge over potential regional adversaries.

articles.title: NATO drills new layered air defence over Romania
articles.body:
NATO has carried out a multinational air and missile defence exercise over Romania as the Alliance shifts from traditional air policing towards a broader system designed to counter aircraft, drones and cruise and ballistic missiles, according to Allied Air Command.
The Flexible Deterrent Option training on 9 September brought together fighter and tanker aircraft from France, Greece, Romania, Spain and Türkiye, alongside NATO Airborne Warning and Control System aircraft and a tanker from the Multinational MRTT Unit.
The main focus was Integrated Air and Missile Defence, with the participating forces also conducting Close Air Support training with Romanian ground forces. Aircraft taking part included French Rafales, Romanian and Greek F-16 Fighting Falcons, Spanish F/A-18 Hornets and Turkish F-16s. Spain also deployed an A400M Atlas tanker, while Turkey contributed a KC-135 Stratotanker.
NATO said the activity formed part of a wider move away from an Air Policing framework primarily concerned with safeguarding Alliance airspace against aircraft and uncrewed systems, towards a multi-layered air defence posture capable of dealing with a wider range of threats.
The new framework is intended to cover threats including conventional aircraft, uncrewed aerial systems, cruise missiles and ballistic missiles, using sensors, command-and-control systems, fighters and other capabilities as parts of a single integrated network.
Spanish Lieutenant Colonel Alberto B. Calvo López, commander of the Spanish detachment conducting NATO Air Defence duties at Mihail Kogălniceanu Air Base, said: “The evolving threat also reminds us of the importance of collective, layered air defence, in which sensors, command and control systems, fighters and other Allied capabilities must be able to operate as a single, integrated system.”
The exercise used a “Red” versus “Blue” scenario focused on Integrated Air and Missile Defence.
NATO AWACS aircraft acted as the principal command-and-control element for the “Red” force, directing tanker aircraft and coordinating with Romanian forces on the ground. The training was designed to test how airborne and ground-based systems could be brought together in real time, with information shared between participants and command procedures rehearsed against a simulated air threat.
NATO’s Combined Air Operations Centre at Torrejón in Spain oversaw the activity, providing operational-level command and control while coordinating aircraft and supporting capabilities across the exercise. AIRCOM said the new Air Defence framework brings the Alliance’s air and missile defence activities under common rules, guidelines and command procedures regardless of the type of threat being faced.
The intention is to give NATO commanders greater flexibility to move and combine forces supplied by different member states, synchronising sensors, aircraft and other assets across several domains. The Romanian exercise was also intended to test how quickly allied forces could be assembled and integrated under a Flexible Deterrent Option, with those activities used to rehearse collective defence arrangements before they might be required during a crisis.

articles.title: Ukrspecsystems equips the RAM-2X drone with terminal guidance system with target lock up to 3 km – photo
articles.body:
Ukrspecsystems equips the RAM-2X drone with terminal guidance system with target lock up to 3 km – photo
The Ukrainian RAM-2X drone by Ukrspecsystems has been equipped with a terminal guidance system that allows it to complete an attack independently after locking onto a target.
Source: Andrii Rymaruk, Deputy Director of Ukrspecsystems, in an interview with Defender Media.
Quote: "If the pilot locks onto a target at a distance of up to 3 km, presses the 'Attack' button and then loses communications, the system will automatically engage the target. Once it has locked onto a target, it will not let go, even if the target is moving."
Details: Furthermore, visual navigation was implemented in the RAM-2X, allowing the drone to navigate through space without a GNSS satellite signal. According to Rymaruk, this makes it less dependent on the impact of electronic warfare assets.
"The system positions itself in space, making the operator's job easier," he noted.
Ukrspecsystems is also working on a fully autonomous version of the RAM-2X, which they plan to release by the end of 2026.
Quote: "The crew will no longer have to be involved in every second of the flight: reconnaissance identifies a target, passes on its coordinates, and the aircraft sets off on an autonomous hunt."
Details: It is noted that the RAM-2X has been used by the defence forces of Ukraine since 2024.
According to Rymaruk, around a hundred units of the defence forces currently use the RAM-2X. With the help of these drones, an average of 50 to 60 units of Russian equipment are struck per month.
Background:
- Earlier, Ukrainska Pravda reported that Ukrspecsystems had publicly presented the RAM-2X at the MSPO 2026 defence exhibition in Poland. The drone is designed to strike high-value targets at distances of up to 180 km, can remain airborne for over two hours, and carry a warhead weighing 2.7 or 3.5 kg.
- The RAM-2X can also work in conjunction with the SHARK-M reconnaissance drone, which provides target designation and acts as a relay. According to the manufacturer, RAM loitering munitions have already struck over 450 targets.

articles.title: West's toying with nuclear weapons causes particular concern — Russian MFA
articles.body:
MOSCOW, September 18. /TASS/. The Western countries' toying with nuclear weapons is a matter of particular concern, and the situation holds grim prospects, Vladislav Maslennikov, Director of the Russian Foreign Ministry's Department of European Cooperation and Russia's Senior Arctic Official, has told a news briefing.
"For decades, the Baltic Sea was a very stable, peaceful region. As soon as NATO decided to venture there – or rather, its member states decided they needed to strengthen their defense (in their view) in the Baltic (though it is, in fact, more of an offensive posture) – the Baltic ceased to be the peaceful and stable region it once was. Now, generally speaking, we are witnessing the beginning of that same process in the Arctic region," he noted.
"Against this backdrop, the attempts of our Western Arctic neighbors to toy with nuclear weaponry is a source of particular concern. A recent development adding to this picture – which is, let us say, grim rather than promising – was Finland joining the French nuclear deterrence initiative. This follows Helsinki's decision this summer to lift restrictions on the importation of nuclear weapons into the country, at least during peacetime," Maslennikov emphasized.
The senior diplomat added that Russia is the only country in the Arctic Council that is not a member of the NATO alliance.
"Such erosion of the non-proliferation policy and deliberate actions to further undermine it can only be described as utterly reckless and extremely dangerous. The European Union is creating additional obstacles to the development of the Russian Arctic and international cooperation in the North by adopting successive packages of sanctions that are illegitimate under international law," he noted.

articles.title: Israel will seek to purchase new weapons systems from US as compensation for Saudi F-35 sale
articles.body:
The United States informed the Prime Minister's Office that it intends to sell F-35 fighter jets to Saudi Arabia in a $25 billion deal, an Israeli official confirmed to Walla on Friday.
Israel is expected to seek "compensation" from Washington in the form of weapons systems that the US has so far declined to sell to Israel.
A source familiar with the details told Walla that the IDF would prefer that no other country in the Middle East receive the stealth fighter, in order to preserve Israel's qualitative operational advantage. However, the source stressed that even if the deal is signed soon, Saudi Arabia would receive its first aircraft only in five years.
Walla was also told that Israel continues to hold a clear operational advantage over other countries that have purchased the aircraft from the United States. That advantage stems not only from the extensive operational experience accumulated by the Israel Air Force and its pilots over the past three years, but also from Israeli-made weapons systems that Israel has received approval to integrate into its Adir aircraft, the Israeli version of the F-35.
Israel also operates an Adir test aircraft used to develop advanced capabilities for the fighter. The United States, for example, does not operate an aircraft of this type.
Another defense official sought to play down concerns, saying the Israel Air Force's advantage lies "not just in the machine, but mainly in the people."
Following the Saudi-US deal and the wider arms race in the Middle East, Israeli officials are already planning to approach negotiations with the US administration differently over future procurement deals.
Israel seeking to participate in production of classified weapons systems
Israeli officials will also seek participation in the development and production of classified weapons systems.
The IDF's focus is not limited to advanced fighter jets and the next generation of stealth aircraft. It also includes the development of space-based weapons and US participation in the development and production of interceptors for the Arrow 4 and Arrow 5 systems, which are intended to address future threats.
There are also advanced munitions that the United States has declined to sell to Israel. These include systems in the field of bunker-busting weapons, systems designed to operate underground deep inside rocky mountains, autonomous strike systems, and swarms of unmanned aerial vehicles.
Israel is currently struggling to finance a third F-15 squadron and additional F-35 squadrons.

articles.title: Russia kills captain of Tanzanian-flagged ship in latest attack on civilian shipping in Black Sea

Foreign vessels repeatedly targeted

Attacks threaten Ukraine’s maritime trade
The repeated attacks have also disrupted Ukraine’s maritime trade route.
In July, Russian strikes on civilian cargo ships brought traffic through the Black Sea corridor close to a standstill at the height of the harvest, with shipowners temporarily stopping vessels from entering Ukrainian ports.
The Ukrainian ministry called for an international response and coordinated action to strengthen the protection of civilian shipping and the security of international logistics routes.

articles.title: West seeking ‘pretext’ for major Russia-NATO war – Fico
articles.body:
NATO member warns bloc seeking pretext for war with Russia
Europe is moving dangerously close to a direct clash between NATO and Russia, Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico has warned, accusing the West of seeking a “pretext” for a major conflict between the two sides.
Fico made the comment in a Facebook post on Thursday, which accompanied the remarks he delivered before traveling to Ukraine for a meeting with Vladimir Zelensky and several European leaders.
“I am deeply concerned that they are merely looking for a pretext for a major conflict between NATO and Russia,” he wrote.
Reflecting on the Ukraine conflict, Fico said that the hostilities had “gotten out of control,” while accusing European nations of engaging in increasingly bellicose rhetoric which he said risked dragging the continent into a broader war. “The situation has never been as serious and tense regarding the possibility of a pan-European war conflict as it is now,” he said.
Fico also warned that Bratislava could face pressure from NATO to commit troops if the bloc’s Article 5 – a collective defense clause applied if a member state is attacked – is invoked. “Can anyone imagine being told to prepare 5,000 soldiers, 10,000 soldiers, and that they would go somewhere to fight? We don’t know with whom, why, or for what reason,” Fico said.
“I don’t want Slovakia to be part of any military conflict because of some Article 5,” he stressed, adding that, though his country still “cares about collaboration and fulfilling obligations”. “As prime minister, I will do everything to ensure that Slovakia is never drawn into a war,” Fico stressed.
Fico has consistently opposed military support for Ukraine since returning to office in 2023 while halting government weapons shipments to Kiev. He has also opposed Kiev’s accession to NATO, and insisted that Ukraine’s EU membership is only possible if it meets all the requirements.
He has also argued that the West’s strategy to “bring Russia to its knees” had “completely failed.” “The European Union does not need more weapons and Russophobia. The European Union needs more diplomacy and concrete plans to help the economy,” Fico said last month.
Russia has accused the EU of rapid militarization, with Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov saying the bloc is directing increasing military capabilities against Moscow while portraying it as an enemy.
President Vladimir Putin has consistently rejected claims that Moscow intends to attack NATO countries, but warned last week that deploying European forces to Ukraine “would mean war with Russia.” Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov also stressed that Russia has no intention of attacking the West but warned that if Europe attacked first, the resulting conflict would be “very short.”
