articles.title: Britain contracts drone-ship sensors to track air threats
articles.body:
Project HORUS, the Royal Navy effort to deploy persistent air-search sensors on uncrewed maritime platforms, is now under contract as the service moves ahead with a distributed system intended to detect and track airborne threats.
The status of the project was confirmed in a written parliamentary answer from Defence Readiness and Industry Minister Luke Pollard, following a question from Conservative MP Ben Obese-Jecty asking for the scope of the programme.
Pollard said: “Project HORUS is supporting urgent operational requirements for a rapidly procured, persistent air-search capability using uncrewed maritime platforms fitted with sensors to detect, track, identify and report airborne threats. The project is on contract and is intended to help the Royal Navy generate distributed sensing that reduces risk to personnel, and will inform future procurement decisions.”
The confirmation represents a step forward from the market-engagement stage reported by the UK Defence Journal in March, when the Navy was seeking mature systems that could be brought into service at pace. At that point, the requirement called for “a rapidly procured and persistent air search capability” able to detect, track, identify and report threats including drones, fast jets and cruise missiles from sensors carried aboard maritime platforms.
The original market notice envisaged moving rapidly from industry engagement to an initial capability. It stated that the intention was to select credible solutions, place contracts and deliver the first capability within four to six months, with an emphasis on mature products and suppliers able to work quickly.
HORUS is built around distributing sensors across multiple lower-cost uncrewed platforms rather than relying entirely on crewed ships or a small number of high-value assets.
The earlier requirement described a “System of System Approach” intended to introduce greater mass through numerous lower-cost sensors operating from uncrewed platforms in areas where sending personnel could carry greater risk. Persistence was also central to the concept. The March requirement sought platforms capable of remaining on station for 30 days as a threshold requirement and as long as 90 days as an objective, without in-person human intervention or maintenance.
The performance targets outlined during that earlier market engagement included the detection of NATO Class 2 uncrewed aircraft, anti-ship and land-attack cruise missiles and third and fourth-generation fighter-bombers at distances of at least 15 nautical miles.
Industry was also asked to consider how the system could eventually be expanded to detect surface threats, including fast attack craft and uncrewed vessels. The initial requirement envisaged persistent surveillance across an area of around 2,500 square kilometres, pointing towards several sensor-carrying platforms operating together rather than a single picket.
Alternative commercial approaches were also being considered, including what the Navy described as “SENSE as a service”, potentially allowing industry to provide the sensing effect rather than Defence purchasing every element outright.
Those figures and performance requirements were set out during the earlier market-engagement phase and do not necessarily describe the final contracted configuration. Pollard’s latest answer confirms, however, that HORUS has moved beyond that initial stage and is now on contract in support of an urgent operational requirement.

articles.title: Russia confirms rocket launch behind viral sky “jellyfish”
articles.body:
- Russia's Ministry of Defense confirmed on Sept. 18 that a Soyuz-2.1b rocket launched a classified satellite from Plesetsk the previous evening.
- The glowing shape that fueled online missile-launch claims was a documented "space jellyfish" effect caused by sunlight hitting the rocket's exhaust plume.
Social media users shared widespread footage Thursday evening of a glowing, tentacled shape in the night sky, with some posts claiming it showed a missile launched toward Ukraine. Within hours, astrophysicist and satellite tracker Jonathan McDowell offered a more mundane explanation, and Russia’s Ministry of Defense confirmed it the next day.
“Russia appears to have launched a Soyuz from Plesetsk at around 1650 UTC Sep 17, probably with another Glonass navigation satellite, but no official confirmation yet,” McDowell wrote on X on Thursday.
By Friday, Sept. 18, Russia’s Ministry of Defense released video of the launch, identifying the rocket as a Soyuz-2.1b lifting off from the Plesetsk Cosmodrome carrying a satellite for the ministry’s own use. The ministry did not name the satellite or describe its mission, following its usual practice of keeping military payload details classified.
The glowing shape that alarmed observers is a well-documented optical effect known as a “space jellyfish.” It happens when a rocket climbs high enough into the atmosphere to catch direct sunlight during evening or morning twilight, while observers on the ground remain in darkness. The rocket’s exhaust plume expands rapidly in the thin upper atmosphere, and the illuminated, billowing gas cloud can resemble a glowing jellyfish trailing tentacles across the sky. The same phenomenon has accompanied SpaceX Falcon 9 launches over Florida and California this year, as well as previous Soyuz launches from Russian and Kazakh spaceports.
Plesetsk, located in Russia’s Arkhangelsk region roughly 800 km (500 miles) north of Moscow, is the country’s primary military launch site and has hosted a steady stream of Soyuz-2.1b missions carrying Defense Ministry satellites throughout 2026, including launches in February and April. Those earlier missions were also witnessed and photographed across Finland and Scandinavia, consistent with the rocket’s typical flight path toward high-inclination orbits to the north. That trajectory runs opposite the direction claims about a strike on Ukraine would require, since Ukraine lies south of Plesetsk rather than along the rocket’s ascent path.
McDowell’s guess that the payload was another Glonass navigation satellite has not been confirmed by Russian officials, who described the cargo only in general terms as serving the Ministry of Defense’s interests. Russia has not disclosed the satellite’s orbit, designation, or intended function.

articles.title: Russians vote in elections with no party opposing Putin or war in Ukraine
articles.body:
The three-day vote will fill 450 Duma seats and 11 regional governorships, with only parties backing Putin and Russia's ongoing war in Ukraine on the ballot. Despite official denials of a new draft, fears of mobilisation are overshadowing the vote.
Russians began voting Friday in a tightly controlled three-day election that will likely see President Vladimir Putin tighten his grip on power after 26 years at the helm, as Russia's all-out war in Ukraine continues well into its fifth year.
Only parties backing Putin and his war in Ukraine are on the ballot: the ruling United Russia, the Communist Party, A Just Russia, the nationalist LDPR and New People.
Yabloko, Russia's only publicly anti-war party still operating inside the country, was barred from participating. The party saw a surge in social media support, particularly among young people, after it was initially allowed to stand.
An unnamed European diplomat said the elections were "pretty much a sham" but described them as "a ritual the Kremlin considers necessary," adding that it would seek to ensure a high turnout.
Independent observers have previously documented the use of state resources to influence results, including bussing voters to polling stations, pressuring employees of state institutions to vote for the ruling party, and pushing online voting as it is easier to monitor and control.
"As in the Soviet era, elections must demonstrate the loyalty of citizens," Russian political scientist and Head of Analysis of Transformation Processes at the NEST Centre Nikolai Petrov said.
The election will fill 450 State Duma seats and the governorships of 11 federal regions, with the country's only remaining anti-war party excluded from the ballot and fears of mobilisation overshadowing the vote.
Running from 18 to 20 September, the election will also choose deputies to regional legislatures in 39 federal subjects.
Voters will choose eight of the 11 regional heads directly, while regional parliaments will elect the remaining three. Polling stations have been opened at Russian border crossings with Poland and the three Baltic states.
Half of the 450 Duma seats will be allocated through nationwide party lists and the other half through single-member constituencies.
Voting in Russian elections is also taking place in parts of Ukraine occupied by Moscow's troops, a move that neither Kyiv nor the West recognises as legitimate.
Kremlin pushes pro-army narrative
Almost 200 candidates in these elections have taken part in Russia's war in Ukraine, according to electoral commissions.
The Kremlin has promoted them as part of Russia's "true elite," but the initiative is primarily a recruitment tool to boost Moscow's troops on the front lines, with few standing any real chance of being elected.
Ahead of the vote, Putin urged Russians to vote to show troops that "behind our fighters stand millions of people" and to deliver an "answer to those who want to weaken Russia".
Meanwhile, Russians fear another wave of military mobilisation, despite Putin personally denying plans for a call-up twice in three days in September alone.
Independent Russian media have counted 17 official denials of an imminent mobilisation. Russia called up 300,000 reservists in the autumn of 2022 in a move that triggered significant public alarm and a mass departure of men of fighting age from the country.
Tatiana Stanovaya of the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Centre, which is banned in Russia, said she considered a new draft unlikely.
"They have put so much effort into persuading Russians not to worry about this," she said. "I would be very, very surprised if it happened."
In the streets of Moscow today, few visible signs indicate an election is even under way.
Fears of mobilisation have been further compounded by Ukrainian long-range drone strikes on Russian infrastructure in a bid to defund its war machine, causing fuel shortages and economic losses running into billions of euros.
Many Russians feel the attacks break what Stanovaya described as the Kremlin's tacit bargain with the population over the war.
In prison, in exile, dead
All of Putin's main political opponents are in prison, in exile or dead. Alexei Navalny, his most prominent challenger, died in a Russian penal colony in 2024.
Putin's political opponents have mostly been driven into exile and his main opponent Alexei Navalny died in an Arctic prison in 2024.
Russia's exiled opposition has urged anti-Kremlin Russians not to boycott the elections but instead vote "against Putin's party".
Navalny's widow Yulia Navalnaya also called on anti-war Russians to cast their ballots at noon on Sunday.
Yabloko — which critics say outlived its usefulness after the Kremlin allowed it to exist for many years to create a pretence of political plurality as a catch-all for liberal and discontented voters — disagreed, arguing that it was better not to vote.
"You are suggesting that we once again go, like sheep, dancing to their tune, and vote for those who have caused the deaths of people in Russia and Ukraine?" party chairman Nikolay Rybakov said this week.
'Mad printer'
Parliamentary elections were previously a source of significant political tension: in 2011, mass fraud during the Duma vote and Putin's return to the presidency from the post of prime minister triggered the largest street protests in Russia since the collapse of the Soviet Union.
Putin has ruled Russia since 1999 and his United Russia party has dominated politics since the early 2000s.
Under Putin, the Duma's powers have been substantially curtailed, reducing it largely to approving legislation initiated by the Kremlin — a role that has earned it the popular nickname "the mad printer" to mock the speed at which it rubber-stamped highly restrictive and controversial laws.
Any criticism of the war is treated under Russian law as "discrediting the army" and can carry a prison sentence.
Older voters remain among Putin's strongest supporters, although many still complain about living standards.

articles.title: US to sell fighter jets to Saudi Arabia – why is the plan controversial?
articles.body:
The administration of US President Donald Trump has announced the approval of the sale of nearly 50 F-35 fighter jets to Saudi Arabia, a policy shift that has raised concerns among some members of Congress, the BBC reports.
For years, Saudi Arabia has sought to acquire the world’s most advanced fighter jets, which are equipped with stealth technology to evade detection. Washington had long been reluctant, primarily because it supplies F-35 jets to its ally, Israel. US law mandates that Israel is guaranteed access to top-tier American weaponry. Congress now has 30 days to review or block the potential 24 billion dollars deal with Riyadh.
On the 17th of September, Representative Raja Krishnamoorthi (Democrat from Illinois) spoke out against the sale of fighter jets to Saudi Arabia. He warned that the move could place the “crown jewels” of American military technology within reach of the Chinese Communist Party. Other Democratic politicians and some US defense officials have expressed similar concerns. They believe that Riyadh, based on security cooperation between the two nations, could share sensitive information with China.
In announcing the agreement, the US State Department stated that it would support US foreign policy and national security objectives. The deal with Riyadh is expected to strengthen the security of a major non-NATO ally—a force for political stability and economic progress in the Persian Gulf region.
The proposed sale of military equipment would not alter the military balance in the region.
Trump shares a close relationship with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman; bin Salman visited the White House last November. The two also met in Riyadh last May, where an agreement was concluded for the sale of 142 billion dollar worth of arms to Saudi Arabia.
The latest deal will include 48 F-35 fighter jets manufactured by Lockheed Martin. This would place Saudi Arabia on par with Israel, which possesses 50 such jets. Israel’s Foreign Ministry announced in May that it plans to purchase additional F-35s, bringing the country’s total to 100. A single F-35 costs approximately 82.5 million dollars. Congress had previously questioned deals with Riyadh following the 2018 killing of Saudi journalist Jamal Khashoggi. The administration of U.S. President Joe Biden considered selling F-35s to Saudi Arabia if it normalized relations with Israel, but diplomatic efforts failed.
The proposal to sell the fighter jets comes as Saudi Arabia is engaged in a conflict with Houthi rebels in Yemen. The Houthis have seized control of Yemen’s Red Sea coast.
Read also: Gulf states cancel meeting with Iran; Houthis attack Saudi Arabia

articles.title: Lublin and Rzeszów airports suspend flight operations for third consecutive day due to Russian strikes on Ukraine
articles.body:
Amidst fresh Russian strikes on Ukraine, the airports in Lublin and Rzeszów have suspended flight operations for the third day in a row, the Polish Air Navigation Services Agency (PANSA) reported on the social network X.
PANSA noted: "Airports in Lublin and Rzeszów have suspended flight operations."
Specifically, the agency reported operational restrictions at the airports starting September 16 due to Russian attacks on Ukrainian territory.
The Operational Command of the Polish Armed Forces had announced the commencement of military aviation operations in Polish airspace in response to renewed Russian air attacks on Ukraine.
"In accordance with established procedures, the Operational Command of the Polish Armed Forces—through the Air Operations Center-Air Component Command—deployed the necessary forces and assets at its disposal. Ground-based air defense and radar surveillance systems were placed on alert," the message reads.
The command emphasized that these measures were precautionary, aimed at ensuring the safety and protection of airspace, particularly in areas adjacent to the zones under threat.
Subsequently, the Operational Command announced the conclusion of the military aviation operations in Polish airspace, which had been conducted to ensure safety during the Russian strikes on targets in Ukraine.
"Ground-based air defense and radar surveillance systems have returned to standard operating mode," the command noted.
It also reported that no violations of the Republic of Poland's airspace were recorded.

articles.title: Indonesia gets its first aircraft carrier amid debate over cost and military ambitions
articles.body:
Indonesia has received its first aircraft carrier, a former Italian warship that the government says will strengthen the archipelagic nation’s maritime security and disaster response capabilities.
The 41-year-old former ITS Giuseppe Garibaldi, with capacity for short takeoff and vertical landing aircraft and helicopters, arrived Friday morning at a naval base in North Jakarta’s Tanjung Priok port, where it was welcomed with a military ceremony.
Italy in March agreed to give the carrier, which was retired in 2024, to Indonesia in a move aimed at boosting Italy’s broader defence engagement with the south-east Asian country. Italy is seeking deals on submarines and aircraft, and gifting the carrier to Indonesia also saves it the cost of decommissioning the ship.
The transfer would make Indonesia only the second country in south-east Asia with a carrier in its fleet. The first was Thailand’s HTMS Chakri Naruebet, which was commissioned in 1997 after being procured from Spain along with carrier-capable AV-8S Matador jump-jets.
The carrier will be formally commissioned into the Indonesian Navy next week as the KRI Gajah Mada, named after the famed 14th-century Majapahit-era military leader, whose campaigns and vision of a unified archipelago have made him one of Indonesia’s most celebrated historical figures.
Defence development was one of the top priorities for president Prabowo Subianto’s administration, as he has advocated an expansion of the military through the purchase of submarines, frigates, fighter jets, missiles and pushed for more defence cooperation with various countries.
But the Garibaldi acquisition has sparked a fierce debate among defence analysts, economists and opposition politicians who question whether Indonesia needs an aircraft carrier at all and whether the government should be spending millions of dollars to refurbish and operate an ageing warship while facing mounting fiscal pressures at home.
Indonesia’s finance ministry approved $450m in financing for the aircraft carrier program in 2025. However, some lawmakers have warned the overall bill could be far higher. TB Hasanuddin, a member of parliament’s Commission I, said the cost of retrofitting the carrier alone could reach 16tn rupiah (about $900m).
Unlike major naval powers that use aircraft carriers to launch fighter jets far from home shores, Indonesia views the vessel as a mobile command centre and support hub for helicopters, drones and maritime operations across its thousands of islands.
Speaking during a disaster management meeting early this month, Prabowo said the vessel would help authorities combat forest and peatland fires that regularly blanket parts of south-east Asia with hazardous haze.
Prabowo said the carrier could accommodate up to 10 medium-sized helicopters, including aircraft with capabilities comparable to the Black Hawk and Mi-17, and could carry large quantities of water and be deployed to areas with large numbers of fire hotspots.
He also outlined plans to operate drones from the ship and use it as a mobile platform that could be rapidly deployed to help in the event of natural disasters, which are common in Indonesia, a nation that sits in the Pacific “Ring of Fire.”
Operating a carrier is extremely costly, however, and experts have questioned whether Indonesia’s leadership has thought through whether one is necessary for the country’s defence or disaster-relief needs.
The acquisition comes as Indonesia’s economy faces growing fiscal pressures. Prabowo’s government has been funding a free nutritious meals program – which has been tainted by multiple food poisoning incidents – and other costly initiatives while economists have warned about slowing growth, weaker state revenues and widening budget constraints, prompting closer scrutiny of major government spending projects.
“The plan to acquire the Garibaldi must be based on genuine operational needs and our ability to operate it, rather than being driven by pride or other considerations,” said Muhammad Fauzan Malufti, of the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
He said policymakers must weigh not only the vessel’s acquisition and modernisation costs, but also the Navy’s ability to sustain its operations, including personnel, maintenance, fuel, weapons systems and supporting infrastructure.
Fauzan said the government should be transparent about those considerations, particularly given the vessel’s age. He cited Thailand’s carrier as a cautionary example, saying it has spent much of its service life in port because of operational and budget constraints.
“The bottom line is that this should not be forced. Otherwise, the benefits could be outweighed by the costs,” Fauzan said. “The money might be better spent on other priorities, such as increasing the number of frigates in the fleet.”
Military analyst Khairul Fahmi of the Institute for Security and Strategic Studies said aircraft carriers are not a priority for Indonesia, which is focused on preventing adversaries from operating freely in the country’s territorial waters.
“Indonesia has a greater need for submarines, frigates and asymmetric weapons systems to protect its maritime sovereignty,” he said.
But he added that if Indonesia is seeking to position itself as a major maritime nation, “an aircraft carrier can be both a symbol of national power and a multifunctional platform capable of supporting a wide range of military and non-military missions.”

articles.title: Iran reconstructing nuclear test-linked Taleghan 2 site after IDF strikes, satellite imagery shows
articles.body:
New satellite imagery from Vantor Technologies appeared to show the Iranian regime rapidly attempting to reconstruct the Taleghan 2 facility in the Parchin military complex, the Institute for Science and International Security stated on Thursday.
The facility is located approximately 30 kilometers southeast of Tehran. It was initially destroyed in Israeli strikes in October 2024, before being partially rebuilt starting in May 2025. Israel again struck it in March 2026 during Operation Roaring Lion, and it has been heavily damaged since.
The satellite imagery appears to show the regime having erected a tarp above the hardened buried facility, which has been tied to nuclear bomb testing as part of Iran's AMAD program.
The tarp seems to be an attempt to hide reconstruction activity from satellite view or aerial reconnaissance, the institute assessed.
This assessment was boosted by significant activity being seen throughout the construction site, including various construction vehicles, such as dump trucks, bulldozers, concrete pump trucks, concrete mixers, and cranes being seen at the site in the latest satellite imagery.
The "repair and rehabilitation work began in June," the institute stated.
The first step Iran took in its reconstruction project was to repair and place concrete caps over penetration holes caused by bunker-buster heavy bombs dropped on the facility, the institute said.
Iran reinforces nuke test facility with 'concrete apron' during reconstruction project
Iran also appears to have built a new "concrete apron reinforcement on the right side of the facility," the institute said, adding that it will "provide additional blast protection from an aerial attack."
"Significant questions remain as to Iran's plans for the facility; not least is why Iran keeps rebuilding it," the institute stated.
"What is clear is that Iran remains committed to rebuilding this facility, a deeply concerning development considering the long history of nuclear weapons research and development activities that occurred there," it warned.

articles.title: A war-fatigued and anxious Russia picks a new parliament
articles.body:
A war-fatigued and anxious Russia picks a new parliament
September 17, 2026
Russians are increasingly anxious. Nearly half of those surveyed by state pollster FOM say a sense of alarm is the prevailing mood among the people around them.
According to data by independent pollster ExtremeScan, 60% of Russians believe that the war against Ukraine has had negative consequences for their day-to-day lives.
"Anxiety and war fatigue are driven by increasing uncertainty," Margarita Zavadskaya, a sociologist and senior research fellow at the Finnish Institute of International Affairs in Helsinki, told DW.
She says this year has seen a shift in public opinion. Rising prices, internet crackdowns, fuel shortages caused by Ukrainian strikes on oil refineries and rumors of another mobilization drive are making it harder for Russians to plan for the future. Some are even leaving the country, afraid they could be drafted after the elections.
Sociologist and the founder of ExtremeScan Elena Koneva said people were starting to ask the question: "How much does this war cost me and my family? And am I ready to pay this price? "
That could pose a problem for the Kremlin.
From September 18 to 20, Russians are voting for a new parliament (the State Duma) for the first time since 2022. It's the first parliamentary election to take place in Russia during the Ukraine war. And although there are unlikely to be any surprises in the official results, the Kremlin will be closely monitoring turnout.
Why are these elections important for the Kremlin?
"The Kremlin is confident it can fabricate whatever figures it needs. The question is how high of a price it will have to pay," said Zavadskaya.
Although elections in authoritarian systems like that of Russian President Vladimir Putin have little to do with democratic change, they still serve an important purpose. They are a reality check on whether the population remains loyal. And for Putin, that is especially important right now.
"They are crucial for him because they demonstrate that the majority supports the main party, the party of war, and that he has legitimacy for further escalation and the continuation of this war," Russian opposition politician in exile Ilya Yashin told DW.
In the fifth year of the war in Ukraine, there is little sign the Kremlin is willing to end the conflict. United Russia, a party de facto led by Putin, is campaigning on a platform that lists victory in the war among its priorities. Its candidate list is headed by people presented as veterans of the war against Ukraine.
But many Russians appear to want the opposite.
"The silent majority just wants the war to end," opposition politician Yulia Galyamina, who still lives in Russia, said in a recent interview with online media-outlet Bereg. Most of these people still support Putin, but they are becoming increasingly anti-war, she said.
That mood is also reflected in polling. Six in 10 Russians favor peace negotiations with Ukraine, according to independent pollster Levada Center. Recent Kremlin hints at a new round of peace talks in October may be a tactic to calm the electorate, Zavadskaya said.
Support for Yabloko has been rising
One party has sought to capitalize on this anti-war sentiment: Yabloko.
The liberal opposition party is the only registered political force opposing the war in Ukraine.
Although its rating was below 5% in July, the party has seen a surge in popularity since then. Many people, especially younger Russians, are joining Yabloko and volunteering.
According to the independent pollster ExtremeScan, 18% of Russians would have voted for Yabloko. But they will not be able to: In a recent court decision, Yabloko was barred from running in the parliamentary elections.
"This support for Yabloko is, in fact, a demonstration of people's attitude toward the war," Koneva told DW.
What will anti-war voters do?
Now, with Yabloko out of the race, are there still ways for Russians to express that attitude?
Yulia Navalnaya, the widow of Alexei Navalny, and opposition politician in exile Maxim Katz are urging supporters to back any party except United Russia in an effort to reduce the ruling party's result in the election.
Yabloko has taken a different approach, encouraging voters to spoil their ballots.
Yashin says neither choice matters. What matters, he says, is showing up at polling stations at noon on Sept. 20.
"These queues will be a visible expression of public discontent," he said. "No need for flags, banners, or symbols. Everyone will know: the queues at noon are made up of people who do not want the war to continue."
DW Russian asked its readers anonymously whether they plan to vote in the upcoming election. Most of those who responded said they would follow Navalnaya's and Katz's advice.
"Elections have long become a farce and a political spectacle. But I will vote because I want to show that I have a position," one user said.
Others decided to stay away from the elections. One respondent wrote: "I don't want to legitimize Putin's regime."
Sergei Satanovskii contributed reporting.
Edited by: Carla Bleiker

articles.title: IDV unveils upgraded British VIKING UGV with EW and strike roles
articles.body:
IDV has unveiled the latest generation of its British-built VIKING uncrewed ground vehicle in electronic warfare and precision-effects configurations, with the upgraded platform gaining an electric-only range of up to 30km.
The two variants were shown at DVD 2026 at Millbrook, demonstrating how the same vehicle architecture can carry significantly different payloads. One VIKING was equipped with precision effectors, while another carried Leonardo’s Guardian Vantage electronic warfare and signals intelligence system. The latest version of VIKING has been designed to improve range, usability and autonomous operation. Its electric-only range has been extended to as much as 30km, allowing the vehicle to move with a reduced acoustic and thermal signature.
The platform can be transported internally by Chinook helicopter or carried as an underslung load, and can also move under its own power or be towed.
Geoff Davis, Managing Director of IDV UK, said: “As demand for uncrewed capabilities accelerates across NATO, platforms such as VIKING are becoming an essential element of modern land operations.”
He added: “VIKING embodies this approach, offering a flexible and scalable platform that can be configured for a wide range of roles, from ISTAR, electronic warfare, counter-UAS and precision effects to logistics and casualty evacuation.”
The electronic warfare configuration pairs VIKING with Leonardo’s Guardian Vantage system, while a portable Guardian Shield unit can be carried aboard the vehicle and left in position separately. The systems are designed to passively detect transmissions, identify emitters and determine their direction before, when required, moving to active jamming.
IDV said the uncrewed vehicle could therefore carry out what it described as a “jam and scoot” role, operating away from the troops it is supporting, transmitting when required and then moving before the position can be targeted.
The VIKING’s series-hybrid powertrain is particularly relevant to that role. The electronic warfare payload can run from the vehicle’s battery while the engine is switched off, reducing both its thermal and acoustic signature while it listens passively. IDV argues that power generation is becoming an important distinction between different classes of uncrewed ground vehicle, particularly as increasingly demanding sensors, electronic warfare systems and other payloads are fitted to them.
Guardian Vantage and Guardian Shield are designed in the UK and manufactured at Leonardo’s Basildon plant. IDV said both use components and software supplied by British small and medium-sized companies and carry no US International Traffic in Arms Regulations restrictions.
VIKING itself is developed and built at IDV UK’s facility at MIRA Technology Park in Nuneaton, using a British supply chain. The company says the vehicle has undergone more than a decade of trials with armed forces in Britain, Europe and the United States, with initial orders now placed by allied armies. The vehicle’s modular architecture is intended to allow different mission systems to be fitted to the same basic platform, with IDV listing possible roles including reconnaissance, electronic warfare, counter-drone operations, precision effects, logistics and casualty evacuation.
IDV also displayed its MUV Military Utility Vehicle in an ambulance configuration and an 8×8 protected logistics vehicle from its Modular Military Range, but the upgraded VIKING represented the company’s clearest move towards higher-end autonomous battlefield roles.

articles.title: Iranians rally in biggest show of defiance since US war began
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iranians rally by the hundreds of thousands in biggest show of defiance since US-Israeli war began
Hundreds of thousands of Iranians rallied Friday in a government-organized show of defiance after months of war, pledging their readiness to take up arms in the biggest such demonstration since the United States and Israel launched the war in February.
Iran's government has sought to rally the people and stress national unity, even as the economy worsens under a US naval blockade of Iranian ports and new US sanctions meant to increase Tehran's economic pain.
Estimates varied of the number of people volunteering to receive limited military training and defend the country in an effort described as "Janfaday-e Iran," or the "ones who sacrifice their lives for Iran." They marched through downtown Tehran in combat uniform, carrying flags, as onlookers cheered.
For days, state media have encouraged Iranians to join the campaign, saying training with assault rifles would begin soon. The volunteers would be an additional layer of security to the powerful Revolutionary Guard paramilitary and its all-volunteer arm, the Basij.
Tehran’s Guard chief, Gen. Hassan Hassanzadeh, told the state broadcaster that over 600,000 people had registered to participate, with over 1 million expected to take part in the training. On Friday morning, the broadcaster estimated over 300,000 people were on the streets.
The new head of the Basij, Hossein Taeb, declared in a speech as the rally began that the volunteers will be ready for “full-fledged defense” and similar rallies will take place in other cities soon.
The new trainees will make a “nightmare” for Iran's enemies, Taeb added, as President Masoud Pezeshkian, military commanders and other senior officials watched the march.
Some participants trampled flags of the U.S. and Israel. Others chanted “Death to America” and “Death to Israel.”
"I am here to tell Trump that we Iranians have no fear about his threats against our homeland," said Marzieh Afaghi, 24, who attended the rally with her toddler and husband. "No one in history could invade Iran and remain there."
The rally was also a chance for Iran to show off military hardware. Anti-aircraft batteries were on display, while female Guard members in black headscarves sat with truck-mounted machine guns.
The Guard displayed drones that have been widely used against ships in the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran has asserted control since the war began, severely affecting the Gulf region’s shipments of oil and natural gas to the rest of the world.
Friday's events also suggested that hardliners like Taeb among Iran's leadership will be more prepared to suppress any future demonstration against the theocracy.
In January, shortly before the war, Iran saw some of its largest nationwide protests in history, which began over the struggling economy and turned to wider grievances. Activists have said a crackdown killed over 7,000 people and saw tens of thousands detained.
In May, government officials said more than 30 million people in Iran—home to a population of some 90 million—had volunteered via an online form or at public gatherings to lay down their lives for the theocracy.

articles.title: Carney Says Canada and E.U. 'Are Not Fair Weather Allies' as Trump Threatens Europe Over 'Hostile Act'
articles.body:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Thursday welcomed the prospect of Canada becoming an “associate member” of the E.U., just hours after U.S. President Donald Trump dismissed the proposal as “laughable.”
Addressing the European Parliament as a guest of honor in Strasbourg, France, Carney insisted “Europe and Canada are stronger together” and said “Canada and the European Union can anchor our ground to hold our values while forming a protective canopy under which our citizens can thrive.”
Carney’s pivot toward Europe comes as he seeks to establish stronger international ties and curtail Canada’s reliance on the American market amid an all-out trade war. Canada’s retaliatory tariffs came into effect last week, matching the economic pressure imposed by the U.S. after negotiations collapsed last month. Trump’s repeated threats against Canadian sovereignty and calls to make it the “51st state” have added to the months-long tension.
While Carney did not directly mention Trump or his Administration while addressing European lawmakers, he appeared to make nods to the current volatility of Canada-U.S. relations and condemned economic coercions. Speaking about the "current geopolitical rupture," he said a "new dimension was needed.”
“Economic integration is now being weaponized, tariffs being used to exert pressure,” he said. “Financial mechanisms have been used for coercion. Supply chains constitute weak points to be exploited.”
Championing the burgeoning E.U. alliance, Carney focused on what he said were shared values between Canada and the bloc, insisting: "We are not fair-weather allies. We believe that our prosperity grows when it is shared."
“I'm not proposing a third bloc in order to become a 'great power' rival, only with better manners,” Carney continued. “We do not seek power to dominate others. On the contrary, we are pursuing resilience so no one can control our open markets, impair our sovereignty, threaten our territorial integrity, or undermine our freedoms, our democracies, our rule of law.”
Carney, who began his speech in French—one of Canada’s official languages—before continuing in English, with splatterings of German, welcomed how European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen had on Wednesday opened the door for Canada becoming an “associate member” of the 27-member bloc.
When speaking about forging closer ties with the E.U., Carney referenced seeking strategic autonomy through “deep co-operation in the full range of strategic capabilities, including critical minerals, defense industrial capacity, AI and compute, energy security, space and payments.” He insisted Canada and Europe must not be dependent on “individual nations or individual companies” as this “creates vulnerabilities, particularly when supposedly global companies prove national in the breach.”
He also hinted at a potential freedom of movement between the E.U. and Canada that would allow “youth to work, study, and live where they want, on either side of the Atlantic.”
Carney’s passionate advocacy for the deepening of ties with the E.U.—a move he says Canadians have shown they’re in support of—came after Trump lambasted the idea of a new European dawn for Canada.
Speaking to reporters Wednesday, Trump called the proposal “laughable” and threatened economic punishments if the E.U. moves forward with von der Leyen’s plan.
"If they do that, if I think it's at all a hostile act, I will put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe on many things," Trump said en route to an event in North Carolina. "If it's a good intention, that's fine. If it's a bad intention, we'll put very heavy tariffs on Europe.”
In response to Trump’s remarks, a European Commission spokesperson told TIME: “As president von der Leyen made clear [on Wednesday], the proposed strengthening of our partnership with Canada is not against anyone else, but for our common strength.”
Carney welcomes new alliances on visit to Europe
Carney's speech to the European Parliament came on the final day of his stay in Europe, where he sought to cement and deepen Canada’s international relationships.
The E.U. is Canada’s second-largest global trading partner for goods and services, with bilateral trade worth approximately C$178.6 billion in 2025.
The Canadian leader also traveled to Liverpool, England, to meet British Prime Minister Andy Burnham. The pair attended a football game and watched Everton—the team they both support—secure a victory against the Wolverhampton Wanderers.
"The leaders began by underscoring the close co-operation between the U.K. and Canada and emphasized the importance of building similar close ties with European partners, particularly on trade and defence,” a Downing Street spokeswoman told TIME.
Ahead of the meeting, Burnham called Carney a “great progressive leader” with whom the U.K. shares “so many values, but also with whom we have a shared opportunity on defense co-operation, on trade” and AI.
Canada applies to join U.K.-led military coalition
Following Burnham and Carney's meeting, it was announced that Canada has applied to join the British-led Joint Expeditionary Force military coalition.
The force, formally launched in 2014, consists of 10 North Atlantic NATO member states that deliver rapid response and security operations.
“Prime Minister Carney announced that Canada has formally applied to join the Joint Expeditionary Force and welcomed the U.K.’s support for Canada’s participation in this important initiative,” Carney’s office said in a statement.
Canada, already a NATO member, is seeking to diversify its defense dependency from the U.S. with new partnerships across the Atlantic.
In February, Canada became the first non-European country to participate in the "Security action for Europe” (SAFE) instrument, which provides up to €150 billion in low-interest loans to help member states purchase military and defense equipment.
What happens next as Canada seeks "associate" membership with the E.U.?
Following von der Leyen’s proposal, a European Commission spokesperson told TIME that the executive cabinet will work “in close coordination with [its] member states and the European Parliament” to “create a new form of partnership that has not existed until now–building the closest imaginable form of association with a partner outside Europe.”
The proposed alliance is set to include deeper economic ties, a technology alliance, greater integration of defense industrial bases, and efforts to make the Arctic a flagship joint project. It could also expand cooperation on energy, critical minerals and batteries, as well as AI, quantum technology, cybersecurity, and economic security.
The E.U.-Canada summit set to take place in Montreal in late October will “provide the first meaningful opportunity to discuss these issues further,” the spokesperson told TIME.
The proposal has been welcomed by many European lawmakers across the bloc.
Member of the European Parliament (MEP) for Spain Javier Moreno Sánchez, who also serves as chair of the parliament’s delegation for relations with Canada, told TIME the decision to bring Canada in as an “associate member” was “politically and symbolically significant,” but warned it “must now be followed by concrete actions.”
Irish MEP Barry Andrews told TIME that the announcement is a clear “win-win for both sides,” adding that “in an ever more insecure world, truly democratic countries must come together and stand up to Trump, [Chinese President] Xi Jinping, and [Russian President Vladimir] Putin.”
Germany, the E.U.’s largest economy, also embraced the move, with government spokesperson Stefan Kornelius saying Berlin “welcomes the initiative for a particularly close partnership with Canada.”
The E.U., much like Canada, is seeking new partnerships amid a weakening alliance with the U.S. under Trump, following disputes over tariff threats, his lashing out at the NATO alliance, and his push to annex Greenland.
Espen Barth Eide, Norway’s Foreign Affairs Minister, told TIME the world is "living through the most serious security situation since the Second World War.”
“At a time like this, it is welcome that the E.U. is strengthening cooperation on European security. We also welcome the E.U.’s efforts to involve Norway, the United Kingdom, Canada and Iceland. Such an approach strengthens European security,” he said.
Norway and Iceland are not members of the E.U., but both belong to the European Economic Area (EEA), giving them close economic ties to the bloc through trade and free movement—a model from which Canada could draw inspiration.
Elsewhere, the “associate” membership proposal faced backlash.
French MEP Manon Aubry, co-chair of The Left group, told TIME there was “a serious question of method,” arguing that “a decision of such magnitude cannot be made by the president of the European Commission alone.”

articles.title: Trump hails ‘major progress’ on setting up US Army base in Poland
articles.body:
Trump hails ‘major progress’ on setting up US Army base in Poland
The US has made major progress in negotiations to establish a military base in Poland, President Donald Trump has announced.
His remarks came as Russia warned that it would retaliate if the territory of Poland or the Baltic states were used for a NATO attack against the country.
Poland, which borders the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad to the northeast, is a key logistics hub for delivering Western military aid to Ukraine and is one of Kiev’s main supporters in Europe.
“GREAT NEWS! Thanks to the bold leadership of my friend, Karol Nawrocki, President of Poland, major progress is being made toward establishing a US Army base in Poland,” Trump wrote on Truth Social on Thursday.
“If this happens, the location will be announced very soon. This will be a historic step for our Great US/Polish Alliance.”
Nawrocki responded by promising to find “the best possible location” for the base. “We are ready to continue our efforts to strengthen our defense cooperation: seriously, responsibly, and always together,” he wrote on X.
The US already maintains a permanent Army garrison and command headquarters in Poland, although most of the 10,000 US troops stationed in the country serve on a rotational basis. During Trump’s first term in 2018, Poland offered to host a permanent base tentatively named ‘Fort Trump’.
Under Trump’s successor, President Joe Biden, the US established a garrison headquartered at Camp Kosciuszko in Poznan and permanently stationed the V Corps Forward Headquarters in the city.
Tensions between Russia and NATO have flared in recent months as eastern members of the US-led military bloc have accused Russia of launching drone incursions. Moscow has dismissed the allegations as unfounded.
Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski said during a trip to Kiev over the weekend that “if Russia attacked us and we took our gloves off, I think we would defeat Russia quite quickly.”
Russian presidential aide and former security chief Nikolay Patrushev responded to Sikorski by warning that “Polish statehood would cease to exist within two or three days” if a conflict breaks out.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov reiterated this week that the country has no intention of attacking NATO members, but said that if the bloc attacks Russia, the war would be “very short.”

articles.title: UN finds grounds to believe US committed war crimes in Iran
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
UN mission finds grounds to believe US committed war crimes in Iran, and Tehran crimes against humanity
A UN fact-finding mission on Iran said on Thursday it had reasonable grounds to believe the United States was behind two military strikes on a school and sports facility in Iran in February, and that these constituted war crimes.
It also found that Iranian authorities committed crimes against humanity during their deadly crackdown on anti-government protests.
The findings in a new report by the Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran, to be submitted to the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva, examined US conduct during the Iran war that began in February and the Iranian government's response to nationwide unrest that began in late December.
The Pentagon declined to comment on a report conducted by an outside organization.
"Our investigation remains ongoing, and we have nothing to announce at the moment," it said in a statement. White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly said in response to the report that the UN Human Rights Council had "accomplished nothing for human rights," adding that Iran was the only party in the current conflict that had committed war crimes.
The Iranian permanent mission in Geneva did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment.
U.S. officials have previously said military operations are conducted in accordance with the law of armed conflict, while Iran has consistently rejected allegations of systematic rights violations.
UN Fact-Finding missions are investigative, not judicial bodies, and therefore do not initiate any criminal cases.
Their findings, however, can be used in criminal investigations by national courts or international tribunals such as the International Criminal Court. States will discuss the findings of the report when it is presented to the Human Rights Council in Geneva on Monday.
MINAB SCHOOL STRIKE
The UN experts said they found reasonable grounds to believe U.S. forces were responsible for an attack on the Shajareh Tayyebeh Primary School in the city of Minab, where more than 150 people were killed, including around 120 schoolchildren, according to Iranian officials.
The attack constituted an indiscriminate attack causing civilian deaths and damage to civilian infrastructure, amounting to a war crime under international law, the mission concluded.
According to the report, the US failure to update information in relation to the school, which was adjacent to an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps naval complex, in its targeting databases and to confirm the building was a military objective amounted to more than mere negligence.
"Rather, the US directed the strikes at the building of the school while being aware of a substantial risk of striking a civilian object and acting recklessly as regards the possibility that this would happen."
In June US President Donald Trump said that "nobody" purposefully attacked a girls' school in Iran in February, citing an investigation into the incident. Reuters news agency first reported that an initial internal US military investigation showed US forces were likely responsible for the fatal strike in Minab in southern Iran.
The Pentagon has since elevated the probe but it has not published any preliminary findings.
UN experts said the school was a clearly identifiable civilian object and found no evidence that it was being used for military purposes.
The experts reached a similar conclusion over a strike on a sports centre in Lamerd. The report said the attack damaged nearby residential buildings and a school and killed and injured 22 civilians. It concluded that the strike was indiscriminate and therefore constituted a war crime.
U.S. Central Command said in a statement in March that U.S. forces did not launch any strikes into the city of Lamerd on that day.
IRAN ABUSES
The UN mission probe found that the Iranian authorities carried out a widespread and systematic attack against civilians during protests that erupted in late December last year, involving unlawful killings, torture, arbitrary detention, enforced disappearances and severe restrictions on freedom of expression.
Rights groups say bystanders were among those killed during the biggest crackdown since Shi'ite Muslim clerics took power in the 1979 revolution. Tehran blamed "terrorists and rioters" backed by exiled opponents and foreign foes the U.S. and Israel.
The probe said it could not independently verify the death toll, but that it believed the number of dead and injured was likely far higher than official figures which say 3,038 people were killed, and 25,000 people injured.
The government's response to the protests — including violence and killings, cutting off the internet and use of the death penalty — marked a significant escalation from previous patterns of suppressing dissent, the report said.

articles.title: U.S. Air Force joins Navy in funding Castelion hypersonic missile maker
articles.body:
- The Air Force Research Laboratory added $16.4 million to Castelion's contract for its Blackbeard hypersonic weapon, bringing that deal's total to $37.2 million.
- The Navy separately placed a production order worth up to $200 million for Blackbeard on Sept. 14, 2026, following a rapid string of earlier awards.
The Air Force Research Laboratory has added $16.4 million to a Castelion Corp. contract for developing a low-cost, mass-producible long-range strike weapon, the latest in a rapid series of government awards backing the company’s Blackbeard hypersonic missile.
The modification brings the total value of this particular contract to $37.2 million, up from $20.9 million. Work will continue at Castelion’s headquarters in Torrance, California, funded by fiscal 2025 research money, and is scheduled to run through June 30, 2028. Wright-Patterson Air Force Base’s research laboratory manages the contract, separate from a parallel string of Navy awards that have funded the same missile.
Blackbeard is designed to fly faster than Mach 5 while maneuvering within the atmosphere, built in both an air-launched version for aircraft such as the F/A-18 and a ground-launched variant compatible with the HIMARS launcher. Castelion, founded in 2022 by three former SpaceX engineers, has pitched the weapon as the first U.S. hypersonic system built from the outset for industrial-scale, commercial-style manufacturing rather than the smaller test batches typical of earlier hypersonic programs.
The Navy has moved unusually fast on the missile. After initial Army and Navy integration awards in October 2025, the Navy selected Blackbeard in February 2026 as its first weapon candidate under the Multi-mission Affordable Capacity Effector program, known as MACE, an effort to field large numbers of cheaper, longer-range strike weapons instead of relying on smaller numbers of expensive ones. That was followed in April by a $105 million contract to integrate the missile onto the F/A-18E/F Super Hornet and run live-fire testing in the Indo-Pacific Command area.
In June, the Navy ordered 50 early operational capability prototypes for $23.4 million, and in August it added nearly $90 million to push the weapon toward becoming a formal program of record, including design changes meant to speed up future sales to allies. Just this month, on Sept. 14, the Navy placed a production order worth up to $200 million, moving Blackbeard out of prototype status entirely.
Congress increased MACE program funding by more than $140 million in the fiscal 2026 defense appropriations act, more than doubling its base funding. Much of Castelion’s production capacity runs through Project Ranger, a 1,000-acre manufacturing campus the company built in Rio Rancho, New Mexico, at a cost it has put above $250 million. Castelion has said its longer-term goal is producing 500 of the weapons a year.
The U.S. Army was one of the first services to back the program, placing an integration award alongside the Navy in October 2025, before the Air Force Research Laboratory and the Navy’s own contracts expanded rapidly through 2026.

articles.title: Russian drones devastate shopping mall in Zaporizhzhia city
articles.body:
The Amstor shopping mall, on the city’s right bank, was struck by Russian drones late on Thursday, 17 September. Emergency service footage showed firefighters battling flames across the complex, which Ukraine's State Emergency Service later described as “practically destroyed”. Rescue operations were completed on Friday morning.
Fire crews had to repeatedly take shelter because of the risk of further Russian attacks before returning to the site and eventually extinguishing the blaze.
Local media reported that children in a nearby outdoor skatepark survived the explosion by taking cover in concrete recesses built into the skate bowls.
Ukrainian authorities said other civilian infrastructure, including businesses, buses, bus stops and commercial facilities, was also targeted or damaged.
The attack comes as Zaporizhzhia, a major city in southeastern Ukraine, remains exposed to regular Russian drone and missile strikes.

articles.title: Russian officials trying to move assets abroad and open foreign bank accounts amid mobilization rumors, Bloomberg reports
articles.body:
Russian officials trying to move assets abroad and open foreign bank accounts amid mobilization rumors, Bloomberg reports
Amid rumors of a new mobilization, senior Russian officials have spent recent months trying to open accounts at foreign banks and move their assets abroad, Bloomberg reported, citing documents it had obtained.
According to Bloomberg, draft office employees are doing the same, and advising friends and relatives to leave Russia.
Bloomberg’s report offered no further details.
Speculation that Russia could announce a new mobilization after elections to the State Duma, the lower house of Russia’s parliament, has circulated for several weeks, echoed by Meduza sources, Western media, and Ukrainian officials. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has said that Russian authorities are allegedly planning to mobilize up to 300,000 people this fall.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov has said Ukrainian officials are trying to “ideologically stir up the situation” in Russia with their statements about a possible mobilization. Commenting on the rumors, Vladimir Putin has said that “there is no scenario today that would require a mobilization,” and has called the reports “utter nonsense” and an “information attack” on Russia.

articles.title: Slovak PM says Slovakia should not go to war "because of some Article 5" of NATO
articles.body:
Slovak PM says Slovakia should not go to war "because of some Article 5" of NATO
Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico has said he does not intend to fulfil Slovakia's obligations under NATO's Article 5 or take part in defending its allies in the event of a Russian attack.
Source: Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico during a speech to students and hospital staff in Prešov
Details: Fico did not once mention Russia as an aggressor state or a source of military threat to Europe. Instead, Fico accused European leaders of using "war-mongering rhetoric" and acted as though he did not understand who exactly NATO was supposed to defend itself against.
Quote: "It seems... that sometimes there is a tendency to replace the inability to solve problems such as illegal migration, competitiveness and high energy prices with these war-mongering conversations: let's go, let's fight. For God's sake, who do we want to fight? Who?"
Details: Fico publicly expressed his unwillingness to fulfil the obligations under Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty, which provides for a collective military response by NATO in the event of an attack on one of its members.
Quote: "Can you imagine, ladies and gentlemen, that Article 5 of the NATO treaty would be invoked? Can anyone imagine it? Can anyone imagine being told: get 5,000 soldiers ready, or 10,000 soldiers, and they'll go off somewhere to fight? And we won't even know who we're fighting, why or what for.
I don't want Slovakia to be part of any military conflict because of some Article 5. As prime minister, I will do everything to ensure that Slovakia is never drawn into a military conflict."
Background:
- After returning to the post of Slovak prime minister in autumn 2023, Robert Fico immediately halted military aid to Ukraine and began regularly making anti-Ukrainian statements while justifying Russia's invasion.
- Throughout 2024-2025, Fico consistently opposed Ukraine's membership of NATO and threatened to veto the process. He argued that Ukraine joining NATO would be a direct route to a Third World War.
- In June 2026, ahead of the NATO summit in Ankara in July, Fico came out strongly against further large-scale financial and military support for Ukraine.

articles.title: US considering arming AUKUS submarines with nuclear warheads — Russian MFA
articles.body:
GENEVA, September 18. /TASS/. The United States is openly considering the possibility of arming SSN-AUKUS submarines with strategic nuclear warheads, Russian Foreign Ministry Ambassador-at-Large Andrey Belousov said at the 70th session of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) General Conference in Vienna.
AUKUS is a trilateral security partnership between Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States. One of its key areas of cooperation is the creation of a nuclear-powered submarine fleet for Australia.
"SSN-AUKUS submarines are technically capable of carrying strategic warheads, and the United States is openly considering them as potential carriers of such weapons. Moreover, if the relevant decision is made, all the necessary infrastructure for this purpose will already have been established in Australia. We can see from open sources that the United States and the United Kingdom are moving full steam ahead with the military development of Australian territory," he said.
The diplomat explained that military contingents are being deployed in Australia and infrastructure is being built there to accommodate the weapons of nuclear-armed states.

articles.title: Sybiha: IAEA resolution on Ukraine's nuclear safety secures 63 affirmative votes
articles.body:
The resolution on nuclear safety, security, and safeguards in Ukraine, adopted during the 70th session of the IAEA General Conference, received 63 affirmative votes, Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha announced.
“It reaffirms fundamental principles: nuclear safety and security must be guaranteed, international law upheld, Russia’s unauthorized military and other personnel withdrawn from the Zaporizhia Nuclear Power Plant, and Ukraine’s full sovereign control over the facility restored,” he wrote on the social network X overnight into Friday.
Sybiha thanked Canada for its leadership in advancing this resolution, as well as all IAEA member states that supported it.
He noted that it is equally important that 49 countries and the European Union supported a joint statement calling for the immediate release of the detained Ukrainian personnel from the Zaporizhia Nuclear Power Plant. Sybiha emphasized that real people—whose rights Russia continues to violate—stand behind this demand.
“Serhiy Korzh has been held since 2022. Serhiy Potyng has endured torture in captivity and is now suffering serious health problems. Ruslan Lavryk has reportedly been subjected to torture and urgently needs medical care. They are nuclear professionals whose expertise is essential for the safe operation of the ZNPP. They cannot be treated as bargaining chips in Russia’s war against Ukraine,” the minister said.
Sybiha emphasized that Russia's actions at the Zaporizhia NPP demonstrate a profound disregard for nuclear safety.
“Occupying and militarizing a nuclear facility while detaining and mistreating the professionals responsible for its safe operation creates risks that extend far beyond Ukraine. Such disregard for nuclear safety cannot come without consequences. Russia must be held accountable for the risks it deliberately creates,” he noted.

articles.title: UK seeks allies for space-based missile warning network
articles.body:
Britain is working with NATO allies and other partners on future sensing capabilities for missile defence, including space-based systems intended to help detect, assess and track threats across the Euro-Atlantic.
The work was outlined in a written parliamentary answer to Conservative MP Ben Obese-Jecty, who asked what progress had been made in finding partners for the next-generation persistent surveillance capability proposed in the 2025 Strategic Defence Review. The SDR called for an overhead intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance capability able to sense, warn of and track threats across the Euro-Atlantic in support of Integrated Air and Missile Defence.
Defence Readiness and Industry Minister Luke Pollard said: “Defence is also improving the sensing capabilities that underpin Integrated Air and Missile Defence through a layered NATO-integrated approach, drawing on ground-based, airborne, maritime and space-based sensors to improve the ability to detect, assess and respond to threats across the Euro-Atlantic.”
Pollard said the money would initially be directed towards foundational elements of the system, including command and control, new radars and other sensing infrastructure.
He said: “For Integrated Air and Missile Defence (IAMD), the Defence Investment Plan invests a further £790 million in dedicated homeland IAMD, focused on improving foundational capabilities through enhanced Command and Control and sensing systems, including new radars and control systems.”
The Government is also investing in long-range weapons and Deep Precision Strike, including Precision Strike Missiles, as part of the wider effort to improve the ability of the Integrated Force to detect and respond to threats. The future sensing architecture is intended to work as part of NATO rather than as an isolated national system, bringing information from different domains into a common air and missile defence picture.
Pollard said Defence was “working closely with NATO as part of a layered and integrated approach to the defence of the UK and the Euro-Atlantic.”
On international participation, he said the National Armaments Director was already working with allies and partner nations to identify opportunities for joint development and procurement.

articles.title: U.S. Army tests a cheap missile made to intercept drones
articles.body:
- Perseus Defense tested its Mk-III interceptor, built for about $2,500 each, at Yuma Proving Ground alongside U.S. Northern Command, NORAD and JIATF-401.
- The low-cost kinetic system is part of a broader Pentagon push for cheaper counter-drone options following the 2023 Langley Air Force Base drone incursion.
A counter-drone startup tested a low-cost interceptor missile at Yuma Proving Ground this month, loading it into an eight-shot launcher during a homeland-defense experiment involving U.S. Northern Command, NORAD and the Pentagon’s Joint Interagency Task Force 401.
Perseus Defense, a company that went through Y Combinator’s 2025 batch, said each Mk-III interceptor it fired cost roughly $2,500 to build. The company demonstrated the system to a group of distinguished visitors at the test event, showing the launcher running what it described as Lattice-level integration, a reference to Anduril Industries’ command-and-control software, following an earlier demonstration at Fort Carson’s Operation Jailbreak exercise.
The Mk-III is built to physically strike small drones rather than jam or spoof their signals, a kinetic hit-to-kill approach the company says is harder to defeat than electronic warfare against drones flying on fiber-optic links or preprogrammed waypoints that don’t rely on jammable radio signals. Perseus has said it is targeting a cost per engagement far below the $100,000-plus kinetic interceptors currently used against drones that themselves can cost as little as a few hundred dollars.
The push for that kind of low-collateral kinetic option traces back to a specific incident. In December 2023, dozens of unidentified drones flew over Joint Base Langley-Eustis in Virginia, forcing the base to temporarily relocate its F-22 fighters and exposing gaps in how U.S. installations could legally and physically respond to drone incursions over American soil. Similar sightings followed at other bases into 2024 and 2025, and the Department of War stood up JIATF-401 in 2025 specifically to speed up counter-drone capabilities for U.S. forces and installations at home.
The Perseus system was fired at Cibola Range Site 17, Yuma Proving Ground, as part of Falcon Peak 26.2, a counter-small unmanned aircraft systems experiment run by the North American Aerospace Defense Command and U.S. Northern Command. The exercise is designed to demonstrate new counter-drone technologies, expand the military’s focus on low-collateral defeat capabilities, deepen collaboration with mission partners, and give developers fast feedback to speed up the maturity of systems with potential use across the Department of War. This was the first time the campaign was held at Yuma Proving Ground rather than its previous home at Eglin Air Force Base. Other reporting on the event described a Perseus interceptor called Harpe, a 61-centimeter missile with a stated 2-kilometer engagement range fired from a launcher weighing less than 36 kilograms (79 pounds), tested alongside other short-range counter-drone systems to help U.S. Northern Command weigh mobility, cost per shot and magazine depth for base defense.
Perseus Defense was founded in 2025 by Jason Cornelius and Steve Messinger, who studied aerospace engineering together at Penn State, and the company has raised $6.5 million in seed funding.

articles.title: U.S. approves Saudi F-35 sale after year of signals
articles.body:
- The U.S. State Department approved a possible $24.3 billion sale of 48 F-35 fighter jets to Saudi Arabia on Sept. 17, 2026.
- The notification follows a Houthi claim a day earlier that it shot down a Royal Saudi Air Force F-15 over Marib governorate.
The U.S. State Department has approved a possible sale of 48 F-35 fighter jets to Saudi Arabia, a $24.3 billion deal that would make the kingdom just the second country in the Middle East, after Israel, cleared to fly the stealth aircraft.
The Defense Security Cooperation Agency notified Congress of the potential sale on Sept. 17. The package covers 48 conventional-takeoff F-35A jets and 49 Pratt & Whitney F135 engines, one spare beyond the 48 needed to power the aircraft. It also includes secure communications and navigation equipment, electronic warfare support, training simulators, spare parts and years of maintenance and logistics support. Lockheed Martin Aeronautics in Fort Worth, Texas, and Pratt & Whitney Military Engines in East Hartford, Connecticut, would be the main contractors.
A congressional notification is not a signed contract. It starts a review period during which lawmakers can object to the sale before formal negotiations between the U.S. and Saudi governments can begin, and the State Department’s release included standard language saying the deal would not disrupt the regional military balance and would not require sending additional U.S. personnel to Saudi Arabia.
The move follows nearly a year of on-again, off-again signals from the Trump administration. President Trump first said the U.S. would sell F-35s to Saudi Arabia in November 2025, ahead of a Washington visit by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, when the two countries also signed an agreement designating Saudi Arabia a major non-NATO ally. Trump repeated the commitment in March 2026, calling the F-35 “perhaps the most capable fighter jet ever built.” The sale had drawn scrutiny inside the administration over concerns about preserving Israel’s military edge in the region and the risk that F-35 technology could eventually reach China, concerns that also stalled a similar proposed sale to the United Arab Emirates.
Saudi Arabia’s current fighter fleet, built mainly around F-15 variants and Eurofighter Typhoons, has taken losses in the kingdom’s long war against Yemen’s Houthi movement. The Defence Blog reported on Sept. 16 that Houthi forces said they shot down a Royal Saudi Air Force F-15 over Marib governorate, the latest in a string of aircraft losses Riyadh has suffered during years of fighting. That vulnerability adds a practical dimension to Saudi Arabia’s interest in a stealth aircraft that carries none of the current fleet’s radar signature.
The State Department’s notification says the sale would strengthen Saudi Arabia’s homeland defense and improve its ability to operate alongside U.S., regional and NATO forces, describing the kingdom as capable of absorbing the new aircraft into its military without difficulty. No offset agreement, the arrangement where a seller commits to investment or work-share in the buyer’s economy, has been proposed yet; any such deal would be negotiated separately between Saudi Arabia and the contractors.

articles.title: S. Korean president rejects Trump to send troops to ME
articles.body:
South Korea has maintained a naval presence off the coast of Somalia in an anti-piracy mission, while resisting calls from U.S. President Donald Trump to play a more active military role in supporting Washington over the war in Iran, NBC News reported.
“There won’t be deployment that would involve or enter war. I can tell you that very clearly,” Lee said at a news conference. “We won’t deploy military assets in any form to that end.”
He added, however, that it “is also clear that we must do the minimum as other countries do to protect our commercial shipping and crude shipments, and also the safety of our people.”
Trump has criticized Seoul for what he called insufficient support for the Iran war and scaled back major joint military drills by the two countries’ armed forces this summer, a move that unsettled the U.S. ally.
Asked about progress in reaching an agreement with the United States on Seoul’s U.S. investment commitments under its trade deal with Washington, Lee said concern over the commercial viability of the package was the main sticking point.
