articles.title: Poland deploys its military aircraft in response to Russian strikes on targets in central Ukraine
articles.body:
Poland has deployed military aircraft in its airspace in response to Russian strikes on targets in central Ukraine.
"In connection with subsequent strikes carried out by the Russian Federation using airborne assault means on targets in the central part of Ukraine, military aviation is operating preventively in Polish airspace," the Operational Command of the Polish Armed Forces reported on the X platform.
According to the statement, the necessary forces and assets at the disposal of the Operational Command of the Polish Armed Forces were deployed through the Air Operations Center – Air Component Command.
Poland's ground-based air defense and radar reconnaissance systems have been placed on alert.
The Operational Command said these measures are preventive in nature and aimed at ensuring the security and protection of Polish airspace, particularly in the eastern part of the country.
"The Operational Command of the Armed Forces is monitoring the current situation, and the subordinate forces and means remain ready for immediate response," the statement reads.

articles.title: Homes damaged in southern Russia as air defenses down 629 drones overnight
articles.body:
MOSCOW, September 18. /TASS/. Air defenses shot down 629 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions, the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov overnight, the Russian Defense Ministry said.
More than 350 drones were detected flying toward the Moscow Region between 8:00 p.m. Moscow time on September 17 and 8:00 a.m. Moscow time on September 18 (5:00 p.m. - 5:00 a.m. GMT), Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said.
Over five private houses and eight apartment buildings were damaged in the southern Rostov Region, Governor Yury Slyusar said.
TASS has gathered the key information about the consequences of the attack.
Scale of attack
- Air defenses shot down 629 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions last night, the Defense Ministry said.
- The drones were downed over the Astrakhan, Belgorod, Bryansk, Vladimir, Kaluga, Kursk, Oryol, Rostov, Ryazan, Smolensk, Tula, Krasnodar, Moscow and Adygea regions, as well as Crimea, the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov.
- More than 350 drones were detected flying toward the Moscow Region between 8:00 p.m. Moscow time on September 17 and 8:00 a.m. Moscow time on September 18, Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin wrote on the Max social media platform.
- He said that most of the drones had been shot down on distant approaches.
- Sixty-four drones were destroyed on the outskirts of Moscow, Sobyanin added.
- Air raid warnings have been issued in 30 Russian regions since midnight, according to TASS calculations.
- Air defenses shot down seven drones over the Kaluga Region, regional Governor Vladislav Shapsha said on Max.
- More than 50 unmanned aerial vehicles were destroyed in the Rostov Region last night, Governor Yury Slyusar wrote on Max.
- Air defenses destroyed 45 Ukrainian drones over the Tula Region last night, Governor Dmitry Milyayev said on Max.
Consequences
- The windows of a private house were damaged in the city of Bataysk, Rostov Region, Slyusar said.
- In Azov, the windows, roofs and fences of five private houses were damaged, as well as four cars.
- Gas pipelines supplying four households were damaged, and gas supplies were suspended.
- Power lines were broken in two areas.
- In the Neklinovsky District, the roofs and windows of eight apartment buildings were damaged, along with four cars.
- Once emergency response teams have completed their work, administration officials will assess the damage, Slyusar added.
- Affected residents will be provided with the necessary assistance.
- Falling drone debris damaged two private houses in the Krasnodar Region, the regional crisis center said on Max.
- Besides, drone fragments also damage a school gym and a utility building.
- Emergency response personnel are working at the sites.

articles.title: In the Arctic, the ice is moving – and so is the India-Russia agenda
articles.body:
In the Arctic, the ice is moving – and so is the India-Russia agenda
Russian-Asian rapprochement in the Arctic is currently unfolding along two distinct tracks: the first driven by logistics and operations, and the second focused on resources and investment.
Russia’s new Trans-Arctic Transport Corridor (TATC), whose key section is the Northern Sea Route (NSR) running along its Arctic coast, is intended domestically to connect major Russian ports – from St. Petersburg through Murmansk to Vladivostok – and link them to inland cities and towns via land, rail, sea and inland waterway networks.
On the international front, the larger TATC is aimed at linking the consumer markets of Europe and Asia via shorter, safer, more cost-effective, and alternative maritime routes. Similarly, on the resource and investment side, Russia remains keenly interested in developing Arctic and Siberian potential in critical minerals, energy resources, and infrastructure projects that require capital and technology.
The overall Russian approach in the Arctic remains focused on linking its energy and mineral projects in mainland Russia, the Arctic, Siberia, and the Far East to the TATC through multimodal transport connectivity.
The ice is moving
Last month marked a turning point for container transit along the NSR when Sea Legend Shipping launched its regular container service – the China-Europe Arctic Express – consisting of eight voyages, that are scheduled between August and early October 2026. The first shipment, which set sail from China’s Ningbo-Zhoushan port on August 15 via the Northern Sea Route, reached the Port of Teesport in the United Kingdom on September 9 – in just 25 days.
The goal is to deliver high-value and time-sensitive cargo including electronics, lithium batteries, electric vehicle components and photovoltaic modules to multiple European ports (Felixstowe, United Kingdom; Rotterdam, Netherlands; Hamburg, Germany and Gdynia, Poland). Sea Legend Shipping is making use of Russian ice breaking services, and is delivering good to its European clients in far less time than via traditional routes. So far it hasn't faced any kind of criticism or sanctions from Europe.
Similarly, South Korea’s PanStar Group has conducted its own pilot voyage along the NSR to European ports, carrying chemical products. South Korea’s Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries and Panstar reported on Monday that the containership Panstar Arco has completed the first leg of its demonstration voyage, reaching the UK and Rotterdam on September 12 and 13 respectively – successfully covering the route in 21 days. The vessel will then sail to Gdynia, Poland, where it is expected to load additional cargo before beginning the return trip. The vessel is currently scheduled to return to Busan on October 12.
While Seoul hopes this pilot test will position Busan as a leading Arctic shipping hub, currently there are no plans to move regular commercial traffic along the NSR until 2030.
India’s logic of engagement
Against this backdrop, India’s interest in the Russian Arctic is positioned quiet differently. It is primarily about integrating into the resource and investment aspect of the region. The economic viability of sending goods to Europe from India by transiting the entire NSR remains unfavorable for the foreseeable future, but it does offer a secure, strategic alternative maritime route to the traditional shipping lanes, given ongoing geopolitical challenges.
For India, in shipping terms, Russia’s proposed TATC offers greater potential if cargoes are picked up from, or delivered to, Vladivostok and then sent either to other points in Russia via the TATC’s multimodal transport network or to India through the Eastern Maritime Corridor (EMC), also known as the Chennai-Vladivostok Maritime Corridor.
Similarly, some segments or shipping connectivity between India and Eastern ports of Russia along the NSR can become viable options for enhancing point-to-point shipping connectivity between both the countries, if Russia becomes successful in integrating those with its energy and mineral development projects in the region.
New prospects for India-Russia partnership
The India-Russia partnership dates back to the 1971 Indo-Soviet Treaty of Peace, Friendship and Cooperation. Despite contemporary global geopolitical challenges, the underlying character of India-Russia bilateral cooperation has remained intact.
On bilateral trade and economic fronts, it in fact has grown exponentially. Despite western pressures, India’s oil imports for Russia have continued and it has emerged as a significant factor in supporting the Russian economy in challenging times. In 2022, India’s oil imports from Russia surged to $45.9 billion and crossed $79 billion last year.
Russia’s Pivot to the Arctic and its planned large-scale projects in terms of shipping, energy, and mineral development need Indian industrial attention to take these trade figures between the countries to new highs in the future.
Critical minerals
India’s projected demand for rare and critical metals is expected to increase four to tenfold by 2047. India is heavily dependent on imports of lithium, cobalt, nickel, and a number of other rare-earth elements. Furthermore, India’s net cumulative demand for minerals such as copper, graphite, silicon, and nickel is also expected to increase exponentially between 2025 and 2070. Russia’s resource base appears almost ideally complementary to such Indian needs.
The Pavlovskoye lead-zinc deposit in the Novaya Zemlya archipelago; the Tomtor deposits, which constitute one of the largest deposits of niobium and rare-earth elements in Yakutia; and the Angara-Yenisey cluster for the deep processing of non-ferrous and rare metals in Siberia are some of the potential projects that could fulfill India’s future mineral resource demands. Any significant progress in terms of joint investments and partnership could open new prospects for India-Russia economic partnership and reduce Indian reliance on traditional hegemons for these resources.
Energy imports to refined exports
India’s demand for oil is expected to be around 14 million barrels per day by 2050, while its gas consumption is also expected to rise to 103 billion cubic meters annually by 2030. Of this, around 65 billion cubic meters would be supplied by India’s LNG imports.
Crude continues to remain the key commodity in the India-Russia trade basket, and Russia’s vast LNG potential, mainly its Arctic projects, remains largely untapped by India. LNG imports require specialized vessels, and longer distances add to its transportation costs, which ultimately affect its final price. New investments in Russian Arctic LNG projects could offer a strategic diversification and long-term solutions for meeting India’s energy demands in any future geopolitical scenarios in West Asia if both sides are successful in factoring in pricing and transportation aspects.
India, on the other hand, possesses substantial refining capabilities in terms of crude and its related derivatives while Russia is currently facing difficulties in meeting its own demand for refined petroleum products. This is opening another avenue for greater cooperation between the two sides. India has recently scaled up deliveries of refined petroleum products to Russia to meet its domestic needs.
Shipping synergy
In March this year, New Delhi allocated approximately $8.4 billion to bolster shipbuilding, shipbreaking, and maintenance infrastructure under the ‘Make in India’ initiative. Concurrently, Russia’s growing demand for vessel construction and maintenance presents high-value opportunities for Indian shipbuilding and ship-repair enterprises. Synergizing these capabilities directly aligns with both nations’ strategic interests, offering a mutually beneficial avenue for bilateral maritime cooperation. Both Russia and India are placing significant emphasis on developing sustainable maritime operations for the future.
Both countries are pursuing major reforms to build greener ports and cleaner maritime infrastructure, promote alternative fuels, deploy hybrid and electric vessels, and launch green shipping corridors. They are also focusing on advanced technologies and AI to modernize ports and improve logistics and cargo handling – creating strong potential for high-value economic cooperation between India and Russia.
In its efforts to advance its artificial intelligence (AI) capabilities, India has recently allocated about $1.25 billion to the IndiaAI mission. Similarly, India’s ‘Semicon India Programme’ aims to build a self-reliant semiconductor ecosystem in the country. Such initiatives create new avenues for collaboration in high-growth digital sectors between India and Russia.
A way forward
Russia’s Arctic pivot to the East is the sum of several parallel experiments at different stages of maturity. Container shipping along the NSR remains niche, seasonal, and dependent on who ultimately assumes the commercial risks. Russia’s Atomflot tariff depends on a vessel’s gross tonnage, ice class, distance, and the period of escort. Added to this are the higher costs of icebreaker escorts, high insurance premiums for Arctic voyages, and the need for crews trained to operate in Arctic conditions. Despite these challenges, countries like China and South Korea are already sending test consignments to Europe via the NSR and are competing for the benefits of first movers.
Russia’s total foreign trade turnover reached $697.3 billion in 2025, of which 73.4% was accounted for by Asia. India contributed approximately $63.6 billion, and remains Russia’s second-largest trading partner after China, significantly ahead of the UAE, Brazil, Iran, and South Africa.
India has highlighted its plans to send its first cargo via the NSR by 2027, but its broader comprehensive plans for the region are still at the nascent stage of development. Opening up of the Russian Arctic offers immense new untapped business potential for India and Russia, requiring a stronger government push and greater Indian industrial exposure.
This would not only help India and Russia to reach their bilateral trade target of $100 billion by 2030, but to surpass it in the future.

articles.title: CCA Drones to Fly at Large-Scale Air Force Exercise in December
articles.body:
NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.—The Air Force’s new Collaborative Combat Aircraft will take part in their first large-force engagement exercise in December, the head of the drones’ Experimental Operations Unit said Sept. 15.
The Emerald Flag exercise, which will take place at Eglin Air Force Base in Florida, will be CCAs’ “first dip of the toe in an actual force integration,” Lt. Col. Lyndon Bartlett, commander of the unit, said in a panel at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference.
Flying CCAs alongside manned fighters will help build the foundations necessary to one day use them in real-world operations, Bartlett said.
“That will, in [my] mind, be the first time that we will ever do some CCA end-to-end kill chain live,” Bartlett said. “That’s the first time we’ll ever be integrated in a fourth- and fifth-gen combined [offensive counter-air] push. It’ll be small, but those type of building blocks are where, I think, you get the intangibles like trust in the CCA.”
CCAs are semi-autonomous fighter drones that will, in some cases, fly alongside crewed fighters such as the F-35 or the upcoming F-47, and be directed by those fighters’ pilots using a tablet interface. The Air Force wants to have at least 500 CCAs by 2032, and plans a total fleet of 1,000 or more. So far, the service has committed to buying two CCAs—General Atomics’ FQ-42A Vengeance and Anduril Industries’ FQ-44A Fury—but more are planned.
Since the EOU was stood up at Creech Air Force Base, Nev., in June 2025, it has flown and experimented with CCAs to figure out how Airmen can best use them in combat.
During that time, Bartlett said, the EOU has been “pleasantly surprised” to learn how easy CCAs are to maintain and how small of a footprint they require to operate and sustain.
In a series of recent Agile Combat Employment exercises, he said, “we’re at a one-to-one maintainer-to-airplane ratio, which is crazy small.”
That simplicity will make it easier to have “cross-functional” Airmen take on work generating CCA sorties, even if those duties aren’t in their normal career fields, Bartlett said.
“Because [CCAs are] a little bit simpler, because their role is so focused, what we found … any [Air Force Specialty Code] can be trained to generate sorties, to load weapons,” Bartlett said. “We’ve done some of those things already, and we’re going to do a lot more experimentation over the next couple of years.”
Col. Timothy Helfrich, the portfolio acquisition executive for fighters and advanced aircraft, also said at the panel that the EOU is flying CCA aircraft “multiple times a week.”
Jason Levin, Anduril’s senior vice president of engineering, said the company delivered its FQ-44 Fury drone to the EOU in August. And in recent months, the process for operating Fury has been streamlined to the point where “it’s down to a single operator flying a Fury from a laptop,” Levin said.
“They were doing disaggregated operations, flying from multiple locations,” Levin said. “They were doing hot reloads on Fury, so getting it down from hours down to single-digit minutes to turn the jet. They’re really pushing the envelope, flying with mission autonomy. It was the first time Air Force operators were flying with mission autonomy on Fury multiple times a day, in the airspace with crewed fifth-gen fighters, other CCAs, starting to build that trust.”
David Alexander, president of General Atomics Aeronautical Systems, said that once a foundation has been built for Airmen to autonomously use CCAs and they are comfortable, the program can focus more on Agile Combat Employment operations, where aircraft are flown from smaller, potentially austere and isolated bases, without the same level of support a larger base might have.
At that point, Alexander said, “it’s not an experiment anymore, it’s an everyday event.”
Levin said those ACE exercises are vital, because that’s where operators find the shortcomings of CCA’s software. And if those problems aren’t rapidly fixed, he said, Airmen in the field won’t become comfortable using CCAs.
“When we go out to those ACE exercises and they don’t like something, if we don’t fix it by the next ACE, they’re not going to trust the system,” Levin said. “They’re not going to trust that it does what it needs to do.”
Anduril’s Fury in July fired its first weapon—an AIM-120 Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missile—and General Atomics’ Vengeance will conduct its first live fire test later this year.
The biggest challenge that remains for the CCA concept, Bartlett said, is seeing whether their mission autonomy programming will deliver everything the Air Force needs and contractors have promised.
“Mission autonomy is going to be the secret sauce that lets these things become decisive or not, and we’ll know that over the next couple years, as that develops,” Bartlett said.
The Air Force has decades of established doctrine governing how it employs piloted fighters and other aircraft, Bartlett said, but the book for using CCAs is still being written. And as the Air Force figures out how it wants to use them, it needs to make sure this doctrine is tailor-made for CCAs and doesn’t just rehash existing guidelines.
“Working the nuances of CCA and fielding policies that are not just copy-pastes from old regulations, that are actually something that enables us to move quickly with these things … is, I think, our big challenge right now,” Bartlett said.
But it’s not just the Air Force that needs to adjust for a world with CCAs in it, Bartlett said. The entire nation will also have to get used to the concept of uncrewed aircraft regularly flying in U.S. airspace, he said. That will have policy implications, he said, and the Federal Aviation Administration will have to figure out how to integrate pilotless aircraft into the airspace it manages.
“Our system is not set up for that,” Bartlett said. The U.S. government has “to set policies that make sure the enterprise, and the country, is ready to receive these, and internalize an autonomous fighter that does not have a pilot, that is running on a mission autonomy agent, that doesn’t listen to” air traffic control.

GENEVA, September 18. /TASS/. The further development of the AUKUS security partnership between Australia, the UK and the US could trigger a new arms race and undermine stability in the Asia-Pacific, Russian Foreign Ministry Ambassador-at-Large Andrey Belousov said.

articles.title: Miliband’s Israel speech was a watershed. Now he must deliver
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Miliband’s Israel speech was a watershed. Now he must deliver
Time will tell whether the Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband’s significant speech to Parliament last Tuesday will be viewed as a watershed moment in UK-Israel relations or a flash in the pan. As Miliband knows, time is not on the side of Palestinians as Israel continues to commit genocide, expand settlements, steal more land and violently displace Palestinian communities.
Miliband has certainly gone further than his predecessors, and this is to be welcomed – but it’s a low bar after decades of UK policy falling short of its own legal obligations. Recognising the unlawfulness of Israel’s illegal occupation is a good starting point - one Amnesty International has been pushing the UK toward and was confirmed in the International Court of Justice’s (ICJ) July 2024 Advisory Opinion. The question is whether this recognition leads to a change in policy and practice.
Miliband’s statement indicated a genuine commitment to the “comprehensive reset” he promised of UK policy on Israel. But his diagnosis of the problems was at times selective. For instance, he rightly called out the ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in parts of the West Bank - but pinning it on “settler terrorists”, while stating that the Israeli government has merely “turned a blind eye”, is a distortion he and his officials must surely be aware of.
These rampaging settlers are armed by the state, backed by Israeli forces and incited by senior government ministers. They are not rogue actors. They are proxies for state policy – and Israel bears full responsibility for their actions.
The commitment to “introduce a new comprehensive sanctions regime” on illegal settlements is one Amnesty has pressed for years - it is a welcome departure from previous policy, and one that follows in the footsteps of other states. But a sanctions regime only works if it makes Israel’s settlements unviable. That means covering all forms of trade and investment, including the provision of services such as insurance, banking, IT, digital tourism, security, construction, engineering, real estate and consultancy - not just goods.
It was surprising and disappointing that Miliband announced that it would be six to nine months before the legislation is in place. When Russia invaded Ukraine, the UK announced its first sanctions within hours – and had trade restrictions on goods from Russian-occupied eastern Ukraine within five weeks, by 30 March 2022. Existing legislation is already in place in the form of the Sanctions and Anti-Money Laundering Act 2018, which has been used to impose sanctions on 25 states.
The announcement that the UK will “refuse all licence applications for arms and other exports that materially contribute to the occupation” is also positive and overdue. However, it will be critical to see how the UK assesses whether an item contributes to the occupation.
More problematically, Miliband himself confirmed that this would not apply to F-35 parts - despite evidence of the F-35’s extensive use in Israel’s genocide in occupied Gaza. This is a significant gap in an otherwise welcome commitment.
Amnesty has long argued that ending transfers of F-35 parts to the Global Supply Pool - the international pipeline that supplies parts to every F-35 built, including those operated by Israel - is both necessary to fulfil international legal obligations and possible without jeopardising the wider F-35 programme. BAE Systems, the UK’s largest arms company, says it is responsible for 15% of every F-35 that rolls off the production line. Every F-35 currently in Israel's fleet – used to horrific effect in Gaza - contains significant UK-supplied parts and components.
Breaking Israel's impunity requires accountability mechanisms the UK has, at times, tried to block. In May 2021, the then UK government voted against a UN Human Rights Council resolution establishing an Independent International Commission of Inquiry into violations of international law in the Occupied Palestinian Territory.
Certainly, it is a positive step that Miliband has now referenced the Commission's findings - which include stating clearly that Israel has committed genocide in Gaza. This suggests a more amenable approach to such mechanisms in future and would be a welcome reversal - particularly since the Foreign Secretary maintained his predecessor's position of not taking a position on whether Israel is committing genocide.
Whatever the UK does or doesn't say, the legal obligation to act to prevent and punish genocide is already triggered. The UN Commission of Inquiry has found that states must, at minimum, recognise the serious risk of genocide being committed against Palestinians. The government should say so plainly - not wait for a final ICJ ruling, which could take years yet to come.
One of the most glaring omissions in Miliband’s speech was any reference to the systematic discrimination against Palestinians - which the ICJ has found breaches the prohibition on racial segregation and apartheid. Given the racism at the heart of Israel’s cruel and brutal treatment of Palestinians, any approach to holding Israel accountable is unlikely to work unless this is addressed.
Miliband’s speech may yet break the logjam of the UK’s acquiescence in Israel’s crimes under international law and, in doing so, help bring an end to the suffering and subjugation of Palestinians. Miliband appears to recognise what’s at stake. But he must implement his promises of comprehensive action quickly and robustly, and others must follow.
For Palestinians subject to Israel’s genocide, ethnic cleansing and apartheid, action can’t come soon enough.
Peter Frankental is Amnesty International UK’s Economic Affairs Director.

articles.title: Lindsey Graham sanctions bill ‘a grand disservice’ to US – Moscow (VIDEO)
articles.body:
Lindsey Graham sanctions bill ‘a grand disservice’ to US – Moscow (VIDEO)
The “Russophobic” new sanctions bill empowering US President Donald Trump to impose steep tariffs on buyers of Russian energy will lead to ever-higher prices at the pumps for Americans, the Russian Embassy in Washington has warned.
The legislation was championed by the late Senator Lindsey Graham, a Russia hawk and staunch Ukraine supporter who pushed for “crushing sanctions” on Moscow before his unexpected death this summer. Named ‘The Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026’ in his honor, the bill allows the president to impose tariffs of up to 100% on goods from major buyers of Russian oil and gas, potentially including China and India, and additional sanctions on Russia and Iran. It cleared the House on Wednesday, removing the final congressional hurdle before reaching Trump, who has said he plans to sign it.
The Russian Embassy in Washington on Friday warned the legislation will likely backfire on American consumers, particularly as Middle Eastern energy supplies are already disrupted by the US war on Iran.
“Russophobic instinct underlying the late Senator Graham’s bill… makes a grand disservice to the current Administration’s efforts to Make America Great Again,” the embassy wrote on X. “Destabilizing energy markets by blocking Russian oil and gas trade as Mideast supply is dramatically cut is an invitation to ever-higher prices at the pump close to midterm November elections.”
The embassy also warned that targeting major buyers of Russian energy could deepen tensions between Washington on one side and Moscow and Beijing on the other. It argued that the legislation runs counter to the Trump administration’s diplomatic efforts with Moscow and that simultaneously confronting Russia and China would create a geopolitical “lose-lose” situation for Washington.
Russophobic instinct underlying the late Senator Graham’s bill approved by the House on September 16th (and earlier by the Senate) makes a grand disservice to the current Administration’s efforts to Make America Great Again.
Destabilizing energy markets by blocking Russian oil… pic.twitter.com/TQR4fFxD5C
US gasoline prices are already under pressure from the Middle East energy crisis. US gasoline averages $4.43-$4.44 a gallon, over $1.10 more than a year ago, while diesel has hit a record $6.40 nationwide, jumping 77 cents in the first half of September alone.
Disruptions to tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical route for Gulf oil exports, have constrained supplies, while instability around the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb Strait due to Iran-allied Yemeni Houthi advances has threatened another major shipping route. Crude prices have climbed above $100 a barrel, raising concerns about further increases at the pump if disruptions persist.
China and India, the largest buyers of Russian energy, have opposed the bill and defended their purchases. Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said on Thursday that Beijing rejects Washington’s “long-arm jurisdiction” as lacking a basis in international law. India has warned that tariffs over Russian oil purchases could affect US-India ties and vowed to “take all necessary measures to protect its trade and economic interests.”
Moscow has long denounced Western energy sanctions as illegal and self-defeating, arguing that they redirect Russian exports while forcing Western countries toward more expensive supplies. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov warned this week that additional US sanctions would make reaching a settlement of the Ukraine conflict more difficult.

articles.title: North Korea warns of ‘more offensive’ response to US-led military drills
articles.body:
Faisal Mahmud
18 September 2026•Update: 18 September 2026
North Korea’s Kim Yo Jong on Friday warned of a stronger response to US-led multinational military exercises in the Asia-Pacific, saying Pyongyang would continue strengthening its nuclear deterrence.
Kim, the sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and a senior ruling Workers’ Party official, accused Washington of being the “main source” of worsening tensions on the Korean Peninsula and across the region, according to a statement carried by the state-run Korean Central News Agency (KCNA).
She singled out Pacific Vanguard 2026, a multinational naval exercise near Guam involving the US, South Korea, Japan, and other countries.
Kim called the exercise a threatening “war game” and accused Washington of seeking to expand its military influence through alliances in the Asia-Pacific.
She also criticized growing US-Japan-South Korea military cooperation, claiming North Korea was its primary target.
“The present situation ... stresses the need to break records in our responsive action, proportional or more offensive in its nature,” Kim said.
She added there would be “never ever change” in North Korea’s course of strengthening its nuclear deterrence and warned Pyongyang could “mobilize all means available” if its sovereignty or security were seriously threatened.
The warning came as South Korean President Lee Jae Myung said Friday that Seoul should make every effort to facilitate renewed dialogue between North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and US President Donald Trump, according to Seoul-based Yonhap News Agency.
“The possibility cannot be ruled out,” Lee told a televised news conference, adding Seoul should do its “utmost” to help make such talks happen. Lee said renewed North Korea-US dialogue could become an important stepping stone toward restarting inter-Korean talks and promoting peace and stability on the Korean Peninsula.

articles.title: Taiwan official warns Xi Jinping could move toward lifelong rule
articles.body:
TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Deputy Mainland Affairs Council Minister Shen Yu-chung (沈有忠) said Friday that Chinese leader Xi Jinping (習近平) could move toward lifelong rule as he further consolidates power.
Shen said Xi has steadily dismantled the CCP's collective leadership system since taking power more than a decade ago, consolidating what Shen described as “one-man rule,” per SET News. He said Xi's centralization of authority and emphasis on comprehensive national security over economic and social development continued to shape China's governance.
He said Beijing had strengthened ideological control through laws including the national security law and the ethnic unity law, while introducing “Xi Jinping Thought on Party Building” this year. He said authorities were also using increasingly sophisticated grid-based governance and AI surveillance to control society.
China's growing military spending could encourage the PLA to take more aggressive actions, Shen said, noting that the country's defense budget increased by 7% this year, according to SET News. He said military purges had not reduced the PLA's gray-zone activities around Taiwan, where Chinese navy vessels, coast guard ships, and research vessels continue to conduct operations in nearby waters.
Shen also warned that Beijing's prioritization of national security had shifted policy resources toward state-owned capital and strategic industries, distorting market allocation. He said China's state-led technology strategy had fueled efforts to recruit Taiwanese talent remotely and conduct commercial espionage, threatening the nation’s high-tech competitiveness and the security of global supply chains.

articles.title: South Korea’s president rejects US request for Iran war support
articles.body:
South Korea’s president rejects US request for Iran war support
President Lee Jae Myung has drawn a firm line against sending troops or assets to the Middle East, defying pressure from Washington
The stance comes amid mounting public opposition to any military deployment and growing pressure from Washington for Seoul to contribute to efforts to secure freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz.
Lee’s government faces the difficult task of balancing its security alliance with the United States against the risks of becoming entangled in a distant conflict that could expose South Korean forces, citizens and commercial interests to Iranian retaliation.
“There will be no dispatch of troops or military assets that would lead to involvement in a conflict. There will be no engagement or involvement in war. I can say that clearly,” Lee said during a televised press conference on Friday. “We’ve been sticking to this principle, and this principle won’t change.”

articles.title: Thousands are starving in occupied Oleshky. People have no food, no way out, and Russian forces bomb incoming aid
articles.body:
Oleshky, a Ukrainian city under Russian occupation in Kherson Oblast, is facing a severe humanitarian crisis, with more than 6,000 people, including around 200 children, potentially trapped there, according to Ukrainian Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets.
Civilians are going without food, drinking water, medicine, and other basic necessities while facing daily shelling and drone attacks, Lubinets said.
The crisis has become so desperate that some residents are trying to escape on their own without waiting for an organized evacuation, crossing mined fields because they see no other way out. They risk being killed by mines or Russian drones, but are attempting to leave because staying in Oleshky has become even more dangerous.
“People need to be saved,” Lubinets said, describing the city as a “death trap.”
Thousands remain trapped
Lubinets said his office has received 176 appeals concerning the humanitarian situation in the temporarily occupied territories of Kherson Oblast and has verified 358 people who urgently need assistance to safely leave the area.
He stressed that these are only people his office has managed to identify. Based on the population of Oleshky and the surrounding area, more than 6,000 people may still remain there, including around 200 children, he said.
The civilians remaining in the city are effectively in a “gray zone,” according to Lubinets. They face daily shelling and drone attacks while lacking food, drinking water, medicine, and other essential assistance.
“The stories make your blood run cold. And so there is only one task — to get our people out of this deadly danger,” Lubinets said.
“There is real hunger there”
Other reporting indicates that the shortages have persisted for months. According to Kherson Regional Military Administration head Oleksandr Prokudin, food deliveries to Oleshky have almost completely stopped, while Russian forces prevent residents from evacuating.
Natalia Soboleva, an Odesa volunteer who tracks the situation in Oleshky, told Espreso that residents are gathering grass and searching through destroyed basements for food.
“There is hunger there, real hunger,” she said.
The blockade has also affected humanitarian efforts. Soboleva said Russian forces attacked humanitarian vehicles attempting to bring food and water into the city. During the latest reported attempt on 1 September, Russian troops shelled four volunteer vehicles.
The crisis in Oleshky has been independently documented by international organizations and media. The UN, Human Rights Watch and the OSCE have all reported severe shortages of food and medical care, dangerous conditions for civilians, and restrictions on humanitarian aid and evacuation.
International monitors confirm Russia’s blockade of occupied Oleshky, where the living starve and the dead go unburied
Russia has not confirmed evacuation, so civilians risk mines to escape
The ombudsman said some people are now trying to leave independently. They are crossing mined areas despite the risk of being killed by a mine or targeted by a drone because they do not see another way to escape.
This desperation has also been documented by Human Rights Watch, which said there is no organized evacuation route from Oleshky and that people attempting to leave face Russian military checkpoints and a dangerous journey through occupied territory.
Lubinets said Ukraine has been pressing for an organized humanitarian evacuation.
Ukraine and Russia had previously reached agreements and established clear procedures for such a mission, he said. Lubinets also secured the International Committee of the Red Cross’ readiness to participate within its mandate.
Ukraine prepared a list of people for evacuation and coordinated with its Security and Defense Forces to establish a ceasefire during the humanitarian mission.
But Russia has not confirmed its readiness to carry out the evacuation, according to Lubinets.
Mined in, starved out, hunted from above—life in the towns Russia demands at the peace table
Months ago, he said, he informed international organizations, including the United Nations and the ICRC headquarters in Geneva, about the critical situation and called for assistance to prevent mass deaths.
Lubinets said his office continues to collect and verify information and coordinate with the ICRC, international organizations and Ukrainian authorities. It is also continuing to press Russia for an urgent evacuation of civilians remaining in Oleshky.
The situation is difficult to independently verify because Oleshky is under Russian occupation and access to the city is severely restricted. But reports of the humanitarian crisis have been corroborated by the UN, Human Rights Watch, the OSCE and other international organizations, as well as Ukrainian and international media.

articles.title: US plans to approve transfer of 10 Patriot interceptor missiles to Ukraine from Germany
articles.body:
US plans to approve transfer of 10 Patriot interceptor missiles to Ukraine from Germany
The US government is prepared to authorise the transfer of 10 interceptor missiles for Patriot air defence systems to Ukraine, initiated by the German government.
Source: a US State Department arms sales notification, published in the Congressional Record, the official journal of the Congress
Details: Ukraine is to receive 10 MIM-104E GEM-T missiles with an initial value of US$29.6 million. The munitions belong to Germany; however, under the terms of such agreements, a purchasing country cannot transfer American weaponry to a third party without US consent.
Quote: "This transfer is consistent with US security assistance objectives. The United States government is prepared to authorise this transfer, having taken into account political, military, economic, human rights, and arms control considerations."
Details: According to the State Department, Ukraine seeks to obtain the interceptor missiles to "bolster its air defence capability against ongoing Russian attacks".
Background:
- In early September, German Federal Minister of Defence Boris Pistorius announced that PAC-2 missiles would be supplied to Ukraine from Bundeswehr (Germany's Armed Forces) stockpiles.
- Earlier, UP reported that Ukraine is signing contracts for the supply of around 1,000 missiles for Patriot air defence systems, according to Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara. Future missile deliveries will take time, making it necessary for Ukraine to receive missiles from its partners' existing stockpiles before winter.

articles.title: Ukrainian orders scaling up missile production at Britain's Thales, restoring country's industrial capabilities – Zaluzhny
articles.body:
Valeriy Zaluzhny, Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of Ukraine to the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland and former Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine (2021–2024), visited the defense technology company Thales UK near Belfast—which fulfills Ukrainian defense orders—and noted that this cooperation serves the UK's interests.
"For the UK and British companies, this is not just about helping Ukraine; it is also an investment in their own national defense. Ukraine offers a unique asset: real combat experience combined with one of the world's most dynamic defense technology sectors. The closer the cooperation between our governments and businesses, the better we can combine Ukraine's practical experience with the creation of new technologies and capabilities for both countries. Successful projects with companies like Thales UK clearly illustrate the potential of the strategic agreement between Ukraine and the UK," Zaluzhny wrote on Facebook on Friday following the visit.
According to him, the plant manufactures Starstreak and LMM/Martlet air defense missile systems; Ukrainian forces used these to shoot down Russian helicopters early in the full-scale invasion, and they are now employed for short-range air defense against Shahed drones and other targets. The Thales UK plant in Belfast also assembles NLAW anti-tank systems.
"Ukraine and Thales UK have already established an industrial partnership. These are long-term investments, not a one-off transfer of weaponry. This model also serves the UK's interests: Ukrainian orders are already helping to expand Thales UK’s missile production in Belfast and rebuild British industrial capacity for air defense," Zaluzhny concluded.

articles.title: Ukrainian forces strike control station for Russian Orion drones in Crimea
articles.body:
Ukrainian forces strike control station for Russian Orion drones in Crimea
Units of Ukraine's defence forces struck a number of Russian military facilities on 17 September and on the night of 17-18 September.
Source: General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine
Quote: "In the area of the settlement of Novofedorivka at Saky airfield in Crimea, a ground control station for the enemy's Orion unmanned aerial vehicles was struck."
Details: The General Staff said that the Orion is a medium-altitude long-endurance drone capable of remaining airborne for up to 24 hours, conducting optical-electronic reconnaissance and target designation at altitudes of up to 7.5 km and carrying up to 200-250 kg of guided aviation weaponry.
The General Staff reported that striking the ground control station significantly limits Russian forces' ability to use these systems in the relevant operational sector.
Quote: "In the area of Donetsk, a storage, preparation and launch site for attack drones was struck."
More details: In addition, according to the General Staff, the destruction of a Russian ammunition depot in the area of Dovzhansk, Luhansk Oblast, and a stores and equipment depot belonging to Russian forces in the area of Kypuche has been confirmed.
Background:
- Ukraine's defence forces struck a number of Russian military assets, including air defence equipment, on 16 September and on the night of 16-17 September.
- The General Staff previously reported a strike on a drone launch site near Donetsk.

articles.title: NYT: Trump considers "appeasing" Russia with business deals before hostilities end
articles.body:
NYT: Trump considers "appeasing" Russia with business deals before hostilities end
The White House is reportedly considering signing certain business deals with Russia even before Moscow ends its war against Ukraine, as a way of demonstrating its good intentions.
Source: The New York Times, citing anonymous sources
Details: According to two people familiar with the details of negotiations involving Trump's special envoys, the administration is already considering signing certain economic agreements with Russia without making it a precondition that hostilities in the war against Ukraine cease.
One of the sources, a US official, said deals before the end of the war were considered possible because they would "show that the United States is serious about a reset relationship with Russia".
Last year, Trump said economic cooperation with Russia could only resume once the Russia-Ukraine war had ended. In particular, ahead of his meeting with the Russian leader in Alaska, he said Russia wanted economic cooperation but that there would be none of that "until we get the war settled".
Trump's negotiators are now reportedly looking for new ways to encourage Moscow to end the war, as it has become clear that Ukraine is not prepared to surrender the unoccupied part of Donetsk Oblast without a fight.
The US official said the administration wanted to create more incentives for Russia's elite to push the country's leadership towards peace. The thinking is that economic deals with the US that appeal to Russia could "help convince anti-American hawks around Mr Putin that Mr Trump really does want to create a new relationship with Russia".
It is not yet known what specific agreements are under consideration. After special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner travelled to Moscow, Kremlin foreign policy adviser Yuri Ushakov said their discussions had touched on "economic issues and potential major mutually beneficial Russian-American projects".
Background:
- Russia has previously tried to entice Trump with the potential benefits of economic cooperation, discussing joint projects involving rare-earth mineral and aluminium extraction, projects in the Arctic and the involvement of US companies in selling Russian natural gas to Europe.
- Following Trump's recent proposal for an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine, the Kremlin said it would also like Ukrainian strikes on its tankers in the Black Sea to stop and Western sanctions on Russian energy resources to be lifted.
